New details are being released following the arrest of a 62-year-old Martin County woman who had 36 dogs living in severely unsanitary conditions inside her home, the Martin County Sheriff's Office (MCSO) said.WATCH BELOW: Dogs rescued after WPTV investigation into suspected animal hoardingPaige O'Donnell was taken into custody on Monday, following a lengthy investigation into animal welfare concerns at her residence. When deputies executed a search warrant, they discovered dogs covered in feces and urine living in a home with no functioning air conditioning and floors covered in waste and garbage, a probable cause affidavit said.The investigation began after a neighbor contacted WPTV with concerns about the conditions at O'Donnell's residence and reports that she was housing a large number of animals. Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services said they reviewed call history at the address and identified approximately 20 related incidents spanning from 2020 through 2026, the affidavit said.Animal Control Officer Tabitha Queen documented a pattern of deteriorating conditions at the residence over several years, according to a probable cause affidavit released by MCSO. On July 22, the officer responded to a complaint that more than 20 dogs were inside the home without air conditioning and had not been allowed outside since 2022."Upon arriving, the officer detected a strong odor consistent with decomposition from the roadway," according to the arrest report. "She could hear a large number of dogs, including what sounded like puppies, barking from inside the residence."When deputies arrived on Monday to execute the search warrant, O'Donnell was taking a bath, deputies said. When asked about the conditions of the home and dogs, she said only that she was in the process of cleaning.Deputies said they observed the residence to be in an unlivable and unsanitary condition, with floors throughout the home covered in feces, urine and garbage. The air-conditioning system was inoperable, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office report.Multiple dogs were found inside the residence covered in feces and urine with severely matted fur, investigators said. Deputies noted the condition of the dogs and surrounding environment was such that the animals were difficult to distinguish from the heavily soiled areas of the residence.Portions of the walls appeared to have been chewed or damaged by the dogs. The only water source observed was an automatic water container inside the master bathroom. No clean food dishes were found anywhere in the residence, investigators said.Animal hoarding cases like this highlight ongoing challenges in animal welfare enforcement and the need for community vigilance in reporting suspected neglect. The case also demonstrates how repeated interventions over several years can escalate when underlying issues aren't addressed.During an August 3 meeting at Jock Leighton Park in Palm City, O'Donnell told the Animal Control Officer she owned only four dogs: Jeep, Jagger, Naughty and True. She presented one dog, "Jeep," a black-and-white Border Collie whose white fur was heavily stained with what appeared to be urine and feces.However, records from Boulevard Animal Hospital painted a different picture, the affidavit said. A hospital employee who had worked there since 2015 knew O'Donnell as a dog breeder who would bring in numerous puppies over the years in filthy conditions. The clinic's computer system identified approximately 38 adult dogs associated with O'Donnell, some documented as deceased.The employee said there were so many puppies brought in with O'Donnell that it was impossible to get an accurate count, according to the affidavit. The last recorded visit was June 25, 2022, when two dogs, Jeep and Naughty, were vaccinated for rabies.Neighbors provided investigators with video recordings capturing evidence of the conditions. One neighbor recorded video of O'Donnell's garage area on August 6, days before the arrest, showing garbage and debris piled nearly to the ceiling of her garage and a large number of dogs barking from within the residence, the affidavit said.Another neighbor told investigators he had not observed any dogs outside the residence or seen garbage placed out for collection since at least 2022, according to the affidavit. He said he continued to notice a strong odor from the residence and had not heard the air-conditioning system operating since approximately 2022.One of the most significant prior incidents occurred April 4, 2020, when Animal Services responded after O'Donnell was placed under the Marchman Act. Deputies said they documented severely unsanitary conditions with approximately 25 dogs on the property that did not have adequate food or water. One dog required humane euthanization due to its deteriorated health, the affidavit said.Following that incident, Animal Services documented that O'Donnell made improvements, rehomed multiple dogs and stated she intended to keep only five dogs going forward, the affidavit said.A similar pattern emerged in June 2022, when Animal Control responded to complaints of 10 to 20 dogs being kept in the backyard covered in feces and flies, the affidavit said. A follow-up inspection found the residence had been cleaned, and O'Donnell voluntarily surrendered three dogs to Farm Dog Rescue.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: 'She really has legally walled us off from investigating,' Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek tells Chief Investigative Reporter Jamie OstroffInvestigators said they identified several inconsistencies in the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning across multiple Animal Control contacts between 2022 and 2023, with numbers ranging from five to 10 dogs.Deputies said they concluded that the conditions observed during the search warrant execution indicated the dogs had been maintained in conditions that failed to provide a sanitary and appropriate living environment and subjected them to unnecessary suffering.A judge set O’Donnell’s total bond at $275,000 and ordered that she may not own or possess either temporary or permanent any animals as conditions of her bond, the Martin County Sheriff's Office said Tuesday.O’Donnell is facing 72 total charges — 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air, the sheriff's office said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The site consists of three parcels located just west of Kanner Highway and south of Southwest 96th Street.Up to 1,200 homes were initially planned on the property.County staff recommended the enclave designation be denied."We reviewed the property tax records for the three parcels in the application, and we found that not all of the property was classified for agricultural purposes from the property appraiser's office," Knobbe said.The Waterside proposal was expected to be discussed at a Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, but the applicant asked for the item to be pulled from the agenda.The property owners declined to comment.How much pushback local governments can mount against the law remains unclear. For the fourth straight year, the Indian River County School District has been graded an A school district. All but one school in the district received an A rating. The only school to receive a B was Dodgertown Elementary School. District Superintendent Dr. David Moore says no matter which school parents choose for their children in Indian River County, they can expect a quality education. Moore says the district is maintaining its A grade by investing in teachers and staff who have helped improve the district over the past six years. He also says that by identifying pain points, school leaders can allocate resources and funding to address those issues and prevent the district from falling in the ratings. Moore says those efforts are also reflected in the number of parents choosing to keep their children in the public school system. "Because of our willingness for the last 6 years to transform the experience, for the second straight year, we are going to exceed the state’s projected enrollment for our community," Moore told CBS12 News. The School District of Indian River County is also ranked in nine out of 12 accountability components. The district says that demonstrates exceptional performance in educating students from the time they begin their education through graduation day.

Proposed change would require no warnings be issued when officers consider the noise ‘so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace.’ FORT PIERCE – For people complaining about neighborhood noise that impedes their sleep, or drivers who feel vibration caused by loud music from other vehicles, Fort Pierce city officials are considering tougher enforcement. According to city statistics, law enforcement responded to nearly 2,000 noise complaint calls in the city between April 1, 2025 and April 30, 2026. And officials say about one in three of those complaints came from the same 14 city locations. Half of all calls currently come in Sundays, between 10 p.m. Now city leaders have proposed ordinance amendments that would expand police enforcement authority, beef up penalties that could include fines of up to $250-$500 per day of violation and allow the city to place unpaid fines as liens against the properties where violations take place. In addition, officials are recommending that parents/guardians be made responsible for the penalties levied against juvenile offenders. District 1 Commissioner Arnold Gaines suggested chronic noise offenders are now using loopholes in the current ordinances that should be closed, giving “more teeth to enforcement.” For example, Gaines said those violators will continue to offend until they get the three warnings from police, then turn down their music. Gaines said violators also may make loud noise in one location where police respond, then move down the street or to another parking lot to continue the obnoxious noise. Police currently issue written “warnings” if violations occur within the same 24 hours at the same location. Proposed change would require no warnings be issued when officers consider the noise “so loud, excessive or disruptive that it constitutes a clear and substantial disturbance or breach of the peace.” In instances not considered severe, the city is proposing penalties when the same individuals are cited during a 48- or 72-hour period at any location in the city. They would get five minutes to comply after the first warning and a citation to appear would be issued if the violation continued another five minutes or if it was a third violation. An arrest would be made for a fourth offense or if another five minutes passed without correcting the current violation. Chronic violations would be defined as three or more verified noise complaints at the same location within 30 days, or six or more within 90 days. If an offender fails to follow a compliance plan or new complaints continue, the incidents could be treated as a public nuisance that’s referred to the city’s Nuisance Abatement Road where daily fines of up to $250-$500 can be ordered. If the fines are not paid, a lien may be placed on the property where the incident occurs and the city can foreclose to collect the lien after three months, affecting the violator and the property owner. Quieter hours would be observed from 10 or 11 p.m. on specified days or seven days a week, depending upon the commission’s final action. Rather than spending an estimated $80,000 to have a sound study conducted to scientifically define “loud” noise, city staff is recommending officers use what a “reasonable person” would consider excessive or audible from a vehicle to an officer at least 25 feet away. “That’s all some of the residents want – more teeth in enforcement,” Gaines said, supporting the recommendations. “If you put citations in their hands, the noise will stop.” An implementation date has not been determined yet. City Clerk Linda Cox said recommended ordinance changes require two public hearings once final ordinance language is drafted. Your comment has been submitted. Palm Beach County is locked in fierce competition with Texas, Tennessee, Virginia and the Carolinas for high-paying corporate jobs and headquarters, according to the county's top economic development executive who warns that the region's economic future depends on how quickly local governments adapt to changing business demands."There's very stiff competition for economic development projects throughout the United States. So, when these companies come in, we have one shot to pitch the Palm Beaches to make it to the shortlist," said Kelly Smallridge, president and CEO of the Business Development Board of Palm Beach County. "This is a competition, and as soon as they walk out our door, internal in the state of Florida, Miami, Jacksonville, Tampa are our biggest."WPTV's Joel Lopez spoke with Smallridge to examine what drives corporate relocation decisions in today's competitive market. The answer, she said, isn't what many residents expect."People think that companies come here for the beaches and the lifestyle. But the first question they ask is draw a 5-mile radius around the building that I would ideally would like to locate to and tell me the skill sets of the residents in that area," Smallridge said. It is the number one factor in whether or not they're going to be competitive."The Business Development Board serves as Palm Beach County's public-private economic development agency, helping recruit companies, retain existing employers and coordinate with municipalities across all 39 cities in the county.Smallridge, a Palm Beach County native who grew up in Palm Springs, said the organization was created more than 40 years ago, because residents wanted to diversify an economy once dominated by tourism, agriculture and construction."The residents came forward and said, 'It's too cyclical, very seasonal in nature. It's very low-paying,'" she said. "We want an entity that goes after high-quality, higher-paying jobs."Today, the county's economy is driven increasingly by sectors like life sciences, aviation and aerospace, technology, manufacturing and financial services. The transformation has been dramatic: the average age in Palm Beach County has dropped from 75 to 48-49, with an average resident wage of $78,000.Currently, 19,077 financial services companies in Palm Beach County create 119,483 jobs with an average salary of $126,340, according to Business Development Board data."We are the creators of the Wall Street South Initiative and tangential to that, we've created this tech and innovation-based initiative," Smallridge said. "AI, cybersecurity, quantum computing is coming to the Palm Beaches."The county's aerospace industry includes roughly 1,700 companies, serving as another major driver of growth. Local universities including Florida Atlantic University, Kaiser University, Palm Beach Atlantic University and Palm Beach State College are working to create workforce pipelines for these emerging sectors.One factor repeatedly determines whether Palm Beach County lands corporate deals: available commercial real estate."Buildings, office buildings, industrial buildings are usually at the top of the list," Smallridge said.That reality has helped cities like Boca Raton and West Palm Beach secure some of the county's biggest corporate relocations. Boca Raton currently has roughly 13 million square feet of office space, while downtown West Palm Beach has another 1.7 million square feet of Class A office space under development.Current office space rankings show Boca Raton leading with 13.1 million square feet, followed by West Palm Beach with 9.5 million square feet and Palm Beach Gardens with 4.1 million square feet.For industrial space, West Palm Beach leads with 2.8 million square feet, followed by Boca Raton with 850,000 square feet and Palm Beach Gardens with 556,000 square feet.Companies routinely ask for school ratings within a five-mile radius of proposed office sites, because employees want strong public school options for their children, according to Smallridge.She acknowledged that school quality varies widely across Palm Beach County and influences where families choose to live.Housing affordability is also becoming increasingly important, especially as companies recruit workers from outside South Florida. While executives may afford luxury communities, employers still need workforce housing options for their staff."What are the affordable housing options for our employees?" has become a routine question during corporate recruitment meetings, Smallridge said.Smallridge stressed that speed matters more than ever in economic development competition."I would suggest not to wait for the company to come to you," she said. "You need the process in order."That includes having shovel-ready sites, clear zoning rules and expedited permitting systems already in place before companies begin evaluating locations."Expedited is very, very critical to winning the deal," she said.The top questions executives ask when considering Palm Beach County relocation include site availability, permit speed, local talent for recruitment, school ratings and housing availability and affordability.Despite competition between cities, Smallridge emphasized that economic development benefits spill across municipal boundaries regardless of where companies physically locate."I never see a company locate to an area, hire everybody from that particular city, do all their business with small businesses in that city, send their kids to all the schools in that city," she said. There's a lot of movement."She cited Oxygen Development, a large cosmetics manufacturer in central Palm Beach County, as an example of a company drawing 800 employees from multiple nearby communities, with the majority coming from Lake Worth Beach.At the center of Smallridge's message was a broader warning: Palm Beach County can no longer rely solely on its beaches, weather and lifestyle to stay competitive."Just because we've had a great 5 to 10 years and we are living in somewhat of a bubble right now does not mean that we will be there in 10 years if we become complacent and sit where we are," Smallridge said. "We have to continue to maintain the very quality of life, the character and the charm that attracted everyone here, along with the balance of growth, good schools, good infrastructure. That all makes a difference to landing the deal and beating the other states."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Residents in The Isles community are mounting opposition against a homeowners association plan that could eliminate more than 300 oak trees in Palm Beach Gardens over the next several years, with some neighbors now demanding citywide changes to tree removal approval processes.The HOA-approved infrastructure improvement plan, which received city approval, targets nearly half of the mature oak canopy that residents say defines their neighborhood's character and provides critical environmental benefits.Brian Rickert, a resident of The Isles community, expressed alarm at the potential environmental impact of removing nearly half of the area's oak trees."Just the thought of 47% of these trees being gone, and the sunlight coming in, the loss of shade, the extra heat on the homes," Rickert told WPTV.While residents support necessary infrastructure improvements, Rickert emphasized the community's unified stance on preserving the tree canopy."The community is 100% in favor of fixing the infrastructure. We are not in favor of taking the trees down," Rickert said. Records obtained by WPTV show Palm Beach Gardens city staff asked the HOA to explore tree preservation alternatives before approving the removal plan. The city requested the HOA consider root pruning, root barriers and relocating mature trees where feasible.However, the HOA's consulting team determined that mature oak trees could not be relocated due to site constraints. The replacement plan calls for smaller species including green buttonwood trees.Rickert criticized the proposed replacement species as inadequate compared to the existing mature oaks."The green buttonwood trees are much smaller than the oak trees," Rickert explained. "They give 50 percent less shade than these beautiful, magnificent oaks do."Ron Lamneck, an arborist working with The Isles residents, is now advocating for changes to Palm Beach Gardens municipal codes regarding tree removal approvals."Nothing in the municipal codes requires anyone to show that all mitigation options were considered first," Lamneck said.In nearby Jupiter, residents of The Bluffs community are dealing with the inverse problem of aging, potentially dangerous trees that haven't received proper maintenance.Tom Wickenhauser, a Bluffs resident, warned about hurricane risks from unmaintained trees in his community."If we don't address it, consequences are going to be even more serious," Wickenhauser said.Despite facing different tree-related challenges, residents in both Palm Beach County communities are calling for increased community participation in decision-making processes."All we're asking for is to be heard with our concerns and for the community to be able to vote on it," Rickert said.The controversy highlights broader questions about balancing infrastructure needs with environmental preservation in South Florida's established residential communities, where mature tree canopies provide crucial benefits including storm protection, energy savings and property values.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A 45-year-old dump truck driver was killed after being hit by another construction vehicle inside a work zone on I-95 just south of Tradition on Monday night, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The driver stepped out of their dump truck on the northbound lanes and was struck by a tractor with a sweeper traveling south, repaving the area as part of an improvement project. The construction worker was transported to Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital, where they later died. The driver of the other truck was arrested on an unrelated warrant, FHP said. FHP s Traffic Homicide Investigation is ongoing.

FORT PIERCE — From locally made gifts to Fort Pierce-themed keepsakes, Sunshine State of Mind Boutique gives residents a place to celebrate home and visitors a way to take a little of it with them. Sunshine State of Mind opened in early June on Second Street, offering Fort Pierce souvenirs, locally made works of art and Florida-inspired apparel and gifts. The boutique is a passion project for Kim Brant, who has worked in downtown Fort Pierce for many years. She spent 10 years at the Original Tiki Bar and has worked at Cobbs Landing for the past five years. Brant said she saw the need for a shop dedicated to showcasing the city’s charm and character. “Every town around us has something like that,” she said, mentioning the Shell Bazaar in Port St. “I just wanted to share how amazing Fort Pierce is. It seems that there’s always been a bit of a cloud over the town, but I think it’s really a paradise!,” Brant added. Sunshine State of Mind offers a unique collection of Fort Pierce souvenirs, ranging from T-shirts and sweatshirts to locally made jewelry and woodwork, reflecting the city and Florida lifestyle. One wall features a shelf labeled “Locals Only,” showcasing work by local artists and crafters. Brant said she keeps all the vendors as local as possible. She even designs most of the shirts and sweatshirts herself. While this is her first endeavor as a business owner, she said “everything is figure-outable.” The shop is a family affair. Her husband, Chris, and their children help so Brant can continue working at Cobbs Landing. Brant said customer feedback has been positive since the store opened. Local resident Miranda Talley discovered Sunshine Boutique on TikTok “I thought it looked super cute, so I had to come check it out,” she said, looking over the display of refrigerator magnets for something to add to her collection. Just a few weeks after opening, Sunshine State of Mind Boutique is attracting residents and visitors looking for keepsakes that capture the spirit of Fort Pierce. For Brant, the shop is an opportunity to highlight the city she loves while giving local artists and makers a place to showcase their work. As downtown Fort Pierce continues to grow, she said she hopes Sunshine Boutique will become another stop that encourages people to discover and appreciate what this unique community has to offer. FORT PIERCE – The City of Fort Pierce is inviting professional artists and artist teams to submit proposals for a permanent outdoor sculpture to be installed at the front entrance of Fort Pierce City Hall, located at 100 N. This public art opportunity is part of the City’s ongoing commitment to enhancing public spaces while celebrating Fort Pierce’s unique identity, history, and culture. Located along one of the City’s most highly visible corridors, this artwork will serve as a welcoming landmark for residents and visitors alike. The selected sculpture should demonstrate artistic excellence, create a strong sense of arrival, engage viewers from multiple vantage points, and be designed to withstand Florida’s coastal climate. Project details • Location: Fort Pierce City Hall, 100 N. Highway 1, Fort Pierce, FL 34950 • Project budget: Up to $50,000 • Artwork type: Permanent outdoor sculpture • Submission period: July 16, 2026 – Aug. 16, 2026 Professional artists and artist teams with experience in designing and installing large-scale, permanent public art are encouraged to apply. Submission requirements Applications must be submitted through the CaFÉ (Call for Entry) online system and include: • Letter of interest • Artist resume • Portfolio of previous work • Preliminary concept statement • Proposed project timeline • Professional references • Artist website and/or social Media Links • Maintenance and protection plan • Comprehensive project budget • Selection criteria Submissions will be evaluated based on: • Artistic excellence and originality • Technical feasibility • Durability and public safety • Long-term maintenance considerations • Reflection of Fort Pierce’s community Identity • Ability to complete the project within the established budget and timeline Proposals must be submitted through the CaF online application portal: https://opportunities.wearecreativewest.org/opportunity/17647/CAFE For more information, contact: Audria V. School buses are equipped with automatic “stop” signs along with flashing red lights which are activated when buses stop along routes. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. LUCIE COUNTY – Public school for all students in St. Lucie County begins on Monday, Aug. The seven high schools will be open for students as early as 7:33 a.m., and the daily start of school for eleven K-8 grade schools is 7:35 a.m. Lincoln Park Academy in Fort Pierce begins its days at 7:23 a.m. Dan McCarty Forest Grove middle schools start sessions at 9:30 a.m.; while the start of school for Southern Oaks Southport middle schools is at 9:40 a.m. With the high schools and elementary schools, that means many students would be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. Lucie County School District and St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office urge all parents/students/motorists to be extra cautious and to observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “Every child deserves a safe journey to and from school,” said Lydia Martin, chief communications officer for St. “By practicing safe habits, following traffic laws, and utilizing tools like the ‘Here Comes the Bus’ app, families and motorists can help us create a safer environment for all students as we begin the new school year. Safety is a shared responsibility, and a little extra patience and awareness can make a big difference in protecting our students.” The Here Comes The Bus app can be downloaded by going to www.herecomesthebus.com . For more information on the school district s bus system, go to www.stlucie.k12.fl.us/departments/transportation . During the first few weeks of school, families should allow extra travel time as traffic patterns increase and students adjust to their routines, Martin said. “My message is simple: slow down, stay alert, and eliminate distractions,” Sheriff Richard Del Toro said in a statement. “Motorists must obey school zone speed limits and always stop when a school bus displays its flashing red lights and extended stop arm. Parents should take a few moments to review bus stop safety with their children, and students should remain attentive, follow the bus driver’s instructions, and never cross the street until they are signaled to do so safely. School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: • Have the child arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early. • Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. • Teach children to stay well off the roadway until the bus comes to a complete stop. • Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. • Ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: • Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street • Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. • Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: • Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. • Never play or run near traffic. • Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. • If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: • Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. • Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. • Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. • Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. • Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. • Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the web site. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. Anyone who sees unsafe driving around school buses, dangerous conditions at bus stops, or suspicious activity near bus stops, is asked to report it to local law enforcement or the St. Lucie Public Schools Transportation Department at 772-204-RIDE. “School safety is a shared responsibility,” Del Toro said. “Our deputies will have an increased presence around schools and along bus routes to promote compliance and protect our students, but the greatest difference comes from the choices each of us makes behind the wheel and at the bus stop. Together, we can ensure every child has a safe start to a successful school year.” By Jeff Alexander HTN Correspondent ST. A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. See also: Miami man faces prison after pleading guilty to online threats against Rubio, Noem Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center , per PSLPD. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.\ Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, said McNally. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. This case does, though, serve as hopefully a powerful reminder that allowing your anger to dictate your actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk, McNally said.

As Murray Middle School students head back to class this week in Stuart, they're returning to a campus that looks much different than when they left. Nearly two years after a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton tore through the school, damaged buildings are now gone, and a major rebuild is taking shape. Students are seeing plenty of construction that’ll continue throughout the school year. But district leaders say the work zone is completely separated from the rest of campus, so students can learn safely while crews rebuild. See also: Palm Beach County schools continue layered approach to campus safety as school year begins The October 2024 tornado destroyed two buildings and left a third with major roof damage. Those spaces housed the school's band, chorus, and agriculture programs. Superintendent Michael Maine says those programs never stopped. Over the summer, crews demolished two buildings. It'll make way for a new administration building and media center, plus modern spaces for band, chorus, and agriculture science. Crews will also renovate the gym. Be excited for the new year. Yes, it's going to take a little bit of time to get there, but it's well deserved. And when those students arrive on campus, there's nothing like seeing the bright smiles of the students to say, Wow, this is ours.’ It's incredible when you walk into a classroom environment that's clean, and new and fresh, and teachers are able to do so much more when we're able to provide the very best, said Superintendent Maine. The gym is expected to be finished by next August. The new administration building, media center, and specialized classrooms are expected to follow in December 2027. The project is being paid for through state support, insurance reimbursements, and district capital funds.

PALM CITY — The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is providing urgent care for 36 border collies, including three puppies up to six months old, after the dogs were removed from another hoarding case. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office arrested Paige O’Donnell yesterday, and she is facing felony charges for animal cruelty and improper confinement, according to Sheriff John Budensiek. Upon intake, the dogs were fed and given water after arriving in deplorable conditions, covered in feces. Most have skin infections, several have eye infections, and many appear withdrawn and catatonic. Some are being shaved under mild sedation due to their emotional distress and physical pain. In some dogs, sharp pieces of metal and glass were found within the matted hair. Given the dogs’ medical condition and emotional state, the humane society is not projecting when they will be available for adoption. Many will need foster care first as they recover. There are many ways the community can help. Monetary donations are HSTC s biggest need now as the cost of care continues and the time needed to place these animals remains ongoing. To donate, go online to www.hstc1.org/emergency-medical-fund . Although the border collies are not yet available for adoption, many other animals are ready to find their “fur-ever” homes. Adopting or fostering a current dog, cat, guinea pig or rabbit helps make room for rescued animals while they are being treated. The Humane Society s Name Your Price adoption special is continuing until further notice. Adoptable pets and real-time availability may be viewed at www.hstc1.org/Adopt . Short- and long-term fostering opportunities also are available. Learn more at www.hstc1.org/foster . Your comment has been submitted. Reported There was a problem reporting this. Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County, just three weeks apart, are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals.The first case unfolded at the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, where the Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats. Weeks later, 36 dogs were rescued from a Palm City home on Alligator Street.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult under current law."The laws are not tough enough. It's too easy to escape incarceration if you engage in these horrible acts of animal cruelty," Aronberg said.He said Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own, which creates a barrier for prosecutors."Hoarding by definition is not considered a crime under Florida law, so you need, I think, perhaps an anti-hoarding law to make it easier to prosecute these individuals [...] A specific anti-hoarding law that lowers the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases," Aronberg said.Aronberg explained even when cases do rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time. As a felony, some jail time is possible, but only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm.Martin County Sheriff John Buddensiek explained to Chief Investigator Jamie Ostroff in an interview last week that limited visible evidence of abuse prevented deputies from acting sooner on neighbor concerns in the 36-dog case."Federal law, state law only allows you to go so far when you have any type of investigation," Buddensiek said. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that, you know, dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of, we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there."Aronberg said the stakes extend beyond animal welfare. Studies show animal cruelty can escalate to child abuse and domestic violence, making enforcement a public safety issue."It's a gateway crime and that's why you need to treat it very strictly at the beginning. If you give it a slap on the wrist, you're just inviting more outrageous conduct that can hurt people," Aronberg said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A slithering 2-foot cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag. Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.RECENT SPORTS NEWS | Bob Iger, Josh Kushner to buy Lakers in historic $12.5 billion dealCottonmouths are the second-most venomous snakes found in Arkansas.Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he wasn't bitten."It was unreal," Davis said. The Los Angeles Lakers are being sold to businessmen Josh Kushner and Bob Iger for a record-breaking price, the second such sale in a year.This sale agreement is $12.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the terms who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity Wednesday because neither side revealed specific details.ESPN first reported that Kushner and Iger are buying the NBA's most valuable franchise, which was valued last year at $10 billion when Mark Walter purchased a controlling stake from the Buss family. The two businessmen had been involved in trying to get an expansion team for Las Vegas.By buying the Lakers, Iger and Kushner simply don’t have to wait for that decision. Expansion, if it happens, could take place in the 2028-29 season.The sale still will need approval from the NBA’s board of governors, and that process can take several weeks. The next board meeting is set for next month in New York.The $12.5 billion price tag is not only record-setting for U.S. pro sports but it continues a trend of NBA franchise values skyrocketing. Only three years ago, Michael Jordan sold his majority stake in the Charlotte Hornets for a $3 billion valuation, and the Boston Celtics were sold last year at a valuation of just over $6 billion -- which was then a record.

Matt Hasselbeck took some nasty hits to the head during his 17-year NFL career, four years at Boston College and a childhood full of sports, but the quarterback seems to have emerged from more than two decades of collisions relatively unscathed, enjoying middle adulthood with his wife and three children.The 50-year-old knows that some of his friends and former teammates haven't been as lucky.That's why the three-time Pro Bowl selection recently spent two days at Boston University, going through a battery of scans and tests to determine how much all those collisions affected his brain. The hope is that it will be a small step toward a goal that has eluded doctors — diagnosing chronic traumatic encephalopathy in the living."They need guys like me — they need people who are feeling good to step up to the plate and volunteer," Hasselbeck said. "I played quarterback, so I didn't take some of the hits that a lot of my teammates took."But the guys who were blocking for me, or playing special teams, or trying to get the ball back for me on defense, I wanted to do something. They had my back, so in a way I'd like to have their back."A degenerative brain disease that has been linked to concussions and other head trauma common in military combat and contact sports, CTE has been diagnosed in more than 100 former NFL players, casting a pall over the United States' most popular sports league. Some high-profile football players diagnosed with CTE after their deaths include Hall of Famers like linebacker Junior Seau and quarterback Ken Stabler, along with former Patriots tight end Aaron Hernandez.Right now, CTE can only be diagnosed after death.CTE can affect regions of the brain involved with regulating behavior and emotions. This can lead to memory loss, depression, violent mood swings and other cognitive and behavioral issues, though researchers note these symptoms can also be linked to other illnesses.Hasselbeck's participation is just a small part of a study that Michael Alosco, co-director of clinical research at the Boston University CTE Center, hopes will expand to hundreds of participants in multiple locations. Alosco is the principal investigator in Boston and there are also sites in California, Arizona, Texas and Florida with potentially more to come.The study seeks two types of people: Those who played professional or college football and those who have been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease and never played contact or collision sports and have no history of repetitive head impacts.Alosco said there are many similarities between Alzheimer's and CTE because both are degenerative brain diseases, but there are also some key differences, and mapping out those discrepancies is key to figuring out a way to diagnose CTE properly."We've applied what we've known worked for Alzheimer's disease, but we've learned it does not work for CTE," Alosco said. "We've really got to push discovery efforts and find the marker that's specific to the protein of CTE versus Alzheimer's because they're different."How we're going to get there is through the research we're doing right now."Nicholas Ashton, the principal investigator in Phoenix, said roughly 10 patients have participated at the Arizona site. He said that currently, diagnosing CTE in the living is mostly guesswork because so many of the symptoms mimic Alzheimer's."The more people involved, the more information we get and the closer we get to an answer," Ashton said. "Treatments exploded with Alzheimer's once we were able to accurately diagnose. We're trying to get to the same spot with CTE."Hasselbeck said he went through a variety of mental tests — like counting backward from 100 by sevens and reciting the alphabet backward. He also had a blood sample taken, an MRI on his brain and a PET (positron emission tomography) scan that injects a small amount of safe radioactive tracer that maps out the brain's function.The former quarterback said the procedures were eye-opening and humbling."I've got a healthy respect for people who are dealing with serious brain trauma, whether it's tumors or cancer," Hasselbeck said. "I walked in there feeling completely healthy and you still get a little anxious when you're doing a brain scan, an MRI. You come out and you're looking at your brain."Hasselbeck also is donating his brain for research after he dies.Not everyone in the study is a famous former NFL player.Bryan Savage, a 56-year-old who lives in Maryland, is a former linebacker at Union College in Schenectady, New York — an NCAA Division III school. He traveled to Boston for the study and also has committed to donating his brain.Savage said he's lucky to be relatively healthy but that he's been diagnosed with depression and ADHD over the past few years."I was interested because of some of the things that I've gone through physically and mentally," Savage said. "You wonder if it's just getting older, a midlife crisis or if it's related to any brain trauma I might have had playing football."Savage praised the researchers who were with him during the study and said he was relieved to find out his brain scans look normal for a man in his mid-50s. He's reached out to some of his former teammates, encouraging them to get involved in the study."I'll talk to some of my former friends and they're going through a lot of the same things," Savage said. "They'll say — 'Why do I feel like this? I've never been depressed. Things that I used to be passionate about I don't care about anymore.'"Alosco said the main reason Alzheimer's research is much more advanced than CTE research is sheer numbers: Alzheimer's research dates back decades and there have been countless people who have been studied.By comparison, CTE research is relatively new. Volunteers like Hasselbeck and Savage are crucial to bridge the gap. The National Institutes of Health is sponsoring the current study, awarding $15 million for the research in 2025."The (Alzheimer's progress) is through years and years of research, of people donating their brains, and also collecting data during life," Alosco said. "While we've been studying CTE for a while, we haven't had the point where we've had all this data during life, that have also donated their brain. We need to get to that place."He added: "I'm really hopeful about detecting CTE — I don't think that's too distant. Once we can accurately diagnose, that's when we can start some treatment trials."Hasselbeck — who played in the NFL for the Green Bay Packers, Seattle Seahawks, Tennessee Titans and Indianapolis Colts — said he had three concussions before he even started college, one playing football, another on the basketball court and another while goofing around while ice skating. He had a few concussions during his college or NFL career, but he wasn't sure of the exact number because some might have gone undetected since there was a culture of toughness in locker rooms, particularly early in his career.Hasselbeck's pro career spanned from 1998 to 2015 and the quarterback said there was a huge change regarding head injuries during that time. Early in his career, the only acceptable answer after a hit to the head was "I'm good," but by the mid 2010s, players were much more honest about potential concussions.Hasselbeck's proud of that change. Now he hopes his participation in the current CTE study can continue that progress."I've always had a passion for making the game safer," Hasselbeck said. One of the things I'm most proud of as an NFL guy is not just as a player, but the entire time I worked with the league and NFLPA for ways to make the game safer."

A different approach to public education is taking shape in Indian River County this school year as district leaders expand school choice and reorganize several campuses. Families in the district have more flexibility in where their children attend school. Parents can choose to enroll their children at schools across the district, rather than being limited to the school assigned to their neighborhood. The district has also converted several campuses into K-8 schools and operates five charter schools. One of the biggest changes this school year involves the district’s former all-freshman high school. See also: Indian River County launches new feature to track school buses in real time The Freshman Learning Center has been converted into Vero Beach Middle School. Moore says the freshman center was expensive to operate and did not provide students with high-quality educational programs. He says moving ninth-graders back to traditional high schools will also give them earlier access to more academic opportunities. From a student’s perspective, it allows them access to programming that was only being offered at the high school. You shouldn’t have to wait until you’re in 10th grade to take some of those courses, Moore told CBS12 News. District leaders say the two high schools, Sebastian River High School and Vero Beach High School, have enough capacity to accommodate incoming freshmen. That means all incoming ninth-graders this school year will attend either Sebastian River High School or Vero Beach High School. The changes are part of the district’s broader effort to give families more educational options while restructuring how its schools serve students.

One person is in custody as Martin County sheriff’s deputies investigate what authorities describe as a serious animal hoarding case involving Border Collies at a Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said deputies were serving a search warrant Monday at a home at 1245 SW Alligator Street. The search follows an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff’s detectives, who have been working to determine the scope of the situation and the animals' condition. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home so far, while deputies and animal services officers continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some of the dogs were skittish and hiding in the home. The woman who was arrested was identified as Paige O'Donnell, 62. She is being charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. "She, on purpose, kept these dogs trapped in this jail that she has behind us and abused them for lack of a better word," Sheriff Budensiek said. The conditions inside the home were described as extremely concerning. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said those conditions were making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals; they also said it was extremely hot and that she may not have had A/C. "It's just stacked with garbage. There's feces over every square inch of the house," Sheriff Budensiek said. "It's really sad to see them in such rough shape. But also I'm very happy to see them finally getting out," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor. Investigators and animal services personnel are continuing to assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. WARNING: DISTURBING IMAGES IN VIDEO BELOW Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided an update on the investigation. He said the dogs were running loose in the house and conditions in the house were very bad. "The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces," Sheriff Budensiek explained. See also: Targeted in broad daylight: Boca Raton police search for multiple gunmen This case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home. Budenseik says O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges. She is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. She's supposed to be an animal breeder and she's gonna let the animals live like that? That's just, there's something wrong with her," said Kimberly Todd, another neighbor who lives on SW Alligator Street.

A two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge ended safely after Indian River County deputies talked a man wanted for burglary back from the edge. According to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office , deputies were called to the bridge on Sunday, August 2, after receiving information that a man wanted on a Port St. Lucie Police Department warrant for burglary with battery had contacted his mother and made concerning statements. Viewer discretion is advised. The following video contains footage involving a person threatening to jump from a bridge. Some viewers may find the content disturbing. Deputies located the man on top of the 17th Street Bridge after he climbed over the railing and threatened to jump. The Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team spent about two hours talking with him while the Marine Unit launched a boat below the bridge. Fire Rescue also staged nearby as a safety precaution. See also: Animal Services responded to Palm City home roughly 20 times since 2020 Body camera footage shows negotiators working to keep the man talking and convince him to come back over the railing. "At the end of the day, you're still around to be with your family," one negotiator told him. The man said he was worried about going to jail and the financial burden his family could face. Negotiators continued talking with him, eventually learning that he enjoyed playing video games. As the conversation continued, deputies told him his mother was heading to the base of the bridge. The man eventually agreed to climb back over the railing. There's a big, bright future for you," the negotiator told him. Body camera footage shows deputies encouraging him as he grabbed a ladder and climbed back onto the bridge. The man was then taken into custody without incident. Two moms whose children struggled to read launched a movement nearly 15 years ago. Now, four schools in Indian River County have reached a 90% reading proficiency goal.WATCH BELOW: 'From third grade on, you're reading to learn,' Rosewood principal Adam Faust tell WPTV's Jon ShiainmanIndian River County's schools are drawing national attention for a community-driven literacy program that started with a simple but ambitious goal: get 90% of third graders reading at grade level.The effort is called the Moonshot Moment, born in 2012 through The Learning Alliance, a nonprofit co-founded by parent Liz Remington, whose son struggled with reading."You are afraid and looking for answers and we really struggled with what is going on and how do we problem solve," Remington said.The nonprofit brings together schools, philanthropists, and business owners to fund added resources, including reading coaches, in elementary classrooms."It means the community has to come together and be an unstoppable team," Remington said.When I first met Remington in 2017, just 56% of third graders in the district were reading at grade level. Today, four schools have reached the 90% milestone, including Rosewood Magnet School."From birth to third grade, you're learning to read. From third grade on, you're reading to learn," said Rosewood principal Adam Faust.Faust said the achievement came down to the final day."We had six kids to test to make the 90%. We needed three to be at proficiency or above, and it turned out five of those kids made it," Faust said.At Osceola Magnet School, principal Jennifer Norris said students will return to a new campus building and a new reading challenge after the school also cleared the 90% threshold."We're shooting for 95% this year," Norris said.The stakes behind that goal are significant."If students are reading at grade level by third grade, the data show they are going to be proficient readers for the rest of their life," Norris said.Other school districts across Florida are now looking at adopting the Moonshot Moment model — a continuation of a mission that started with one parent's child and has since helped thousands of students."Put the systems in place and you build your team and implementing collectively and collaboratively and it's so powerful," Remington said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Victor Lopez walked back into HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce eight months after a life-threatening motorcycle crash, this time to thank the team that helped save his life. Lopez, who is now back home recovering and cherishing time with his family, returned to the hospital to express his gratitude to the medical professionals and first responders who cared for him during his critical moments. "Very good, meant to be," Lopez said. A Moment of Joy: News We Love His girlfriend, Stefany Sorto, described the reunion as "very special." She added, "Everybody cares and to see him, he's way better." Last December, Lopez was brought to the hospital in a coma-like state after a serious motorcycle crash. Doctors feared he might not survive. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 "We were very concerned about significant traumatic brain injury. Also signs of anoxic brain injury, which is lack of oxygen to the brain from a significant head injury," said Dr. Jason Moore, a trauma and acute care surgeon at HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. As the medical team worked to stabilize Lopez, his family could only wait. Sorto, who was pregnant at the time, gave birth to their daughter, Juliet, in January while Lopez was still hospitalized. Lopez spent nearly three months in the hospital before he was able to return home to Sorto, their son, and their newborn daughter. Now, he has reunited with the EMS crew and medical team who cared for him during his darkest hours. "I arrived on scene with the crews. He had heavy damage from a motorcycle accident. We immediately called a trauma alert, notified the local trauma center here at Lawnwood so they would be prepared," said Donny Stefani, deputy chief of operations for the St. Lucie County Fire District. Tradition Lakes K-8 in St. Lucie County has delayed its opening by a week. Construction is still underway at the school. Some parents are now concerned about safety and scrambling for childcare options. The school, originally scheduled to welcome 1,600 students on Monday, will now open on Aug. 17, according to district officials. Prince released a statement explaining that after inspecting the school, he did not feel staff had enough time to "adequately prepare it for parents and children," leading to the decision to push the opening. Parents and residents expressed concerns about the delay and the state of the school. "The kids' safety needs to come first. I don’t know how they’re going to do it," one grandmother said. "I’m concerned that they’re going to bring 1,600 kids with it looking like construction. There are signs all over that say hard hat area." Parent Robyn Johnson questioned whether the school would be ready in time. "It doesn’t look at all done, especially towards the back there," she said. Tradition Lakes K-8 is expected to provide much-needed classroom space for one of the county’s fastest-growing communities. However, some parents feel the process has been mishandled. "It’s a nice idea, absolutely wonderful that they have a new school coming, but they haven’t run this, in my opinion, the right way. But hopefully, they get it done," a grandmother said. The district said it will share community childcare options for families during the delay. An open house is scheduled for next Friday. The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked in connection with the case and faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O'Donnell appeared before a judge on Tuesday. Her bond was set at $270,000 and she was told she could have no pets if she is released on bond. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. According to the arrest report, Monday’s search was the culmination of an investigation that stretched back weeks and drew on years of previous Animal Services contacts involving O'Donnell’s home. The latest investigation developed after authorities received renewed concerns about the number of dogs at the SW Alligator Street residence and their living conditions. In June, investigators observed the property from the roadway but did not make contact with anyone at the home. The following month, the Sheriff’s Office received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about conditions at the property dating back several years. On July 22, Animal Services responded to another complaint alleging more than 20 dogs were inside the home, that several deceased animals may have been in the garage, that the home did not have functioning air conditioning and that the dogs had not been allowed outside since 2022, according to the report. An investigator reported smelling a strong odor from the roadway and hearing what sounded like a large number of dogs, including puppies, barking from inside. O'Donnell later met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but, according to the report, would not allow investigators inside her home. The dog she brought to the meeting was described as having heavily stained, matted fur. Investigators said O'Donnell told them she had buried one of her dogs and named several others she still owned. Investigators also checked veterinary records. According to the affidavit, an employee at a local animal hospital said O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some that were brought in deceased. The employee also told investigators the dogs were frequently dirty. The arrest report says Animal Services had a long history of responding to complaints involving the residence, with roughly 20 related incidents documented from 2020 through this year. One 2020 investigation documented about 25 dogs and described the home as severely unsanitary, with feces and urine covering the floor. Investigators said one elderly dog was in such poor condition that humane euthanasia was recommended. Another complaint in 2022 led investigators to report 10 to 20 dogs being kept in a backyard covered in feces and flies. The arrest report says the home's air conditioning was not functioning and investigators observed feces inside the residence. At a follow-up inspection a week later, authorities said the home had been cleaned, the air conditioning repaired and three dogs surrendered to a rescue. In December 2023, investigators again responded to complaints about more than 20 dogs. According to the report, they detected an overwhelming odor of urine and feces and heard more than 10 dogs barking inside, including what sounded like puppies. Neighbors say they'd been raising concerns for years. "Very frustrating, very angry. They say if you hear something, say something, and we said something, probably over a hundred times," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor on SW Alligator Street. "When you called the Sheriff's Office, what did you tell them?" we asked her. "The dogs are in the house. They haven't been let out in years at this point. There's no A-C, 'cause the windows are open. When the wind blows, you can smell it," Weidenheimer explained. "What did they tell you?" we asked her. "As long as the dogs have food and shelter, it's fine," she said. Investigators said the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning changed during different contacts, and records did not always establish what happened to dogs she had previously said were in her possession. "Our interaction with her started back in 2020 when she was an AKC breeder and back then we had several calls for service that involved her maybe mistreating animals. Our Animal Control Officers came out at that point. She was not actually--didn't appear to be mistreating animals," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. According to the Sheriff, they learned from a previous animal hoarding case, that it's not always a smart decision to rush in and take all the dogs. "Unfortunately, 20 plus years ago, we experienced that here at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. We hit a house that had over 100 dogs in it. Seized them all, fostered them all out and then we were sued and lost the lawsuit. And worse than losing the lawsuit, we had to return those animals to the deplorable conditions which we took them from. So learning from our mistakes years and years ago, we weren’t going to do that again," Sheriff Budensiek said. In the days before the search warrant was obtained, investigators returned to the Palm City property and again reported smelling feces and urine. A neighboring resident also provided video that, according to the arrest report, showed garbage and debris piled high inside the garage while numerous dogs could be heard barking inside the home. Investigators also reviewed a photograph from a 2020 case showing at least 12 Border Collies in a room where the dogs and floor appeared to be covered in fecal matter. Based on those observations, prior complaints and O'Donnell’s documented history with Animal Services, investigators obtained a search warrant. When authorities entered the home Monday, the arrest report says the residence was unlivable and unsanitary, with floors covered in feces, urine and garbage and an air-conditioning system that was not working. Investigators said the dogs were severely matted with feces and urine and that portions of the walls appeared to have been repeatedly chewed. Thirty-six dogs were removed from the residence. Sheriff Budensiek separately described the conditions as extremely concerning, saying some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces that they appeared nearly solid black. Deputies and Animal Services employees wore protective clothing while working inside the house. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says viewers and residents can help the 36 Border Collies by donating to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast to help with medical and recovery care for the animals. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the dogs’ conditions and determine the full scope of the case.

Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County, just three weeks apart, are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals.The first case unfolded at the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle, where the Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats. Weeks later, 36 dogs were rescued from a Palm City home on Alligator Street.Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult under current law."The laws are not tough enough. It's too easy to escape incarceration if you engage in these horrible acts of animal cruelty," Aronberg said.He said Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own, which creates a barrier for prosecutors."Hoarding by definition is not considered a crime under Florida law, so you need, I think, perhaps an anti-hoarding law to make it easier to prosecute these individuals [...] A specific anti-hoarding law that lowers the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases," Aronberg said.Aronberg explained even when cases do rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time. As a felony, some jail time is possible, but only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm.Martin County Sheriff John Buddensiek explained to Chief Investigator Jamie Ostroff in an interview last week that limited visible evidence of abuse prevented deputies from acting sooner on neighbor concerns in the 36-dog case."Federal law, state law only allows you to go so far when you have any type of investigation," Buddensiek said. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that, you know, dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of, we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there."Aronberg said the stakes extend beyond animal welfare. Studies show animal cruelty can escalate to child abuse and domestic violence, making enforcement a public safety issue."It's a gateway crime and that's why you need to treat it very strictly at the beginning. If you give it a slap on the wrist, you're just inviting more outrageous conduct that can hurt people," Aronberg said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Palm Beach County’s growing culinary scene is earning international recognition after several local restaurants received honors from the MICHELIN Guide Florida, including one West Palm Beach restaurant making history.Monday, 10 restaurants were awarded 2026 MICHELIN plaques by Discover The Palm Beaches.Emelina, a 16-seat tasting-menu restaurant in West Palm Beach’s Flamingo Park neighborhood, earned Palm Beach County’s only MICHELIN Star this year. According to Discover The Palm Beaches, Emelina also became the first Cuban restaurant in the world to receive a MICHELIN Star.Several other Palm Beach County restaurants received MICHELIN recognition through recommendations and Bib Gourmand honors, which recognize quality food at a good value.MICHELIN inspectors evaluate restaurants based on ingredient quality, flavor harmony, cooking techniques, consistency and the chef’s personality reflected in the cuisine.In Palm Beach County kitchens, chefs are chasing perfection and now, MICHELIN is noticing.Chef Pushkar Marathe said MICHELIN inspectors visit anonymously.“They never really shared that they’re going to be in your restaurant,” Marathe said.Marathe’s Palm Beach Gardens restaurants, Stage Kitchen & Bar and Ela Curry & Cocktails, both earned MICHELIN recommendations this year. His first reaction after learning about the recognition focused on improvement.“First thought was, how could we do better to get a star?” Marathe said.Marathe explained that MICHELIN recommendations place restaurants within reach of earning a future star.“When you’re recommended, you’ve been considered for the star, but there’s still some things you need to work on,” he said.Chef Tim Lipman’s Coolinary and the Parched Pig also received a MICHELIN recommendation.“You don’t necessarily strive for the award, but you strive for excellence,” Lipman said.Lipman said the recognition has helped local restaurants stand out in a competitive dining market.“Definitely needle in a haystack, right? There’s so many great restaurants out there,” he said.Aioli in West Palm Beach earned a Bib Gourmand designation for the second consecutive year. Owners Michael and Melanie Hackman said the recognition validates their commitment to scratch-made baking and consistency.“We are a scratch sourdough bakery,” Michael Hackman said. “It’s definitely why MICHELIN noticed us. We’re doing stuff the right way. We’re not cutting corners."Aioli’s sourdough takes more than three days to ferment. Hackman said even pop culture trends have influenced customer interest.“They said, ‘I’m only here, because Taylor Swift makes sourdough. I want to learn how to make sourdough,’” Hackman said.Melanie Hackman said maintaining MICHELIN recognition can be even more challenging than earning it initially.“Earning it the first time was huge, but retaining it was even bigger for us,” she said.Restaurant owners also said the recognition is helping business during the slower summer months.“We are in the dead of summer and grateful that our restaurant is full every day,” Melanie Hackman said.Milton Segarra, president and CEO of Discover The Palm Beaches, said culinary tourism is becoming increasingly important to Palm Beach County’s economy.“Normally visitors come here for the beaches and the experiences we can offer. Now they are returning, because we became this powerhouse in the culinary scene,” Segarra said.Segarra said tourism investment tied to culinary marketing efforts has generated measurable returns for the county.“For every dollar that we invest on behalf of the county, we have a return of $3.55 in TDTs,” he said, referring to tourist development tax revenue.Why this matters now: MICHELIN recognition continues to reshape Palm Beach County’s reputation beyond beaches and luxury resorts. As more nationally recognized chefs and restaurants open across the region, local leaders see fine dining and culinary tourism becoming a growing economic driver for South Florida.From scratch bakeries to chef-driven tasting menus, Palm Beach County’s restaurant scene is earning attention from diners around the world — and local chefs say they are still striving for more.2026 Palm Beach County restaurants recognized by Michelin Guide FloridaMICHELIN Star • Emelina — West Palm BeachBib Gourmand • aioli — West Palm BeachMICHELIN Recommended• Stage Kitchen & Bar — Palm Beach Gardens• Ela Curry & Cocktails — Palm Beach Gardens• Coolinary — Palm Beach Gardens• būccan — Palm Beach• Moody Tongue Sushi — West Palm Beach• Nicholson Muir — Boynton Beach• The Butcher’s Club — Palm Beach GardensWhat do MICHELIN distinctions mean?• MICHELIN Star: Awarded for exceptional cooking and culinary excellence.• Bib Gourmand: Recognizes high-quality food at a good value.• Recommended: Honors restaurants serving standout meals with quality ingredients and strong execution.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? Students in Palm Beach County headed back to school with new shoes and a confidence boost Thursday morning thanks to a community initiative supported by R&B singer Mark Morrison.WATCH BELOW:Morrison, best known for the hit song "Return of the Mack," splits his time between the United Kingdom and Palm Beach Gardens.The VIP shopping event took place on Thursday morning Shining A Light segment at the Mall at Wellington Green, where students from the Student & Athlete Mentoring Program, known as S.T.A.M.P., received $100 to shop for new sneakers before the start of the school year.S.T.A.M.P. founder Mark Brown said the organization focuses on helping students succeed academically, athletically and personally.“Stamp is all about mentoring kids, helping them academically through the summer,” Brown said. “We specialize in math and reading and personal development, teaching them how to be successful.”Brown said the program’s mission goes beyond sports and academics.“We call it prepped, pressed, and dressed,” Brown said. “So we prep them mentally, and we prep them. We’re gonna get their hair done and their hairdos and haircuts, and they gotta go school with some shoes.”The Student & Athlete Mentoring Program serves children and teens ages 8 to 17 in Palm Beach County through enrichment camps and mentoring opportunities.
