A Palm City woman is in custody on a $270,000 bond after authorities discovered 36 Border Collies living in severe neglect inside her home on Alligator Street, leading to 72 charges of animal cruelty. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the animals were in "deplorable conditions." The case dates back to 2020, when animal services first investigated Paige O'Donnell’s home and dogs. Court records show complaints continued through 2022 and 2023, with renewed concerns in 2026 leading to surveillance and multiple attempted inspections. After officers observed one dog this month, they obtained a search warrant, which led to the discovery of the 36 dogs and O'Donnell’s arrest. During her first court appearance, O'Donnell was ordered, "You may not possess either temporarily or permanently any animals as a condition of your bond." All 36 dogs are now being cared for at the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. (To donate to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast, click here.) Sarah Fisher, a spokesperson for the organization, described the severity of the animals’ condition. "We had not only the matted and the underweight and the skin issues, we had glass and metal. We had their tongues were bleeding from them biting their tongues. There was feces in their mouths. Their tails might be falling off. I mean, it's the worst that I've seen," Fisher said. Fisher added that the focus is currently on assessing each dog’s physical and mental health. "Some of the dogs are just laying there, and they don't know what to do. They don't know to lift their head. They don't know how to interact with people. So you can tell they were institutionalized," Fisher said. Reflecting on the situation, Fisher said, "I don't know whether to be sad for her or angry. Because, you know, at one time in her life, she loved these dogs and she put everything towards these dogs. And somewhere along the way, something happened. And unfortunately, the dogs had to pay for it." The Humane Society said it could take time before the dogs are ready for foster homes or adoption. In the meantime, they are asking for community support to help with the recovery efforts. PALM CITY – The 36 Border Collies rescued on Aug. 10 by Martin County Sheriff’s Office from a home in the the 1200 block of Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City are now getting care from the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Paige Anne O’Donnell, 62, a one-time AKC dog breeder, was charged with 72 counts of animal cruelty on Aug. 10, after the collies were found in what Sheriff John Budensiek described as “deplorable condition.” She faces 36 third-degree felony counts of torture involving pain, serious physical injury or death; and 36 first-degree misdemeanor counts of keeping animals in an enclosure without exercise and air. She was being held in the Martin County Jail on those charges with no bond as of Aug. The home is near Southwest Mapp Road and south of Southwest Martin Highway The rescue came about as a result of an ongoing investigation in which neighbors continually complained about the stench emanating from the home and the incessant barking from many of the dogs, Budensiek said in a press briefing outside the home on Aug. “If the wind blows this way, you smell the stench what the neighbors have been dealing with,” Budensiek said. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office first received complaints in 2020 that animals in O’Donnell’s care may have been mistreated, he said. The animals were found then to be in acceptable condition but soon after, in 2022, O’Donnell reportedly underwent treatment for alcohol abuse through the Marchman Act and began “playing the legal game” to block officials from accessing her home, Budensiek said. O’Donnell, who also lied to sheriff’s deputies about the collies, put up every legal obstacle she could to prevent the sheriff’s office from even looking at the dogs, including building a fence around the property, he said. “She wouldn’t even tell us the true number of dogs in the house,” he said. Recent complaints from neighbors prompted the sheriff’s office to assign a special investigator to the case, Budensiek said. Through that investigator’s efforts, O’Donnell agreed to surrender one dog to the sheriff’s office which then prompted the agency to get a search warrant. “(O’Donnell) was taking a bath this morning when our units arrived here to take her in custody,” Budensiek said. “She was clean but the dogs that she’s supposed to be taking care of were in deplorable conditions. Humane Society tried to help her, DCF tried to help her, Martin County Sheriff’s Office tried to help her but not only did she refuse teh help but she kept these dogs in the jail that she had. Over the years, drywall deteriorated and furniture was destroyed because of the dogs relieving themselves wherever they could, Budensiek said. The house was hot but there was no running air-conditioning, he said. Deputies and animal services officers had to wear Tyvek protective clothing while going into the house because of the extensive accumulation of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the interior. “The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be border collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They’re supposed to be white and black dogs, and they’re solid black from the feces,” Budensiek said. The dogs will be carefully groomed by the local Humane Society and then fostered out to people who can properly care for them, Budensiek said. “We want to make sure that she never, ever owns an animal again, that she never gets any of these dogs back,” he said. The rescue comes about three weeks after a previous rescue by the Martin County Sheriff’s Office at a home in the Foxwoods subdivision where more than 120 dogs and cats were living in similar conditions. Those animals, like the dogs at O’Donnell’s home, were taken to the Humane Society. The Humane Society is asking for the public’s help by making whatever donation it can towards the care of the animals. “We’ve witnessed how deeply our community cares about animals and are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of support these past few weeks. We’re asking again for your help as the financial burden of caring for these neglected dogs comes at a time when our shelter was already facing immense challenges,” the Humane Society said in a Facebook posting. The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked in connection with the case and faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O'Donnell appeared before a judge on Tuesday. Her bond was set at $270,000 and she was told she could have no pets if she is released on bond. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. According to the arrest report, Monday’s search was the culmination of an investigation that stretched back weeks and drew on years of previous Animal Services contacts involving O'Donnell’s home. The latest investigation developed after authorities received renewed concerns about the number of dogs at the SW Alligator Street residence and their living conditions. In June, investigators observed the property from the roadway but did not make contact with anyone at the home. The following month, the Sheriff’s Office received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about conditions at the property dating back several years. On July 22, Animal Services responded to another complaint alleging more than 20 dogs were inside the home, that several deceased animals may have been in the garage, that the home did not have functioning air conditioning and that the dogs had not been allowed outside since 2022, according to the report. An investigator reported smelling a strong odor from the roadway and hearing what sounded like a large number of dogs, including puppies, barking from inside. O'Donnell later met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but, according to the report, would not allow investigators inside her home. The dog she brought to the meeting was described as having heavily stained, matted fur. Investigators said O'Donnell told them she had buried one of her dogs and named several others she still owned. Investigators also checked veterinary records. According to the affidavit, an employee at a local animal hospital said O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some that were brought in deceased. The employee also told investigators the dogs were frequently dirty. The arrest report says Animal Services had a long history of responding to complaints involving the residence, with roughly 20 related incidents documented from 2020 through this year. One 2020 investigation documented about 25 dogs and described the home as severely unsanitary, with feces and urine covering the floor. Investigators said one elderly dog was in such poor condition that humane euthanasia was recommended. Another complaint in 2022 led investigators to report 10 to 20 dogs being kept in a backyard covered in feces and flies. The arrest report says the home's air conditioning was not functioning and investigators observed feces inside the residence. At a follow-up inspection a week later, authorities said the home had been cleaned, the air conditioning repaired and three dogs surrendered to a rescue. In December 2023, investigators again responded to complaints about more than 20 dogs. According to the report, they detected an overwhelming odor of urine and feces and heard more than 10 dogs barking inside, including what sounded like puppies. Neighbors say they'd been raising concerns for years. "Very frustrating, very angry. They say if you hear something, say something, and we said something, probably over a hundred times," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor on SW Alligator Street. "When you called the Sheriff's Office, what did you tell them?" we asked her. "The dogs are in the house. They haven't been let out in years at this point. There's no A-C, 'cause the windows are open. When the wind blows, you can smell it," Weidenheimer explained. "What did they tell you?" we asked her. "As long as the dogs have food and shelter, it's fine," she said. Investigators said the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning changed during different contacts, and records did not always establish what happened to dogs she had previously said were in her possession. "Our interaction with her started back in 2020 when she was an AKC breeder and back then we had several calls for service that involved her maybe mistreating animals. Our Animal Control Officers came out at that point. She was not actually--didn't appear to be mistreating animals," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. According to the Sheriff, they learned from a previous animal hoarding case, that it's not always a smart decision to rush in and take all the dogs. "Unfortunately, 20 plus years ago, we experienced that here at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. We hit a house that had over 100 dogs in it. Seized them all, fostered them all out and then we were sued and lost the lawsuit. And worse than losing the lawsuit, we had to return those animals to the deplorable conditions which we took them from. So learning from our mistakes years and years ago, we weren’t going to do that again," Sheriff Budensiek said. In the days before the search warrant was obtained, investigators returned to the Palm City property and again reported smelling feces and urine. A neighboring resident also provided video that, according to the arrest report, showed garbage and debris piled high inside the garage while numerous dogs could be heard barking inside the home. Investigators also reviewed a photograph from a 2020 case showing at least 12 Border Collies in a room where the dogs and floor appeared to be covered in fecal matter. Based on those observations, prior complaints and O'Donnell’s documented history with Animal Services, investigators obtained a search warrant. When authorities entered the home Monday, the arrest report says the residence was unlivable and unsanitary, with floors covered in feces, urine and garbage and an air-conditioning system that was not working. Investigators said the dogs were severely matted with feces and urine and that portions of the walls appeared to have been repeatedly chewed. Thirty-six dogs were removed from the residence. Sheriff Budensiek separately described the conditions as extremely concerning, saying some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces that they appeared nearly solid black. Deputies and Animal Services employees wore protective clothing while working inside the house. The Martin County Sheriff's Office says viewers and residents can help the 36 Border Collies by donating to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast to help with medical and recovery care for the animals. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the dogs’ conditions and determine the full scope of the case.

The Village of Wellington will soon enforce strict new regulations for electric bikes and scooters after the Village Council approved two new ordinances Tuesday night. The rules establish a minimum riding age of 15, require operators to carry identification, and mandate helmets for younger riders, a move that followed months of debate over public safety.The decision has drawn mixed reactions from a community grappling with the growing popularity of e-mobility devices, particularly among younger residents.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE BELOW:Under the two ordinances passed by the council, several new restrictions will be implemented for e-bikes, scooters, and other vehicles classified as e-motos. Key among them are:Minimum Age: Riders must be at least 15 years old to operate an e-moto.Identification: All riders must carry a government-issued photo ID or a school ID.Helmets: Helmets will be mandated for younger operators.Speed Limits: A speed limit of 15 mph will be enforced on sidewalks and multi-use pathways.Banned Areas: E-motos are now banned from public bridle and equestrian trails, Wellington Town Center, neighborhood parks, and the Heart Trail at Village Park during restricted times.The council chamber was filled with residents who spoke both for and against the measures, with the age requirement proving to be the most contentious point."I believe the village should focus on education, parental responsibility, responsible rules, and enforcement—not simply an age ban," one resident stated during public comment.Seventh-grader Mia Moore attended the meeting to share a letter from her friend, who recently suffered a fractured skull in a scooter accident. Despite her friend's injury, the letter argued that education, not restriction, was the answer for young riders who rely on e-motos for transportation to school."When you turn 15, you don't magically get responsible," Moore told the council. "It's a matter of how mature you already are, or how well you know how to use them."Mayor Michael Napoleone and Council Member Stephen Levin sided with that view, with the mayor calling an age restriction "the lazy way to do this.""We've all seen the kids who are tearing through neighborhoods," Napoleone said. "I think we need to enforce the rules against those kids and punish those kids for misbehaving and reckless behavior."However, other council members argued that a clear, enforceable standard was necessary for public safety."For the parents that say, 'Well, my child's an angel,' sure he is, or she is," said Council Member Johnny Meier. "Are you okay with exchanging your kid's freedom to ride their e-bike for your neighbor's kid to die or get hurt?"Village officials have not yet announced a specific date for when the new rules will take effect. WPTV will provide updates as soon as the implementation timeline is released.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. CBS12 News is continuing our coverage for back-to-school week. The Martin County School District is starting the new year on an academic high. The district earned an "A" rating for the second year in a row, while students also achieved the district's highest state assessment scores on record. Martin County is now celebrating back-to-back A’ ratings after spending seven years as a "B"-rated district. Superintendent Michael Maine credits the students, teachers, families and staff -- but says the work isn’t over. Every district-operated school earned at least a "C rating Stuart Middle, Indiantown Middle, and South Fork High all moved from a "B" to an "A" rating Hobe Sound Elementary improved from a "C" to a "B" Students also posted strong gains on state assessments: English language arts proficiency rose from 55% to 59% Math improved from 60% to 63% Geometry jumped nine points to 69%, ranking fourth in the state The district also finished eighth statewide in civics I'm extremely happy and proud of our teachers and all of the hard work that they do in the classroom every day. Our school administrators just continue to push themselves. We are not going to just settle. Our students deserve the very best, and in order to make sure they're getting the very best, we have to keep pushing at an exceptional level, said Superintendent Maine. To keep that momentum going, Maine says the district is focusing extra support on its five "C"-rated schools this year.

A two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge ended safely after Indian River County deputies talked a man wanted for burglary back from the edge. According to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office , deputies were called to the bridge on Sunday, August 2, after receiving information that a man wanted on a Port St. Lucie Police Department warrant for burglary with battery had contacted his mother and made concerning statements. Viewer discretion is advised. The following video contains footage involving a person threatening to jump from a bridge. Some viewers may find the content disturbing. Deputies located the man on top of the 17th Street Bridge after he climbed over the railing and threatened to jump. The Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team spent about two hours talking with him while the Marine Unit launched a boat below the bridge. Fire Rescue also staged nearby as a safety precaution. See also: Animal Services responded to Palm City home roughly 20 times since 2020 Body camera footage shows negotiators working to keep the man talking and convince him to come back over the railing. "At the end of the day, you're still around to be with your family," one negotiator told him. The man said he was worried about going to jail and the financial burden his family could face. Negotiators continued talking with him, eventually learning that he enjoyed playing video games. As the conversation continued, deputies told him his mother was heading to the base of the bridge. The man eventually agreed to climb back over the railing. There's a big, bright future for you," the negotiator told him. Body camera footage shows deputies encouraging him as he grabbed a ladder and climbed back onto the bridge. The man was then taken into custody without incident. Keeping track of your child’s school bus is about to get easier for families in Indian River County. The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child’s bus in real time. Parents can tap the bus icon in the district’s app to see where the bus is and get an estimated arrival time. The app will also send push notifications when a bus is running late. See also: Palm Beach County students return to school Monday with changes to free meal program Superintendent David K. Moore says the new feature is designed to give parents more peace of mind. You feel good as a parent, speaking as a parent, when your kid’s in school. But when they are on the bus, there’s just a little bit of angst until they get off that bus and walk in that front door, Moore told CBS12 News. Now parents have greater access when they are walking in that front door. The district is also adding another layer of security for students. Students will scan their school ID when they board the bus, allowing the district to keep better track of who is riding each bus. Moore says every school bus driver position is filled, meaning the district is fully staffed. The new tracking feature is expected to give parents another way to stay informed about their child’s ride to and from school especially on days when buses are delayed.

John Abkemeier Jr., a student at Jupiter High School, had learned CPR in his P.E. class just two weeks earlier. Little did he know those skills would soon save his father's life.On June 26, the family was watching soccer at their Palm Beach Gardens home when John Abkemeir had a heart attack."I fell kind of to the side on the couch, the lights just went out on me," Abkemeir recalled. "The next thing I know, I wake up in the ambulance with the paramedics."WATCH: Paramedics filled in the blanks for Abkemeir when he regained consciousness."They asked me what happened, I said no, they said you just had a heart attack," Abkemeir said.Before paramedics arrived, John Jr. "I got my dad off the couch, onto the ground, and started doing CPR for about three minutes," he explained. "Then the ambulance came and took over. Thankfully, my dad was okay."The teenager's quick response came from fresh training. coach, Ben Kennerson, had taught CPR just two weeks before the incident. "It's incredible to know that he rose to the occasion," Coach Kennerson said. "He had his training, trusted it, and applied it. That's phenomenal."The reality of what happened didn't hit the father until he reached the hospital. "They told me your son saved your life with CPR," Abkemeir said.For WPTV anchor Mike Trim, who interviewed the family, the emotion was palpable. "I'm a father myself, so it really touched me," Trim said.John Jr. was recently honored with the Heart Saver Hero Award by the American Heart Association. But for him, the real reward is simpler. "I'm glad he's proud of me," he said. "I love my dad."CPR classes are taught throughout Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast high schools. At Jupiter High School, students learn these vital skills in P.E., history, and science classes. "He saved my life, so he's my hero," Abkemeir said.

At least 18 Palm Beach County teachers are stepping into their own classrooms for the first time this week — not as newcomers to education, but as graduates of a program that let them earn a bachelor's degree while working full time.The School District of Palm Beach County, in partnership with BloomBoard, offers the Palm Beach Associate Teacher Program, a two-year, portfolio-based bachelor's degree pathway for current non-instructional or temporary district employees who hold an associate's degree or at least 60 college credits but not yet a bachelor's degree.WATCH: Participants serve as full-time teachers of record in a paid classroom placement while completing coursework. Graduates earn a fully accredited bachelor's degree in Early Childhood Education, Elementary Education, or Exceptional Student Education.Two of those new teachers, Cindy Mendez-Lopez and Rachelle Jean Louis, are starting their first full-time classrooms this week at Lantana Elementary School — the same school where they completed their training years as teacher's aides.Both said without the program, becoming a full-time teacher would have been very difficult.Mendez-Lopez, now an ESE teacher, said the program made it possible to keep working while finishing her degree — and pushed back on a misconception she said surrounds program graduates."I didn't have to take off for work, especially with how things are now, it's crazy expensive, so being able to have my bachelor's degree now, while still being able to work and get my experience was very, very great," Mendez-Lopez said."I feel like a lot of people have the misconception ok like you know they're not real teachers and this and that, we go through everything we have the state exams and everything we have to do all of that what a traditional teacher does is what we're doing," Mendez-Lopez said.For Jean Louis, a third grade math, science and social studies teacher, becoming a full-time teacher was not part of her original plan until she learned about the program."It wasn't in my mind at all. When I got the email, that. I've already been subbing two years'," Jean Louis said.Jean Louis said the program is well suited for people already working in education who want to teach but cannot step away from work to pursue a degree on their own."If you were already in an associate and you wanna teach, but you don't have the time to go to school and teach at the same time and make the money while you're teaching it would be a good candidate," Jean Louis said.The program is open to current School District of Palm Beach County employees who hold an associate's degree or at least 60 college credits, do not already hold a bachelor's degree, and commit to teaching within the district for at least 4 years after graduation.The Associate Teacher position is full-time and salaried at $33,711.60 per year, with benefits. Tuition is district-supported, though participants are responsible for some program costs and must reimburse tuition if they withdraw.The program's director said it is incredibly popular but also highly competitive, with a thorough vetting process.Employees interested in applying should notify their current principal or director. Application windows open in January 2027 and August 2027.

Moderate Democrat David Crowley won the Wisconsin primary for governor, defeating a democratic socialist who fell short of trying to deliver another win for progressives in a battleground state.Crowley, who is vying to become Wisconsin’s first Black governor, pitched himself as the candidate best positioned to win in November against Republican U.S. Tom Tiffany, who is endorsed by President Donald Trump.Crowley narrowly defeated democratic socialist Francesca Hong, who was hoping to ride the wave of recent victories by progressive candidates, including Abdul El-Sayed in neighboring Michigan’s U.S. Senate race last week.His win was the movement’s first major success in a purple state. It also fed fears in the party’s leaders that such candidates, farther afield and often carrying political baggage of past stances such as defunding the police, would struggle to beat Republicans and imperil the party’s hopes of recapturing control of the U.S. House.RELATED STORY | Flanagan, Klobuchar, Demuth win high-profile Minnesota primariesCrowley didn’t address supporters Tuesday night but was expected at a unity event later Wednesday.“Now, David is focused on bringing people together, earning the support of Democrats, Republicans, Independents, and anyone who believes Wisconsin is at its best when we work together and deliver results," Crowley's campaign manager Garren Randolph said in a statement.Hong’s loss in Wisconsin may have doused the momentum, but it’s far from snuffing it out. A democratic socialist coming close to victory in a battleground state sends a clear message: There’s unignorable angst among the party’s voters.“We have built something that will change politics forever,” Hong told supporters as the outcome of the race hung in the balance late Tuesday. “The work we have done will be remembered forever. I know we don’t have the final results right now, but what I do know is we are ready to keep fighting.”Her campaign manager Becky Cooper said after Hong conceded he race that she was “proud of the race we ran.”“Our team campaigned clean, our souls are intact and we really made meaningful change for the progressive movement,” she said.The Associated Press declared Crowley the winner once Hong’s concession removed the possibility of a recount in the exceptionally close race.Hong could have requested a recount since Crowley’s margin of victory was less than 1 percentage point. But because it was wider than 0.25 points, Hong’s campaign would have had to pay for it.RELATED STORY | Michele Tafoya wins Republican nomination in Minnesota Senate raceSanders and other top progressives stayed out of the Wisconsin raceProgressives had wanted to notch a clear win, but national progressive leaders, most notably Vermont Sen. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, sat out the race and did not endorse.The movement is not entirely aligned. Not all candidates are democratic socialists or have endorsements from Sanders, but they are often tilling similar voter anger with politics and the party: over military aid to Israel, the amount of money wielded in campaigns, the Trump administration’s immigration raids and the inexorable cost of daily life.In New York City in the June primary elections, two democratic socialist candidates and a progressive came out on top, booting two Democratic incumbents from Congress in the process. All three were backed by the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, himself a democratic socialist who framed the upsets as a question of electing “better Democrats.”Democrats in Wisconsin are hoping to capitalize on low approval ratings for Trump in a state he won in 2016 and 2024 to retain control of the governor’s office and flip both chambers of the Legislature to earn full control of Wisconsin state government for the first time since 2010.Wisconsin Democrats are hoping to unite after tight primary battleBoth Hong and Crowley said in the waning days of the race that they expected Democrats to come together and unite to defeat Tiffany, a congressman from conservative, rural northern Wisconsin.“Our ultimate goal is to make sure we don’t have a MAGA extremist occupying the governor’s office,” Crowley said Sunday.Democrat David Zimmerman, a 79-year-old retired industrial engineer professor in Madison, voted for Crowley on Tuesday. He said Hong’s chance of beating Tiffany in November “worries me a lot.”“I think she’s going to have trouble winning,” he said.The photo finish, and possible recount, is just the latest twist in a chaotic primary that saw two major candidates drop out amid scandals. Crowley had also dropped out in early July, but he got back in 10 days later with Gov. Tony Evers’ endorsement.Both of them crisscrossed the state in the final week, making the case that Crowley was the better matchup against Tiffany in a swing state known for close elections where independent, moderate voters often decide the outcome.Democratic socialist shook up Wisconsin race, fueled by national movementHong, a single mother and former line cook, tapped into Democratic anger with the party’s mainstream and Trump’s “Make America Great Again” movement.The 37-year-old known for sprinkling her comments with profanity and leaning into her edgy and sometimes humorous social media profile excited the liberal wing of the party. Hong called for free childcare and healthcare and a moratorium on artificial intelligence data center construction. But she also wrestled with her past support for defunding the police, saying at the race’s only debate that she would not support cutting law enforcement funding.RELATED STORY | Darline Graham advances to GOP runoff to replace late Sen. Lindsey GrahamShe also drew criticism for past social media posts in which she called for canceling Thanksgiving because “we should stop celebrating colonialism” and disparaged Valentine’s Day as “another day capitalism tells you how to show love.”Hong has since downplayed the posts as her attempt at making jokes.Chaotic Democratic primary saw candidates drop, come back inEvers’ decision not to seek a third term created an open race for governor that initially had seven Democrats file to run.Lt. Sara Rodriguez appeared to be making a move to consolidate mainstream Democratic support in July, but she dropped out in the middle of the month amid a campaign finance scandal. That led Crowley, who had dropped out a week earlier and endorsed Rodriguez, to get back in the race, this time with Evers’ backing.Former Lt. Mandela Barnes, who was seen as an early front-runner after nearly beating Republican U.S. Ron Johnson in 2022, bowed out less than two weeks before the election amid questions about inappropriate behavior.In one more twist, reporting the results of about 28,000 absentee ballots from Milwaukee was delayed until early Wednesday morning after a human error related to uploading the data, the city’s election leader said shortly before midnight Tuesday.

Martin County is reviewing its first agricultural enclave proposal under a new state law that could transform farmland across the region.Senate Bill 686, which took effect July 1, allows landowners to build homes and businesses on land designated as agricultural enclaves.WATCH BELOW: Florida's ag enclave law: Martin County reviews first applicationTo qualify, a property must be surrounded on at least 75% of its boundaries by existing development."The property has to have been in continuous use for bona fide agriculture purposes for five years prior to the date of an application," Martin County senior planner Jenna Knobbe said.On the same day the bill became law, the county received its first application for a 396-acre property known as Waterside. The site consists of three parcels located just west of Kanner Highway and south of Southwest 96th Street.Up to 1,200 homes were initially planned on the property.County staff recommended the enclave designation be denied."We reviewed the property tax records for the three parcels in the application, and we found that not all of the property was classified for agricultural purposes from the property appraiser's office," Knobbe said.The Waterside proposal was expected to be discussed at a Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, but the applicant asked for the item to be pulled from the agenda.The property owners declined to comment.How much pushback local governments can mount against the law remains unclear. A crash survivor who was pulled from the wreckage by Martin County firefighters returned months later to thank the crew who helped save his life. In the early morning hours of July 5, Taylor Cantin was the sole survivor of a devastating head-on crash on State Road 710 near Southwest Fox Brown Road , according to Martin County Fire Rescue. Cantin's truck suffered major front-end damage in the collision, leaving him trapped. Firefighters with MCFR's Station 24 say they responded quickly and extricated Cantin from the crushed vehicle. Moments after, LifeStar flew him to the hospital, where he was treated for traumatic injuries. Firefighters wrote that calls like this often end once a patient is safely transferred to medical care. They don't always get the chance to learn what happens next. See also: Large tire fire burns for hours near Belvedere Road But Cantin recently saw a Martin County Fire Rescue open house flyer and knew he wanted to return to thank the firefighters who helped save his life. Over the weekend, Cantin reunited with the Station 24 crew, creating an emotional moment firefighters said reminded them why they do what they do. For the crew, the reunion offered a rare chance to see Cantin beyond the emergency call and learn more about the person they had worked to rescue. Firefighter say Cantin is now on the road to recovery, and firefighters are cheering him on every step of the way.

Two severe animal hoarding cases in Martin County, just three weeks apart, are raising questions about whether Florida's laws do enough to protect animals. The first case unfolded at the 11500 block of Southwest Meadowlark Circle , where the Martin County Sheriff's Office rescued more than 100 dogs and cats. Weeks later, 36 dogs were rescued from a Palm City home on Alligator Street. Former Palm Beach County State Attorney Dave Aronberg said prosecuting these cases is difficult under current law. "The laws are not tough enough. It's too easy to escape incarceration if you engage in these horrible acts of animal cruelty," Aronberg said. He said Florida law does not classify hoarding as a crime on its own, which creates a barrier for prosecutors. "Hoarding by definition is not considered a crime under Florida law, so you need, I think, perhaps an anti-hoarding law to make it easier to prosecute these individuals [...] A specific anti-hoarding law that lowers the threshold for felony prosecution in severe multi-animal neglect cases," Aronberg said. Aronberg explained even when cases do rise to the level of criminal charges, the consequences are limited. As a misdemeanor, these cases typically result in no jail time. As a felony, some jail time is possible, but only if prosecutors can prove intent to harm. Martin County Sheriff John Buddensiek explained to Chief Investigator Jamie Ostroff in an interview last week that limited visible evidence of abuse prevented deputies from acting sooner on neighbor concerns in the 36-dog case. "Federal law, state law only allows you to go so far when you have any type of investigation," Buddensiek said. "If there was something that we could see from the outside that, you know, dogs are being mistreated, malnourished, not taken care of, we would absolutely get a search warrant and go in there." Aronberg said the stakes extend beyond animal welfare. Studies show animal cruelty can escalate to child abuse and domestic violence, making enforcement a public safety issue. "It's a gateway crime and that's why you need to treat it very strictly at the beginning. If you give it a slap on the wrist, you're just inviting more outrageous conduct that can hurt people," Aronberg said. One person is in custody as Martin County sheriff’s deputies investigate what authorities describe as a serious animal hoarding case involving Border Collies at a Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said deputies were serving a search warrant Monday at a home at 1245 SW Alligator Street. The search follows an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff’s detectives, who have been working to determine the scope of the situation and the animals' condition. "The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be Border Collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces. They're supposed to be white and black dogs, and they're solid black from the feces," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home so far, while deputies and animal services officers continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some of the dogs were skittish and hiding in the home. The woman who was arrested was identified as Paige O'Donnell, 62. She is being charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. "She, on purpose, kept these dogs trapped in this jail that she has behind us and abused them for lack of a better word," Sheriff Budensiek said. The conditions inside the home were described as extremely concerning. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said those conditions were making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals; they also said it was extremely hot and that she may not have had A/C. "It's just stacked with garbage. There's feces over every square inch of the house," Sheriff Budensiek said. "It's really sad to see them in such rough shape. But also I'm very happy to see them finally getting out," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor. Investigators and animal services personnel are continuing to assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. He said the dogs were running loose in the house and conditions in the house were very bad. "The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces," Sheriff Budensiek explained. Budenseik says O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges. She is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. She's supposed to be an animal breeder and she's gonna let the animals live like that? That's just, there's something wrong with her," said Kimberly Todd, another neighbor who lives on SW Alligator Street.

The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked in connection with the case and faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O'Donnell appeared before a judge on Tuesday. Her bond was set at $270,000 and she was told she could have no pets if she is released on bond. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. According to the arrest report, Monday’s search was the culmination of an investigation that stretched back weeks and drew on years of previous Animal Services contacts involving O'Donnell’s home. The latest investigation developed after authorities received renewed concerns about the number of dogs at the SW Alligator Street residence and their living conditions. In June, investigators observed the property from the roadway but did not make contact with anyone at the home. The following month, the Sheriff’s Office received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about conditions at the property dating back several years. On July 22, Animal Services responded to another complaint alleging more than 20 dogs were inside the home, that several deceased animals may have been in the garage, that the home did not have functioning air conditioning and that the dogs had not been allowed outside since 2022, according to the report. An investigator reported smelling a strong odor from the roadway and hearing what sounded like a large number of dogs, including puppies, barking from inside. O'Donnell later met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but, according to the report, would not allow investigators inside her home. The dog she brought to the meeting was described as having heavily stained, matted fur. Investigators said O'Donnell told them she had buried one of her dogs and named several others she still owned. Investigators also checked veterinary records. According to the affidavit, an employee at a local animal hospital said O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some that were brought in deceased. The employee also told investigators the dogs were frequently dirty. The arrest report says Animal Services had a long history of responding to complaints involving the residence, with roughly 20 related incidents documented from 2020 through this year. One 2020 investigation documented about 25 dogs and described the home as severely unsanitary, with feces and urine covering the floor. Investigators said one elderly dog was in such poor condition that humane euthanasia was recommended. Another complaint in 2022 led investigators to report 10 to 20 dogs being kept in a backyard covered in feces and flies. The arrest report says the home's air conditioning was not functioning and investigators observed feces inside the residence. At a follow-up inspection a week later, authorities said the home had been cleaned, the air conditioning repaired and three dogs surrendered to a rescue. In December 2023, investigators again responded to complaints about more than 20 dogs. According to the report, they detected an overwhelming odor of urine and feces and heard more than 10 dogs barking inside, including what sounded like puppies. Neighbors say they'd been raising concerns for years. "Very frustrating, very angry. They say if you hear something, say something, and we said something, probably over a hundred times," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor on SW Alligator Street. "When you called the Sheriff's Office, what did you tell them?" we asked her. "The dogs are in the house. They haven't been let out in years at this point. There's no A-C, 'cause the windows are open. When the wind blows, you can smell it," Weidenheimer explained. "What did they tell you?" we asked her. "As long as the dogs have food and shelter, it's fine," she said. Investigators said the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning changed during different contacts, and records did not always establish what happened to dogs she had previously said were in her possession. "Our interaction with her started back in 2020 when she was an AKC breeder and back then we had several calls for service that involved her maybe mistreating animals. Our Animal Control Officers came out at that point. She was not actually--didn't appear to be mistreating animals," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. According to the Sheriff, they learned from a previous animal hoarding case, that it's not always a smart decision to rush in and take all the dogs. "Unfortunately, 20 plus years ago, we experienced that here at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. We hit a house that had over 100 dogs in it. Seized them all, fostered them all out and then we were sued and lost the lawsuit. And worse than losing the lawsuit, we had to return those animals to the deplorable conditions which we took them from. So learning from our mistakes years and years ago, we weren’t going to do that again," Sheriff Budensiek said. In the days before the search warrant was obtained, investigators returned to the Palm City property and again reported smelling feces and urine. A neighboring resident also provided video that, according to the arrest report, showed garbage and debris piled high inside the garage while numerous dogs could be heard barking inside the home. Investigators also reviewed a photograph from a 2020 case showing at least 12 Border Collies in a room where the dogs and floor appeared to be covered in fecal matter. Based on those observations, prior complaints and O'Donnell’s documented history with Animal Services, investigators obtained a search warrant. When authorities entered the home Monday, the arrest report says the residence was unlivable and unsanitary, with floors covered in feces, urine and garbage and an air-conditioning system that was not working. Investigators said the dogs were severely matted with feces and urine and that portions of the walls appeared to have been repeatedly chewed. Thirty-six dogs were removed from the residence. Sheriff Budensiek separately described the conditions as extremely concerning, saying some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces that they appeared nearly solid black. Deputies and Animal Services employees wore protective clothing while working inside the house. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the dogs’ conditions and determine the full scope of the case.

Florida homeowners investing in expensive metal roofs are discovering that durability doesn't always translate to lower insurance premiums, with some residents facing higher costs despite upgrading their homes' first line of defense against severe weather.WATCH BELOW: Florida roof costs and insurance: What homeowners need to knowAnier Sosa installed a new metal roof to replace an aging shingled roof on his West Palm Beach home two years ago, expecting the premium upgrade to reduce his homeowners insurance costs. Instead, the investment had an unexpected result."It's basically the best roof you can put on the house; my premium did not go down, and when I asked them why, (they said) it's because your roof is too expensive, so it's kind of like a lose-lose," Sosa told WPTV.Metal roofs offer superior protection against Florida's harsh weather conditions, lasting up to 40 years compared to traditional asphalt shingles. However, the initial investment can exceed $50,000, roughly double the cost of conventional roofing materials.This price difference creates a complex insurance calculation that doesn't always favor homeowners who make the premium investment."A lot of people are moving towards the metal because it's a better roof," Sosa said, highlighting the growing trend among Florida homeowners seeking long-term protection.As Florida's insurance market continues recovering from recent instability, roof age and condition remain critical factors in determining coverage costs. With hurricane season here and insurance companies scrutinizing risk factors more closely than ever, homeowners need to understand how roofing decisions impact their premiums.Insurance companies typically require roofs to be 15 years old or newer to qualify for the best rates, according to Robert Norberg of Arden Insurance in Lantana."Fifteen typically is the thing. And some companies, it's all roofs they want 15 or newer to get the best rate," Norberg explained to WPTV.After the 15-year mark, premiums generally increase regardless of the roofing material. Recent Florida legislation ensures older roofs remain insurable, but typically at higher premium costs."Previously, the issue in Florida was homeowners policies were being canceled because of roof age," said Mark Friedlander of the Insurance Information Institute.New Florida laws now prevent insurance companies from canceling policies solely based on roof age, though higher premiums often apply to older roofing systems.Insurance experts recommend homeowners take proactive steps to maintain their roofs and potentially qualify for better rates."Realistically, with the weather conditions in Florida as they are between heat and the storms, you should have your roof inspected at least when it's 10 years old, have a professional inspect it because we call the roof the first line of defense," Friedlander advised.Regular professional inspections can help homeowners identify potential issues early and demonstrate proper maintenance to insurance companies, potentially qualifying them for lower premiums.While Florida's insurance commissioner previously suggested phasing out traditional asphalt shingles in favor of more durable materials, insurance experts say such a transition isn't practical given the significant cost differences.Traditional shingle roofs cost approximately half the price of metal alternatives, making them the more accessible option for many Florida homeowners despite their shorter lifespan in the state's challenging climate.Even as Florida's insurance market shows signs of improvement and stability, roof condition and age remain primary factors insurance companies evaluate when setting premiums.Homeowners considering roofing upgrades should consult with both roofing contractors and insurance agents to understand how material choices might impact their long-term costs.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The NCAA has announced it will assist the FBI as the bureau works to protect individuals from the rise of cyber-enabled crimes.The crimes themselves can result in "sextortion" which is a form of blackmail in which a person threatens to share private, sexual photos videos, or information of a victim to the public.The FBI has seen an increase in financial sextortion cases targeting minors, which has resulted in an alarming number of deaths by suicide.According to the NCAA, college athletes have become increasing targets of the cyber crimes. This is often attributed to their public profiles and standing within their community. Because of the increased visibility, the FBI says there is an increase in both exposure to targeting and leverage for what offenders believe they hold.Survivors of sexual exploitation can often be reluctant to come forward to law enforcement, which is why the NCAA says they hope breaking down barriers can make sure anyone who has or may become a target, knows they are not alone.Recently, the Association increased resources, research and monitoring for student-athletes after seeing a rise in online abuse and threats. They have launched an online tutorial which helps student-athletes understand what is classified as harassment, identify prevalence and patterns, and access tools for prevention and management. IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | SafeSport Center to begin publicizing names of people who go on its banned listThey also have a Sexual Violence Prevention Tool Kit to help support safer campus environments for all.“We hope to break down barriers, so law enforcement can help prevent further abuse and connect college athletes who may be targeted with the right support,” NCAA Vice President of Enforcement Jon Duncan said. “If we can play even a small role in preventing these crimes or getting justice or appropriate support for the people impacted by them, we will do everything we can to help.”If you or someone you know is being exploited, contact your local FBI field office, call 1-800-CALL-FBI, or report it online at tips.fbi.gov

Don Nelson, the second-winningest coach in NBA history who won five championships as a player with the Boston Celtics, died Sunday. He was 86.Nelson’s death was announced by the Golden State Warriors, one of the teams he coached. They did not release details.Nelson is one of two coaches in NBA history to have at least 250 wins with three different franchises — Milwaukee, Dallas and Golden State — also serving as general manager for all three franchises. He was a three-time coach of the year and made the playoffs 18 times in 31 seasons. He went to the conference finals three times with the Bucks and once with the Mavericks, never winning a title.Nelson introduced what is now known as the point forward, and his up-tempo style of offense created a buzz. He said the idea of shifting from the dominant big men of the 1970s to an offense focused on speed and the fast break came from his playing days under Celtics Hall of Fame coach Red Auerbach.“The league really hadn’t seen an offense like the one we were running, and the results were undeniable,” Nelson wrote in 2016 in The Players’ Tribune.Nelson said that “without Red Auerbach teaching me the mechanics of running the fast break, none of it would have been possible. He deserves all the credit for Nellie Ball, and for how fast the game of basketball is played today.”Nelson played 11 of his 14 seasons in Boston and was on five Celtics championship teams under four different coaches. He became an assistant coach in Milwaukee after retiring as a player, then took over after coach Larry Costello resigned 18 games into the 1976-77 season. Nelson coached the Bucks for 11 seasons starting in 1976 and won seven straight division titles.In Nelson’s second season, Milwaukee overcame a 29-point fourth quarter deficit to beat Atlanta 117-115 in regulation.“I coached the team as though I was still playing for the Celtics, while implementing a few of my own strategies,” Nelson wrote. “I knew I wanted to play unconventional basketball and use speed to my advantage.”His fast-paced offenses were probably best on display with Golden State in the “Run TMC” era featuring future Hall of Famers Tim Hardaway, Mitch Richmond and Chris Mullin. Nelson said he wanted them on the court at the same time.Nelson spent 11 seasons over two stints with Golden State. The first one was punctuated by a rift with rookie star Chris Webber, who was traded away a month into his second season. Nelson, demoralized by the trade, missed nine games that season due to illness and resigned under pressure three months later in February 1995.In between, Nelson was fired after less than one season in New York in 1995-96, then coached in Dallas for eight seasons, missing 21 games with the Mavericks starting in December 2000 to recuperate from prostate cancer surgery.Nelson’s son, Donnie, joined his father as an assistant coach with the Mavericks in 1998, later became general manager and remained with the organization until 2021. Together they persuaded 20-year-old German star Dirk Nowitzki to pass up European basketball and join the Mavericks. Don Nelson also developed Steve Nash into one of the NBA’s top point guards before Nash went on to win back-to-back MVPs with the Phoenix Suns in 2005 and 2006.At Golden State, Nelson’s “We Believe” Warriors led by Baron Davis upset Nowitzki and the top-seeded Mavericks in the first round of the 2007 playoffs in one of the biggest shockers in NBA history. In his final season as a coach, Nelson mentored rookie Stephen Curry in 2009-10.Nelson retired as the NBA’s career coaching wins leader with 1,335, just ahead of Lenny Wilkens’ 1,332. Nelson kept that top spot for nearly 12 years before close friend and now-retired San Antonio coach Gregg Popovich passed him in March 2022.Nelson was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2012. In 2025 he received the Chuck Daly Lifetime Achievement Award, presented by the National Basketball Coaches Association. Miffed that the Mavericks sent Luka Doncic to the Los Angeles Lakers in a blockbuster trade, Nelson wore a pair of Doncic’s signature Jordan Brand sneakers to the awards ceremony. He called the trade a “tremendous mistake.”Born in Muskegon, Michigan, Nelson attended high school in Rock Island, Illinois, and averaged a double-double in college at Iowa. He spent his retirement years living on the Hawaiian island of Maui and owned several short-term rentals on the island.

The people at the heart of a Jupiter business saw a need for back-to-school time and did something about it.WATCH BELOW: 'How blessed am I,' Mrs. Sue Townsend tells WPTV Anchor Ashley Glass “The coming out of their own pockets for school supplies is a common teacher thing, and I think we need to take care of that as a community and make sure they don’t have to pay," Michael S. of Britto & Herman Injury Lawyers said.WPTV Morning Anchor Ashley Glass was there as the team from Britto & Herman surprised third grade teacher at Jupiter Farms Community Elementary School Mrs. Sue Townsend, the winner of a social media contest they'd been holding for weeks. Townsend was gifted a basket of back-to-school supplies and funding to cover her classroom needs for the entire school year. “How blessed am I," Townsend said as she was overcome with emotion. "Honestly, how lucky am I, because there are so many good teachers.” Many people nominated Townsend through the social media contest, recognizing her as a "one-in-a-million" teacher known for inspiring kids to love to read. Glass covers the Jupiter area for WPTV. If you have a story idea to share with her, reach out via email at Ashley.Glass@wptv.com

The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in connection with an alleged animal hoarding case.Sheriff’s deputies rescued 36 dogs from a home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation. WPTV was told that the hoarding case involves Border Collies.WATCH BELOW: Dogs rescued after WPTV investigation into suspected animal hoardingMartin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the owner of the home, Paige O'Donnell, will face 72 criminal charges — 36 felony torture charges and 36 misdemeanor charges. She's accused of keeping animals enclosed without exercise and air. This comes after investigators said she never let the dogs outside — something that neighbors previously told WPTV had been occurring."The house is so deteriorated that about a foot and a half of drywall is gone. The furniture is destroyed, and the animals are in deplorable condition. The food bowls, the water bowls in there are covered in feces. The animals themselves, the dogs, which are supposed to be border collies, beautiful dogs, are covered in feces," Budensiek said.Monday's search warrant comes after WPTV's investigation revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about dogs and their owners.As law enforcement continued to respond, the homeowner built a fence and stopped letting deputies in — making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant.But after WPTV started asking the sheriff’s office about the house, they decided to look into it once again."We could not legally just run into the house based on what people said. We had to get our own information. So, days of surveillance out here, days of trying to negotiate with Paige… but she agreed last week to surrender one of the dogs to us," Budensiek said.The sheriff said that dog appeared to be malnourished, giving them the probable cause to execute a warrant Monday.Investigators on Monday were busy sweeping the house to make sure no dogs were hiding inside or dead.O'Donnell, a former AKC Border Collie breeder, had been living in this house and was taking a bath when they arrived to serve the warrant. Budensiek said she didn't come to the door, prompting them to bust it open.Budensiek applauded WPTV's efforts reporting the story, which kept the case on their radar."You keeping the story alive in your newsroom kept us engaged, kept us back out here and looking. It’s a collective effort," Budensiek said. Meanwhile, the 36 dogs rescued on Monday will be taken to the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast for care.

The Border Collies rescued from a Palm City home Monday where authorities found deplorable conditions are now receiving medical care, nourishment and grooming as they begin their recovery. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast said it has taken in the dogs rescued by the Martin County Sheriff's Office Animal Services Unit and is assessing their needs while determining the best path forward. Paige O'Donnell, 62, was booked in connection with the case and faces 72 charges: 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O'Donnell appeared before a judge on Tuesday. Her bond was set at $270,000 and she was told she could have no pets if she is released on bond. These innocent dogs were inhumanely kept in deplorable conditions, and while they are finally safe, their journey to recovery is just beginning, the shelter said. Authorities said 36 Border Collies had been removed from the home as of Monday, while crews continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was initially unclear exactly how many animals remained inside because some were skittish and hiding. See also: Homeowner in custody after 36 Border Collies found in Palm City hoarding case The shelter said its immediate focus is on the well-being of the dogs and asked for the public's patience as it works through the complex situation. It is also asking for donations to help cover the cost of caring for the neglected animals, saying the financial burden comes at a time when the shelter was already facing significant challenges. Every dollar makes a difference, the shelter said. Together, we can give these dogs the second chance they deserve. According to the arrest report, Monday’s search was the culmination of an investigation that stretched back weeks and drew on years of previous Animal Services contacts involving O'Donnell’s home. The latest investigation developed after authorities received renewed concerns about the number of dogs at the SW Alligator Street residence and their living conditions. In June, investigators observed the property from the roadway but did not make contact with anyone at the home. The following month, the Sheriff’s Office received a letter and photographs from neighbors documenting concerns about conditions at the property dating back several years. On July 22, Animal Services responded to another complaint alleging more than 20 dogs were inside the home, that several deceased animals may have been in the garage, that the home did not have functioning air conditioning and that the dogs had not been allowed outside since 2022, according to the report. An investigator reported smelling a strong odor from the roadway and hearing what sounded like a large number of dogs, including puppies, barking from inside. O'Donnell later met with Animal Services at a Palm City park with one dog but, according to the report, would not allow investigators inside her home. The dog she brought to the meeting was described as having heavily stained, matted fur. Investigators said O'Donnell told them she had buried one of her dogs and named several others she still owned. Investigators also checked veterinary records. According to the affidavit, an employee at a local animal hospital said O'Donnell had brought in numerous puppies over the years and that records showed roughly 38 adult dogs had been treated there, including some that were brought in deceased. The employee also told investigators the dogs were frequently dirty. The arrest report says Animal Services had a long history of responding to complaints involving the residence, with roughly 20 related incidents documented from 2020 through this year. One 2020 investigation documented about 25 dogs and described the home as severely unsanitary, with feces and urine covering the floor. Investigators said one elderly dog was in such poor condition that humane euthanasia was recommended. Another complaint in 2022 led investigators to report 10 to 20 dogs being kept in a backyard covered in feces and flies. The arrest report says the home's air conditioning was not functioning and investigators observed feces inside the residence. At a follow-up inspection a week later, authorities said the home had been cleaned, the air conditioning repaired and three dogs surrendered to a rescue. In December 2023, investigators again responded to complaints about more than 20 dogs. According to the report, they detected an overwhelming odor of urine and feces and heard more than 10 dogs barking inside, including what sounded like puppies. Neighbors say they'd been raising concerns for years. "Very frustrating, very angry. They say if you hear something, say something, and we said something, probably over a hundred times," said Kelsey Weidenheimer, a neighbor on SW Alligator Street. "When you called the Sheriff's Office, what did you tell them?" we asked her. "The dogs are in the house. They haven't been let out in years at this point. There's no A-C, 'cause the windows are open. When the wind blows, you can smell it," Weidenheimer explained. "What did they tell you?" we asked her. "As long as the dogs have food and shelter, it's fine," she said. Investigators said the number and identities of dogs O'Donnell reported owning changed during different contacts, and records did not always establish what happened to dogs she had previously said were in her possession. "Our interaction with her started back in 2020 when she was an AKC breeder and back then we had several calls for service that involved her maybe mistreating animals. Our Animal Control Officers came out at that point. She was not actually--didn't appear to be mistreating animals," said John Budensiek, Martin Co. According to the Sheriff, they learned from a previous animal hoarding case, that it's not always a smart decision to rush in and take all the dogs. "Unfortunately, 20 plus years ago, we experienced that here at the Martin County Sheriff’s Office. We hit a house that had over 100 dogs in it. Seized them all, fostered them all out and then we were sued and lost the lawsuit. And worse than losing the lawsuit, we had to return those animals to the deplorable conditions which we took them from. So learning from our mistakes years and years ago, we weren’t going to do that again," Sheriff Budensiek said. In the days before the search warrant was obtained, investigators returned to the Palm City property and again reported smelling feces and urine. A neighboring resident also provided video that, according to the arrest report, showed garbage and debris piled high inside the garage while numerous dogs could be heard barking inside the home. Investigators also reviewed a photograph from a 2020 case showing at least 12 Border Collies in a room where the dogs and floor appeared to be covered in fecal matter. Based on those observations, prior complaints and O'Donnell’s documented history with Animal Services, investigators obtained a search warrant. When authorities entered the home Monday, the arrest report says the residence was unlivable and unsanitary, with floors covered in feces, urine and garbage and an air-conditioning system that was not working. Investigators said the dogs were severely matted with feces and urine and that portions of the walls appeared to have been repeatedly chewed. Thirty-six dogs were removed from the residence. Sheriff Budensiek separately described the conditions as extremely concerning, saying some of the normally black-and-white Border Collies were so covered in feces that they appeared nearly solid black. Deputies and Animal Services employees wore protective clothing while working inside the house. The investigation remains ongoing as authorities assess the dogs’ conditions and determine the full scope of the case.

Before the lights dim and the curtain rises at the Raymond F. Kravis Center for the Performing Arts in West Palm Beach, another cast works behind the scenes. For 34 years, volunteer ushers have served as the welcoming faces that help make every performance a memorable experience for thousands of patrons.WATCH BELOW: 'I've been doing it ever since, and I love it,' Karole Crozier tells WPTV's Todd Wilson"I think the most important thing really is friendliness," said Carol Cooney, who helps oversee the volunteer usher program at the Kravis Center.Cooney seeks volunteers with a specific set of qualities that go beyond just showing people to their seats."The desire to help and being flexible because all kinds of things are happening. But I'd say friendliness is the number one thing that we're looking for," Cooney explained.The Kravis Center's volunteer usher program has been welcoming new faces for more than three decades. The very first class trained at the Dreyfoos School of the Arts before the Kravis Center even opened its doors to the public.This program matters now more than ever as live entertainment venues work to create positive experiences that bring audiences back to in-person performances in a competitive entertainment landscape.According to Cooney, volunteer ushers serve as the crucial first point of contact for theatergoers visiting the West Palm Beach cultural landmark."Of course, the show's the main thing, but the ushers are the first person. The volunteers are the first people that the audience interacts with," Cooney said. "They scan their tickets at the front door. They direct them to which floor they're going to, where they can find something to eat. They give them all the information that they need, so that's very important."Among the new recruits, two familiar faces represent the dedication that keeps the program thriving: Karole Crozier and Jason Smith, longtime volunteers helping to welcome the next generation.Crozier, a retired attorney, has been volunteering as an usher for 12 years at the Kravis Center."One of my good friends of probably over 25 years worked here in the founder's room, and she kept telling me about all these shows she was seeing. I said, what are you doing? I've been doing it ever since, and I love it," Crozier said.Smith, a teacher with the Palm Beach County School District, was inspired to volunteer by someone close to home."Behind every good man is a better woman. My wife has volunteered here for, this will be her 6th year, and 3 years ago I decided to also join her because she had such a great time doing it," Smith said.Becoming a volunteer usher at the West Palm Beach performing arts center requires more than just enthusiasm. The process involves several steps designed to ensure volunteers are prepared for their responsibilities."A lot of training, yes, yes. Actually, what we do is we have an orientation. We have a few orientations that gives them the general information," Cooney said.The selection process includes a brief interview, followed by two intensive days of training."It's a lot to learn. You have to learn the seating, the emergency exits. You have to learn where to direct people if they're in the wrong location. So, we have 2 days of training, and this might sound scary, but we also have a test at the end of it," Cooney explained.After passing the required test, volunteers can choose which day they want to work. With nearly 350 performances each year, the Kravis Center relies on a team of 400 volunteer ushers to keep every show running smoothly.The volunteer program represents a significant community investment in West Palm Beach's cultural scene, with hundreds of residents donating their time to support the arts.When asked what keeps volunteers returning year after year, Crozier said the answer is straightforward."You get to see wonderful shows, you meet a lot of very nice people, and you're in these beautiful surroundings, so who can complain about that," she said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

FORT PIERCE – Plans for a massive, new mixed-used development on South Hutchinson Island meet all existing state law requirements, Fort Pierce city planners have concluded, leaving local government no apparent leverage over the 43-acre project. Now it appears a grassroots challenge focused on state lawmakers could be the only remaining roadblock to a five-building, high-rise project designed to include housing, a hotel, commercial space and a marina. Kev Freeman, city planning director, told the Fort Pierce City Commission Monday that provisions of a state law known as Live Local allow the developer to sidestep some traditional density, height, zoning and land use standards because it promises to maintain at least 40 percent of the residential units as “affordable housing” for the next 30 days. While commissioners have expressed unanimous opposition to the plan for Causeway Cove, they suggested Monday that they have no options, save a questionable legal battle that could cost local taxpayers millions with no guarantee of a favorable outcome. Commissioner Michael Broderick, who along with Mayor Linda Hudson lives on South Hutchinson Island, observed that G. FLASH General Partners Inc., West Palm Beach, headed by Ashton DePeyster, a Palm Beach philanthropist and real estate developer, had done “an excellent job” of designing the plan to meet all the nuances of the state law designed to promote affordable housing. “I’m not going to listen to this being the salvation of the city (tax base),” Broderick said. “This is an improper development at an improper location. This is one of the worst written laws of this state. It’s going to be a nightmare out there (South Hutchinson Island) and this city has no control.” Freeman said the city already has consulted with regional and state transportation officials with concerns about the ability of Seaway Drive to accommodate the traffic counts and emergency evacuation plans the development will impact. He said the state has set requirements for driveways, turn lanes, a water taxi connection between Causeway Cove and downtown Fort Pierce, installation of a new public transit stop and providing shuttle service to the beaches. Those are not expected to present roadblocks to development. Live Local provisions require approval of Causeway Cove building heights that meet the highest levels found in commercial/residential buildings located within a mile radius of the proposed location. Freeman said that means state law allows the proposed structures to rise 200 feet. According to Freeman, the city has no choice but to “administratively approve” the plan–without public hearings–because it meets the state’s criteria. Commissioner Arnold Gaines, himself an attorney, said state law is preeminent over contradictory local statutes and he warned other members to “be careful about throwing out hope.” Commissioner Curtis Johnson Jr. attached blame to state lawmakers, saying, “We need to help our citizens understand this was done by people they put in (state) office” and he lauded city planners for “doing their job and doing it correctly.” Hudson said she agrees with community sentiment opposed to the plan. “Do I want a dense development like this? “The property should be developed but not this way.
