This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience. WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy. I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader. "It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good. The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America." And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members. But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride. After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next. But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication. As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades. As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

Martin County commissioners have put the brakes on a proposed ordinance that would change county regulations governing saltwater fishing, including where and when shark fishing could take place on public beaches. STUART — Martin County commissioners have put the brakes on a proposed ordinance that would change county regulations governing saltwater fishing, including where and when shark fishing could take place on public beaches. The proposed ordinance would repeal portions of the county code that regulate saltwater fishing because state law gives the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission authority over saltwater fishing and the taking and possession of marine life. Under the proposed changes, shark fishing would be prohibited on public beaches during hours when lifeguards are on duty and from fishing docks when boats are being launched or removed from the water. However, shark fishing would be allowed on public beaches during unguarded hours. That provision prompted strong opposition from residents who said allowing shark fishing during unguarded hours could increase the use of chum and drones to attract sharks near beaches frequented by swimmers, surfers and families. After hearing from residents, a marine biologist and county attorneys, commissioners voted unanimously to table the ordinance Aug. 5 and directed staff to further study the use of drones in shark fishing and consider whether additional local restrictions can be included. Assistant County Attorney Joseph Baron said the primary purpose of the amendment is to bring the county code into compliance with state law. “Florida statutes reserves the authority to regulate saltwater fishing,” Baron said. “The statute does, however, recognize an exception, allowing local governments to prohibit salt-water fishing on property owned by the county when necessary to protect the public health, safety and welfare.” The proposed amendment would repeal county provisions governing saltwater fishing that are preempted by state law. Senior Assistant County Attorney Melissa Pietrzyk explained that state law does not leave the county without any authority over activities occurring on local beaches. “There is a state statute that has essentially preempted the powers from the county to regulate saltwater fishing and that includes shark fishing,” she said. “Preemption meaning the state says, “County, you can’t control this anymore. The state has to control it.” Pietrzyk said state regulations prohibit chumming from a beach. Chumming generally involves putting blood, bait or other substances into the water to attract fish or sharks. “If a member of the public sees somebody chumming — throwing blood bait — they should be calling FWC so that person can get cited [and] potentially arrested,” she said. County Attorney Elysse Elder suggested that the ordinance could be rewritten to preserve more of the county’s existing language while specifically referencing restrictions already contained in state law. “The ordinance presented today does eliminate our regulation of shark fishing,” Elder said. “If the board wants, we can rework the ordinance to reference state law.” Why residents are concerned Several residents raised concerns about shark fishing during the meeting’s initial public comment period, even though the item was scheduled for later on the agenda. Stuart resident Douglas Adler led the opposition, arguing that eliminating portions of the county’s existing restrictions could create safety concerns at popular beaches. “According to this proposed amendment, we’re going to be striking out some laws and some rules, which really in my opinion are crucial to the safety of the public,” he said. Adler said the county currently prohibits shark fishing within 1,000 yards of a full-service public beach with a bathroom, shower and lifeguard, citing Stuart Beach, Jensen Beach and Bathtub Beach as examples. He also described an incident in late 2024 when he became caught in a shark-fishing line while surfing at Santa Lucia Beach. “I was caught in a shark fishing line that wrapped around my ankle [and] tore through my wetsuit,” he said. “It was one of the scariest moments of my life.” Adler said the fishermen had used drones to take bait several hundred yards offshore while remaining on the beach near the dunes. “If we’re going to be amending these rules, there should be some amendment regarding shark fishing using drones, which has become a huge problem on our beaches,” he said. Robert Wolf, a beach user, swimmer and surfer, also urged commissioners to maintain local restrictions. He said he has seen shark fishermen travel from South Florida to Martin County beaches, catch sharks and post photographs and locations on social media. “If the tourists find out these guys are coming to Jensen and Stuart and Hobe Sound Beach to shark fish and posting these pictures online, that’s not good for our local community, plus it’s not safe,” he said. Hutchinson Island resident Dottie Lancy described a similar situation near her home, saying shark fishermen had used multiple fishing poles, cameras and a drone to chum and attract sharks from the beach. The next morning, she said, a family with two young children set up umbrellas and entered the water in the same area without knowing what had occurred there the previous day. “State rules concerning this do not prevent local government from passing laws of their own restrictions in the interest of public safety,” Lancy said. Scientific concerns Marine biologist Justin Grubich, an avid fisherman and surfer who has researched shark behavior, also spoke in favor of maintaining stronger local restrictions. “I think keeping that language you have now is probably the prudent and best option,” he said. Grubich said chumming adds bait and blood to the water and can attract sharks to specific areas. “There’s accumulated scientific evidence that you can create problem sharks, like problem bears,” he said. “If you have blood-baiting or chumming going on in public beaches, you could get sharks used to coming to that area and eventually you’re going to have a wildlife interaction and that would be a tragedy.” He said recreational fishermen have ample opportunity to fish away from public beaches under existing rules. Commissioners seek more options After additional discussion and public comment, commissioners decided they were not ready to approve the ordinance as written. Staff was directed to further examine the use of drones in shark fishing and whether the county can retain or add restrictions at other public beaches while remaining within the limits of state law. The commission voted unanimously to table the ordinance and send it back to county legal staff for further review and possible revisions. Your comment has been submitted. The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in connection with an alleged animal hoarding case.Sheriff’s deputies rescued 24 dogs from a home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation. Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra — two strangers turned friends, brought together by an incredible act of courage.It happened last Friday around 5 p.m., when Spoelstra was driving along Southeast Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. Spoelstra made a turn, and suddenly a crossing arm came down on top of her car, trapping her on the tracks. Her car's antenna was caught on the crossing arm."I just went to turn, and as soon as I turned, the gate came down on the top of my car," Spoelstra said. "Then I realized that I was trapped; it was absolutely trapped."Dash cam video obtained from a nearby driver shows the close call. As Spoelstra tried to figure out what to do, she hoped someone would come to her aid."I know for sure somebody might come up from behind and help me, but you know didn't happen, and then all of a sudden I looked, and I saw my guardian angel coming over the track," Spoelstra said.That's when Baur, who was on his way home from work, spotted her car. Baur was in a rush at the time and calls the moment a lesson, because he was forced to slow down and help."I looked down on my phone looked back up, and I see Miss Debbie's car stuck on the train tracks with the arm down behind it," Baur said. "As she's trying to move, I was like holy cow, she's stuck in the tracks. She's going to get hit, so I threw it in parking and just took off running."As Baur ran toward her, he was tracking the approaching train. "As I was running, I was trying to see where the train was, how far off it was, how much time and also which side of the track it was on and when I noticed it was on her side of track, I'm like, OK, now or never, we gotta do this," Baur said.Baur lifted the crossing arm, allowing Spoelstra to reverse to safety — just before the train came through."It was incredible, and after he had lifted the gate off, I don't know how many seconds passed by and then the train came right by, so it was a close call. It was very close," Spoelstra said.For Baur, it was a close call, but the right thing to do. "Don't hesitate to help others when they're in need. I didn't sit there and think about it; if I sat there and he hesitated, who knows if I would've got there in time," Baur said. "People say she's a stranger to me, but she's a child of God just like I am."The two believe the moment was meant to be."I think it was a God thing, and for those if you don't believe, I don't know it was just a miracle," said Spoelstra.Spoelstra plans to take Baur and his family out for dinner as a thank you. She also noted an interesting connection — she has a 9-month-old grandson named Josiah. She says she will never forget what Baur did."He's an amazing individual. He is my guardian angel," Spoelstra said. "I'll never forget what he's done ever. I'm truly grateful and indebted to him."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

One person is in custody as Martin County sheriff’s deputies investigate what authorities describe as a serious animal hoarding case involving Border Collies at a Palm City home. The Martin County Sheriff’s Office said deputies were serving a search warrant Monday at a home in the 1200 block of SW Alligator Street. The search follows an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff’s detectives, who have been working to determine the scope of the situation and the condition of the animals. Authorities said approximately eight Border Collies had been removed from the home so far, while deputies and animal services officers continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was unclear exactly how many animals remained inside but that there was at least 29. The woman who was arrested was identified as Paige O'Donnell, 62. She is being charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. The conditions inside the home were described as extremely concerning. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said those conditions were making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals; they also said it was extremely hot and that she may not have had AC. Investigators and animal services personnel are continuing to assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. WARNING: DISTURBING IMAGES IN VIDEO BELOW Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek provided an update on the investigation. He said the dogs were running loose in the house and described the conditions in the house as deplorable. "It's just stacked with garbage. It's disgusting in there," Budensiek said. "There's feces over every square inch of the house." See also: Targeted in broad daylight: Boca Raton police search for multiple gunmen This case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home. Budenseik says O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges. She is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday.

The current view of the 7.84-acre property at 1780 Hartman Road owned by the not for profit Graceway Village. The City Commission voted unanimously Aug.3 to recommend to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit to enable GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct 36 dwelling units of temporary family housing on Hartman Road. The location of the 7.84 acre property at 1780 Hartman Road owned by the not-for-profit Graceway Village. The Fort Pierce City Commission voted unanimously Aug. 3 to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit to enable GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct 36 dwelling units of temporary family housing on the parcel. FORT PIERCE – The City Commission voted unanimously Aug. 3 to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit to enable GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct temporary congregate housing for adults and families on Hartman Road near the non-profit entity’s existing cafe and clothing boutique. The Planning Board previously heard the same requests on July 13, unanimously recommending approval. Assistant Planning Director Chris Suneson introduced the agenda item during the latest meeting. “This is a request this evening to review and approve an application for a major site plan with conditional use to allow adult congregate living facilities at 1780 Hartman Road,” he said. “The owner of Graceway Village Inc. proposes to construct a family shelter community centered on temporary housing with associated site improvements on 7.84 acres. The property contains two buildings [with] a combined 7,563 square feet that houses the applicant’s cafe program, clothing boutique and offices. The facilities were remodeled in 2009 and got some roofing permits in 2021.” Suneson proceeded to emphasize that the property’s underlying General Commercial Future Land Use enabled the location of just such a congregate living facility on the parcel as a conditional use. “The land development code sets forth several basic standards that adult congregant living facilities must meet,” he continued. “The most important of these is that maximum residential densities may not exceed the level determined by the comprehensive plan for general commercial. That maximum is 15 dwelling units to the acre, and with the proposed 36 dwelling units, the project has a density of 4.5 units to the acre.” The assistant planning director also described the site plan, which the applicant proposes to construct in three separate phases. “Phase 1 occupies 10,200 square feet and contains 10 dwelling units and support facilities,” he explained. “Phase 2 contemplates six additional buildings, comprising 17,800 square feet, with each building containing three dwelling units. The final phase is an expansion of the first facility with tri-plex cottages. Each unit will be about 990 square feet. It is an extension of the Phase 1 building, which would expand the family shelter building by an additional 6,300 square feet while also providing eight additional dwelling units and support facilities. Most of the site, 73.72 percent, will be left to open space. This project has been coordinated with the Technical Review Committee [and] all departments have supported the application.” Commissioner Michael Broderick was the first Board member to comment afterward and pose a question to Suneson. “If it was our job to just sit up here and rate the application based on need in the community, this would receive 110 percent approval,” he said. “However, that’s not what we’re here to do: We’re here to participate in a quasi-judicial hearing and determine facts. I reviewed this application in detail, site plans, everything. My only question is, is there any portion of the code that you’re aware of that this application does not meet?” “Not that I’m aware of sir,” Suneson replied. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky raised a question to staff. “Due to the future use of this, congregant living and the possibility of families, is there any provision for transportation at this location, a local bus set aside for transportation?” he asked. Suneson did not have a positive reply to him on that inquiry, however, instead describing other planned improvements on the parcel. “First off, I do not believe this is on a public bus route,” he said. “Second, the applicant has been required by St. Lucie County to provide a sidewalk in front of the property from north to south. Thirdly, if you’re talking about private facilities, I think there’s plentiful parking and driveway access in order to provide that type of service if it’s contemplated in the future by the applicant.” GraceWay Village’s contracted Landscape Architect Brad Currie also addressed the Commission. “Tonight, I’m very grateful to be representing GraceWay Village and their request to expand their existing facility,” he said. Broderick, this is one of the few projects that I’ve brought before the City Commission that I didn’t think you were going to have any comments on, and you did still.” The commissioner, however, admitted this particular development had no apparent controversy or protest. “We usually tend to have a little bit of a friction point, but on this, I think we’re all in agreement,” Broderick explained. “I actually think this is a great location for the project.” Currie did acknowledge some concerns expressed by Planning Board member Krista Story on July 13 about potentially locating so much residential in a commercial use. The applicant’s contracted Project Engineer Mark Landsman attempted to allay her fears that same night. “This is not a permanent residence,” he said during the prior meeting. “These are temporary residences to help people get back on their feet, so it’s not going to be a long-term resident.” While GraceWay Village CEO Chrystal Netherton did not come to the podium during the Commission meeting, she did addressed Storey’s concerns as well during the Planning Board meeting. “The first day of coming to Graceway Village, we are talking about your exit strategy to get into your own permanent housing,” she said July 13. “This really is an opportunity for this family to be self-sufficient [and] learn the skills. Many of them might only need a three-month stay with us.” After no member of the public came forward to comment on Aug. 3, Commissioner Dzadovsky made a motion for approval, with was seconded by Commissioner Broderick and passed unanimously. Florida's chief financial officer was in Palm Beach County on Monday, where he allocated money to local fire departments to help protect the health and safety of firefighters.He was joined by state Rep. Anne Gerwig, R-Wellington, and state Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Highland Beach, and West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James at West Palm Beach Fire Station 1 off North Dixie Highway.WATCH BELOW: Florida CFO holds news conference in West Palm BeachIngoglia awarded $1 million to local fire departments through the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program, the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program and projects that were appropriated in the state's fiscal 2025-2026 budget.According to the CFO's website, this program was established "to help protect the health and safety of firefighters and provide financial assistance to help departments, including volunteer fire departments, procure equipment, supplies and educational training designed to mitigate exposure to hazardous, cancer-causing chemicals.""Fighting fires today is much different than fighting fires 40 years ago," Ingoglia said. "When a structure burned, it was most likely concrete, it was wood. But today, when we ask our firefighters to go into burning structures, there's a lot more than just wood and concrete that are burning. there are things that are being lit up and being absorbed into the skin, into the eye, into the lungs of our firefighters, and unfortunately this has caused occupational cancers, and there's a higher risk of contracting and getting those cancers because of their profession."Funds allocated to local departments on Monday included:West Palm Beach received $19,635 Greenacres received $6,806 Highland Beach received $5,962 "The state of Florida's firefighter cancer decontamination grant is making a real difference here in the West Palm Beach Fire Department and at fire departments across the state," West Palm Beach Fire Chief Diana Matty said. "Whether it is for second sets of gloves, particulate blocking hoods, or on-scene cleansing wipes, or specialized washers, these are very important items that they're accenting in our budgets."The CFO said that the state still has $1 million available through the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program, and another $1 million available for the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program in this year's state budget, urging other fire chiefs to reach out to the state and apply."We must ensure that our fire stations and our firefighters have the equipment they need to keep Florida safe and their families safe," Ingoglia said.Also at Monday's news conference, Ingoglia took questions regarding the upcoming property tax amendment vote and some of the funding concerns that cities and first responders are discussing if the amendment passes.In support of the amendment, Ingoglia said that many county budgets have "exploded over the last six years.""I don't think there is any one of these counties that their budgets have not increased anywhere between 60 to 160% over six years," the CFO said. "They have been an enormous beneficiary of a historic amount of property tax revenue that has flowed into the coffers. Right now, what I'm worried about is an affordability issue here in the state of Florida."Ingoglia said he believes there is a lot of room to offer property tax relief and still fund the necessary items for our first responders."I understand the anxiety of sheriffs and police chiefs and fire chiefs around the state where they're saying that their budgets may wind up being gutted and they might have to lay off people. I don't necessarily agree with that, but I think that also goes to their distrust of the people who are holding their budget because across the state the vast, vast, vast majority of their budgets are controlled by their county commissioners or their mayors. I will tell you that there's more than enough money to go around," Ingoglia said.Matty said at the moment she did not have concerns over response time lagging or budget cuts regarding the property tax amendment.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office conducted a search warrant Monday at a Palm City home in connection with an alleged animal hoarding case.Sheriff’s deputies rescued 24 dogs from a home in the 1245 block of Southwest Alligator Street following a WPTV investigation. WPTV was told that the hoarding case involves Border Collies.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the owner of the home, Paige O'Donnell, will face about 40 charges — one felony and one misdemeanor for each of the dogs they rescued.This search warrant comes after WPTV's investigation revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020 — all related to concerns about dogs and their owners.This isn't the first time law enforcement in Martin County saw filth inside this house on Alligator Street.Last week, WPTV reported neighbors' concerns about this property, which included multiple calls to law enforcement over the years.As law enforcement continued to respond, the homeowner built a fence and stopped letting deputies in — making it hard to find probable cause for a warrant.But after WPTV started asking the sheriff’s office about the house, they decided to look into it once again."We could not legally just run into the house based on what people said. We had to get our own information. So, days of surveillance out here, days of trying to negotiate with Paige… but she agreed last week to surrender one of the dogs to us," Budensiek said.The sheriff said that dog appeared to be malnourished, giving them the probable cause to execute a warrant Monday.Investigators on Monday were busy sweeping the house to make sure no dogs were hiding inside or dead.Meanwhile, the 24 dogs rescued will be taken to the Humane Society in Martin County for care.

A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while attempting to cross a Port St. Lucie intersection against the pedestrian signal.The incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.Police say the preliminary investigation indicates the teenager attempted to cross Crosstown Parkway against the pedestrian signal, entering the roadway in front of oncoming traffic that had the right of way.The teen told investigators they believed they could make it across the street before an approaching vehicle reached them. However, the driver was unable to avoid striking the student.The 16-year-old sustained superficial injuries but declined medical transport at the scene. The teen's guardians were notified of the incident.The vehicle involved in the crash sustained minor cosmetic damage.In March 2024, a 15-year-old student was hit by a car making a right turn onto Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard and was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

A 48-year-old man riding an electric bicycle was killed after being struck by a pickup truck that fled the scene Sunday night in unincorporated Indian River County. According to the Florida Highway Patrol , the crash happened around 8:57 p.m. Sunday at the intersection of A 48-year-old e-bike rider was killed in a hit-and-run crash in Indian River County, and FHP is seeking the driver of the pickup truck.. FHP said the man, who was from Vero Beach, was traveling west on an e-bike in the westbound lane of 8th Street as he approached 14th Avenue. A light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind him in the same lane, investigators said. See also: 19-year-old identified as victim in deadly Boynton Beach shooting As the truck approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action and moved southwest, partially entering the eastbound lane. The truck still struck the bicyclist with its right side, according to FHP. The man was thrown onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane. FHP said the driver fled without stopping to provide aid or contact law enforcement. Investigators say the truck may be missing its right-side rearview mirror due to the crash. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead. Both eastbound and westbound lanes of 8th Street were temporarily blocked during the investigation, per officials. The crash remains under investigation, and troopers are seeking the public's help in locating the truck driver. Anyone with information about the vehicle or driver is asked to contact FHP.

Keeping track of your child’s school bus is about to get easier for families in Indian River County. The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child’s bus in real time. Parents can tap the bus icon in the district’s app to see where the bus is and get an estimated arrival time. The app will also send push notifications when a bus is running late. See also: Palm Beach County students return to school Monday with changes to free meal program Superintendent David K. Moore says the new feature is designed to give parents more peace of mind. You feel good as a parent, speaking as a parent, when your kid’s in school. But when they are on the bus, there’s just a little bit of angst until they get off that bus and walk in that front door, Moore told CBS12 News. Now parents have greater access when they are walking in that front door. The district is also adding another layer of security for students. Students will scan their school ID when they board the bus, allowing the district to keep better track of who is riding each bus. Moore says every school bus driver position is filled, meaning the district is fully staffed. The new tracking feature is expected to give parents another way to stay informed about their child’s ride to and from school especially on days when buses are delayed.

A tree-trimming job turned into a rescue Saturday afternoon in Stuart after a man became trapped about 40 feet in the air on a broken lift. Martin County Fire Rescue says crews were dispatched around 1 p.m. When rescuers arrived, they found the man stuck on the lift after it stopped moving up and down. He had been trimming trees in the area when the equipment stopped working. Because access for a ladder was limited, firefighters used a specialized rescue approach. Crews first removed nearby tree limbs. They then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to safety. Once he was back on the ground, paramedics evaluated him and determined he had minor injuries. The man declined transportation to the hospital. Martin County Fire Rescue credited the C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, Battalion 2, EMS 2 and EMS 22 for the rescue.

After a unanimous vote, the redevelopment of the old Sears space at Gardens Mall is moving forward, with a second vote expected in September.WATCH: Gardens Mall shoppers hear about the possible changesA new Dick's House of Sport and outdoor athletic field are one step closer to replacing the old Sears at the Palm Beach Gardens Mall, following a unanimous vote by local officials.The redevelopment has been years in the making, with plans dating back to 2011. Progress stalled multiple times along the way, including in 2017 when controversy over whether the retailer would sell guns brought negotiations to a halt. Dick's Sporting Goods has since stopped selling guns in its stores, clearing a major point of contention and helping move the project forward.Dick's House of Sport is a larger, experience-focused concept that goes beyond traditional retail. The location would feature rock-climbing walls, HitTrax batting cages, VR sports, and more, alongside an outdoor field for community events, recreational leagues, camps, and other programming. The development would also bring more retail space to the mall.Shoppers in Palm Beach Gardens said the project sounds like an exciting addition to one of the most popular shopping destinations in the city.Suzanne Schoen said:"It's a welcome change."John Schoen said:"I think that's an interesting concept."Amy Smith said:"I think it's a good idea. I mean, I want to try start playing pickleball. That'd probably be a good way to try it."Susan Sands said:"It's convenient, and then it's one-stop shopping. You roam the mall, and it sounds wonderful. So when will they begin it?"The project still requires a second vote in September before receiving final approval. But that vote seems like all but a formality at this point.

Martin County Public Schools has earned its second consecutive A rating from the state, marking a significant turnaround from seven years of B-level performance through innovative teaching methods that prioritize individual student needs over traditional classroom instruction.Superintendent Michael Maine announced the district's back-to-back A grades for the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years, crediting teachers and administrators who shifted away from whole-group instruction to personalized learning approaches that close achievement gapsThe transformation centers on what Maine calls a "game changer" — moving beyond traditional classroom lectures to small-group instruction tailored to each student's skill level."Instead of focusing on all whole group instruction, when the teacher is standing up in front of the classroom and just teaching the entire class, that's happening to introduce lessons," Maine explained. "But teachers are spending a lot more time individualizing the instruction for individual kids, pulling small groups, having smaller groups of students around the kidney table with them."Teachers now use education technology to track student progress in real-time and intervene quickly when students struggle. The data-driven approach allows educators to identify learning gaps and provide targeted remediation through small-group sessions.Martin County's success comes as Florida school districts face increasing pressure to improve academic outcomes while managing budget constraints and staffing challenges. The district's model demonstrates how strategic teaching methods can drive measurable results without reducing class sizes or significantly increasing costs.The district maintains regular class sizes mandated by state rules but transforms instruction delivery through centers and rotations that keep all students engaged at appropriate levels."The teachers are doing a really good job making sure that while he or she's pulling a small group of students, the other students are also in groups working on things that they need," Maine said. Students rotate through differentiated instruction centers, with some working on advanced materials while others receive targeted support.Martin County enters the new school year nearly fully staffed, with 29 teaching vacancies remaining as of early August, with 16 candidates already in the onboarding process. Maine expects the district to be "in a really, really good position" when students return August 10.The transportation department reports all 55 bus routes covered with 56 drivers available. Student enrollment remains steady at approximately 16,000 students, consistent with recent years.Construction continues at Murray Middle School following significant tornado damage that destroyed two buildings and severely damaged a third. The multi-phase rebuilding project will deliver new facilities including band and chorus rooms, agricultural education spaces, a media center, administrative building, and additional classroom space.Maine said certain construction phases will be completed by December 2027, with others finishing by August 2027, depending on progress.The district launched a flexible education program, dubbed "flex tech," offering families alternatives including single-course enrollment, partial schedules, and fully virtual learning through Martin eSchool."We really truly want to be the premier choice, the first choice for all of our families here in Martin County," Maine said. The program targets homeschool families who may need specific courses like advanced chemistry or algebra while maintaining connection to the district.Traditional high school students can also access evening courses or additional classes to enhance their academic preparation.Martin County continues expanding career and technical education programs that provide pathways to skilled trades and high-paying positions immediately after graduation.Programs include HVAC technician training, certified welding, construction trades, certified nursing assistant certification, drone flight operations, and entrepreneurship courses."We have a lot of students that might want to go into a skilled trade right after high school and earn a really high-paying earning job," Maine said.The district continuously evaluates and upgrades security systems, including additional cameras, updated crisis alert badges, hardened front offices, and perimeter fencing improvements."We're always going to be thinking first and foremost about the safety of our students," Maine said. "Anytime we see an area that needs to be improved, our safety and security team is quick to move in and get those fixed."Maine emphasized the district's commitment to living within its means while protecting classroom instruction from budget reductions."We are great stewards of their taxpayer dollars. We do not spend more than we bring in," he said. Any operational adjustments have occurred at the district office level or through efficiency measures, not classroom programs.Looking ahead, Maine set an ambitious target for Martin County to rank among Florida's top 10 school districts while maintaining its A rating."I want to be in the top 10 school districts in the state of Florida. We're working our way towards that goal," he said, emphasizing continuous improvement and professional development for staff.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

What started as a routine drive home from work turned into a terrifying race against time for Debbie Spoelstra. Spoelstra says she was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound Friday evening when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her trapped on the tracks. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments that followed. A train's horn can be heard as it quickly moved closer and closer to Spoelstra's red car as it sat between the crossing gates. Then, a young man runs toward her. I was pretty much frozen, Spoelstra said. Then I thought about getting out of the car, and then at that moment I saw Josiah running across the railroad tracks. That man was 23-year-old Josiah Baur. Baur said he left work late that evening and was on his way home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing. He was on the other side of the tracks when he saw what was happening. You only get a couple seconds to react, Baur said. He immediately ran toward the crossing. I just took off running, he said. Baur reached the crossing and lifted the gate with both arms, giving Spoelstra enough time to back her car away from the tracks before the train came through. He said he first looked to see where the train was. It was on her side, so I ran up and pushed up on it and released it just in time for her to back up, Baur said. Another witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car when she saw what was happening. She and the others in her car could only watch. We were just saying, Please, God, please, God, please, God,’ Dominguez said. We were frozen in the car. After the rescue, Dominguez took a photo of Baur and posted it on social media , hoping to find him and thank him for what he had done. It was very emotional, Dominguez said. We thought, oh, we just witnessed a miracle. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday. When they saw each other, they hugged. Spoelstra said she's grateful to Baur and believes things could have turned out very differently if he hadn't been there. You know, first of all, that a total stranger, would help another person, she said. I won't ever forget what he's done for me. He is a true American hero. Baur, however, doesn't describe himself that way. I’m just very fortunate that God put me right where I was, he said. "He's got a plan and we just got to follow it sometimes. We don't understand why." Witnesses say the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. See also: Foodborne illnesses are rising. What not to eat right now. Spoelstra says she reported the problem to Florida East Coast (FEC) Railway line and was told someone would come out to inspect the gate. The incident remains a powerful reminder of how quickly a dangerous situation at a railroad crossing can unfold and how one person's decision to act can make all the difference. For Spoelstra, there is also a personal connection that makes the story feel even more remarkable. She says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who came to her rescue: Josiah.

Today is the day parents and students have been waiting all summer for -- it's back to school day! And this year, Martin County students will have fewer bus routes this school year. The school board voted to cut three routes -- a move expected to save the district $255,000 a year. The district is reducing its bus routes from 58 to 55. But some employees are raising concerns about what that could mean for already-crowded buses. Superintendent Michael Maine says they aren't eliminating any stops and every bus will continue to operate within its legal capacity. Maine says the district is "right-sizing" its transportation system, combining underused routes serving the same areas. He says it doesn't make sense to have 16 or 20 students on a 77-passenger bus. According to Maine, some routes may take a little longer, but drivers will be paid for any additional time they work. None of the buses are going to be over capacity. We have laws that we have to follow. All of our buses have seatbelts, so, depending on the age, students have to be buckled up. We're never going to run a transportation route or a bus that's over capacity, said Superintedent Maine. While bus stops aren't changing, some students may see a different bus number this year. Maine says families should expect the usual first-week delays as drivers settle into their new routes. Parents can check your child's bus assignment in the focus parent portal or track their bus in real time using the MyReaxium app .

After two years of construction and renovations, West Riviera Beach Elementary is ready to welcome students back this week. The 60-year-old school has been completely transformed with a brand-new cafeteria, media center and updated play areas."With all the new technology and improvements at the school, it's going to be amazing and make my job so much easier," said Crystal Watson, a second-grade teacher at the school.WATCH: But the biggest change isn't just the shiny new facilities—it's how the school will operate. Unlike traditional elementary schools that serve students from kindergarten through fifth grade, West Riviera will focus exclusively on younger learners: pre-K through second grade.Principal Alicia Taylor believes this specialized approach will give students a stronger foundation in reading and math during these crucial early years."It allows my leadership team to really focus on those foundational skills that we need to make sure are rock-solid," Taylor explained.To fill the renovated campus, the Palm Beach County School District has realigned enrollment, moving pre-K, first, and second-graders from Dr. Mary McLeod Bethune and Lincoln Elementary schools. The district expects about 600 students to attend West Riviera this year.For Dr. Camille Long, the school's reopening holds special meaning. Long was once a student at West Riviera Elementary herself, and now serves as the North Regional Superintendent for the School District."I think it's a game-changer to have a state-of-the-art campus, and it's really exciting for the community," Long said.The school will officially welcome students and families when classes begin on Aug.

Buses will be picking students sometimes in the dark as Indian River County public schools begin the 2026-2027 year. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – Public school for all students in Indian River County begins on Monday, Aug. High schools open their doors to students at 7:20 a.m.; middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m.; and elementary schools at 9 a.m. That means many students could be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district’s strategic communications and marketing. “Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas,” she said in a statement. “We also encourage families to remind students to wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street.” Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation , as well as the district s Facebook and Instagram accounts. The School District and Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urge all parents/students/motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “There will be new challenges with drop offs, pickups, buses,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff’s office’s Facebook page. “All the schools are changing and we want to make sure your kids are safe. We’ve got measures in place to make sure that it is a smooth beginning to the school year.” “Please be patient as during drop off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors,” he said. “All of the safety measures we have in place will take some time for everyone to get used to.” School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: * Have the child arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early. * Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. * Teach children to stay well off the roadway until the bus comes to a complete stop. * Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. * Ensure backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: * Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street * Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. * Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: * Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. * Never play or run near traffic. * Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. * If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: * Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. * Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. * Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. * Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. * Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. * Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. “Motorists also play an important role by slowing down, remaining alert in school zones and neighborhoods, and always stopping when required by (state) law for a school bus displaying its stop arm and flashing red lights,” Schafte said. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. Lucie Wednesday released the emotional 911 call from a neighbor after a weekend murder-suicide at a home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. I think my neighbor was shot," the caller said during the 911 call. Authorities identified the victim as 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer for the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Investigators believe Ortega was shot and killed by her longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr., who then shot and killed himself. According to police, Ortega had recently ended their 30-year relationship, but the two were still living together while Varela searched for a new place to live. The neighbor who called 911 said she had been in her backyard with her children when they heard the gunshots. "You heard the gunshot?" the dispatcher asked. There was, like, six of them. And I thought it was maybe on the other side of the street because we do have people that shoot off fireworks all the time. But this one made my house rattle," the caller said. When asked if she saw the gun, the caller responded, "No. We heard it a couple of minutes ago, and I made my kids come inside because it sounded really, really close." The caller said she did not know her neighbors' names but mentioned she often heard them yelling. "Her and her husband were fighting?" the dispatcher asked. "I don't know if they're fighting. They're just always cursing at each other," the caller said. Police arrived at the scene and began their investigation, which they are calling a murder-suicide. Big Brothers Big Sisters of Palm Beach and Martin Counties is preparing for the return of Big Taste of Martin County, a food and spirits event scheduled for Oct. 6 at Atlantic Aviation in Stuart.Organizers say the annual fundraiser brings together local restaurants, chefs and community partners to support mentoring programs for children across the Treasure Coast. The energy was contagious at the annual Glades Teacher Appreciation Breakfast, where educators gathered to celebrate their dedication before welcoming students back to school Monday."This event is fantastic," said Jamie Wyatt, Deputy Superintendent for Palm Beach County Schools. "The Glades Teacher Appreciation Breakfast is one of the most exciting, fun events of the year."WATCH:The celebration highlighted the commitment of local educators, including one remarkable teacher who received a standing ovation for her extraordinary milestone— Rita Schoenfeld, celebrating 51 years in the profession, 50 of those at Glades Day School. For Schoenfeld, teaching has been more than a career—it's been a calling driven by desire to make a difference. You know, knowing that you want to do something for kids and work with the kids," Schoenfeld said.When the room erupted in applause for her milestone achievement, Schoenfeld was both grateful and humble. "It was very cool, but it was embarrassing also," Schoenfeld said and laughed. "You look around and you think, holy mackerel, there's a whole bunch of people that are doing the same thing that I've done, and hopefully they'll keep at it."Schoenfeld's five decades at Glades Day School have created something truly special, as she's now teaching children whose parents, and sometimes grandparents, were once her students. "In teaching as long as I have, I have students that I taught their parents and even sometimes it's sad to say I taught their grandparents," she said. "So it's family, is really what it comes down to."School Board member Marcia Andrews, who brings her own 51 years of education experience including 16 years on the school board, emphasized the importance of recognizing teachers before the school year begins."Teachers work every day, morning, noon, and night, 24/7, to make sure children are successful," Andrews said. "It's certainly not for money. It's about your heart, your desire to see every child succeed."For educators just starting their careers, Schoenfeld offers both practical and heartfelt guidance. That's really the first thing," she said. "And then know that you have a possibility of making a difference in a student's life. Treat them like your own kid. You know, when they need to be corrected, you correct them. When they need the love, you love them."The event showcased the unique spirit that defines education in the Glades area, where teachers and community members work together as partners in student success. "There's greatness out here, and the teachers and the community they rally because they are excited about what they're doing," Wyatt explained. "They believe in what they're doing. They believe in the students. The community wraps their arms around, and we partner together for education."Schoenfeld echoed this sentiment about the teacher appreciation event, noting how it brings together educators who might not otherwise see each other during the school year. "It's awesome because a lot of times we don't get to see each other in the different schools," Schoenfeld said. "As teachers, you don't get a lot of recognition. Sometimes you get all the blame, and now with the (Hand Foundation) giving the kudos to the teachers from the individual schools—it's awesome."District leadership expressed confidence in the year ahead for Palm Beach County's A-rated school district. "We want to let our families and our students know that we're ready for them on Monday," Wyatt said. "We're excited to see them. The teachers have been preparing all week, getting their classrooms set up, and just looking forward to another fantastic school year."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The state then waits at least two years to attempt to contact the owners before setting items up for auction.Any proceeds from sold items are still set aside for the rightful owners.For more information about the Florida Unclaimed Property Auction, click here.

The aerial and location map for the 6.89-acre property home to the current Westside Racquet Club whose new owner had requested a conditional use permit and Phase 1 site plan approval for a significant remodeling and expansion project. The aerial and location map for the 6.89-acre property home to the current Westside Racquet Club whose new owner had requested a conditional use permit and Phase 1 site plan approval for a significant remodeling and expansion project. VERO BEACH – The Indian River County Commission approved the special exception use and Phase 1 site plan Aug. 4 for the renovation and expansion of the existing Westside Racquet Club, a 1970s-era facility that in recent years has fallen into disrepair. The Planning Zoning Commission previously heard the same requests on June 11, voting unanimously to recommend approval but adding a special condition of approval due to concerns about potential noise pollution and light infiltration onto adjacent property owners. Senior Planner Kelly McKinley introduced the agenda item during the latest meeting. “Before you today is the Westside Racquet Club’s special exception use and site plan approval request to expand the existing facility with the intent of restoring it, as well as providing additional enhancements,” she said. “The subject parcel is 6.89 acres located east of 43rd Avenue Southwest, north of 6th Lane Southwest and south of Fifth Place Southwest. The special exception use will cover all four phases, [but] only Phase 1 is before you for site plan approval at this time. The additional phases will subsequently be approved.” McKinley proceeded to provide further details on the color-coded phasing plan for the property, which currently houses a small, existing racquet court building and eight tennis courts. “The white [Phase 1] is going to restore the existing eight tennis courts, construct four new padel courts and construct associated site improvements like utilities, stormwater, parking and landscaping,” she continued. “The green will restore the existing 2,400-square-foot clubhouse and construct two additional padel courts. Phase 3, the pink, will include the pool house as a clubhouse amenity and construct four pickleball courts. Phase 4, the blue, will consist of two additional tennis courts.” McKinley also described the proposed stormwater improvements and landscaping plan, which will include a stormwater pond along the southern part of the project and a swale. Additional landscaping will include a 20-foot buffer along 43rd Avenue Southwest and a 30-foot-Type B landscape buffer around the other three perimeters. Foundation plantings will be installed around the pool and the existing clubhouse building. After she recommended approval and described the P Z Commission’s additional condition of approval, Vice-Chairwoman Laura Moss posed her first question and initial concerns to staff. “I’m just confirming what they’re adding,” she said. “So, it’s four padel courts, a pool and four pickleball courts. Is that reason why this is a special exception?” “The site is zoned RS-3,” McKinley replied. “Within that zoning district, the use itself is the special exception.” Chairman Deryl Loar chimed in with another important fact. “I think it’s also because you’re going over a threshold and you’re expanding the existing use by more than 10 percent,” he said. Vice-Chairwoman Moss then addressed the heart of her concern, the fact that all subsequent phases would be administratively approved and not require any further public hearings. “I think to vote on this, we’re in effect being asked operationally to vote in the blind because I don’t know what it’s going to be in totality,” she continued. “Once we grant the special exception, basically anything goes [and] we lose control of it. On top of that, if we change it, that land maintains the special exception designation no matter who owns it.” Vice-Chairwoman Moss acknowledged that she’d viewed the June Planning Zoning Commission hearing and lamented what she viewed as a lack of technical expertise for the concerned neighboring residents. She also bemoaned the fact the applicant’s representative was not present that day. “Pickleball is very loud, [and] somebody made a really good point,” she said of the earlier hearing. “The noise ordinance only applies when it’s a sustained level of sound. Pickleball’s not a sustained level of sound, so they really don’t have protection in terms of the noise. It was mentioned that the lighting would end up in peoples’ backyards. A privacy fence was suggested. I’m not comfortable that this was thoroughly addressed and will not adversely affect the public interest.” While Chairman Loar responded by insisting her comment about losing control was “not an exact description of our professional staff,” Deputy County Attorney Susan Prado provided a legal opinion of the exact task before commissioners that morning. An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Jacob Craig will perform MacDowell s Piano Concerto No. 2 with the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra during Landscapes Legends. For tickets,visit SpaceCoastSymphony.org or call toll-free (855) 252-7276. VERO BEACH – The Space Coast Symphony Orchestra explores magic and myth during Landscapes Legends on Sunday, Aug. The concert at the Community Church of Vero Beach, 1901 23rd Street, opens with Dukas’ The Sorcerer’s Apprentice, famously depicted in Disney’s Fantasia. Guest conducted by Brevard music educator Patrick Phillips, the vivid, 11-minute orchestral tone poem musically narrates a tale of magic gone wrong. The world premiere performance of Kenneth Fuchs’ Cloud Slant shifts the focus inward, capturing light, motion and atmosphere. A Fuchs album recorded with the London Symphony Orchestra for Naxos won the 2018 GRAMMY Award for Best Classical Compendium. Landscapes Legends continues when Vero Beach music and arts leader, Dr. Jacob Craig joins the orchestra for Edward MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2, a deeply romantic and expressive work in three-movements. Composed in 1885, the work has the distinction of being the first major piano concerto written by an American. Renowned pianist, Van Cliburn chose MacDowell’s Piano Concerto No. 2 at age 18 for his professional orchestral debut. Landscapes Legends concludes with Pines of Rome, the world famous 1924 orchestral tone poem by Italian composer, Ottorino Respighi. Lasting about 22 minutes, it dramatically depicts four different locations around Rome framed by iconic pine trees. Ancient streets, distant echoes, and the sound of a nightingale are sculpted into one of the greatest works of the orchestral repertoire. $35 tickets for Landscapes Legends are available through the orchestra website at www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org or at Marine Bank Trust branches. Tickets at the door are $40. Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about Landscapes Legends, call 855-252-7276 or visit www.SpaceCoastSymphony.org . Collins, Conductor and Artistic Director for the Space Coast Symphony Orchestra, describes what makes the Landscapes Legends concert special. “A good orchestral concert can make the invisible feel real,” said Collins. “The works on this program aren’t just pretty melodies with dramatic flourishes – they create places, characters, atmospheres, and emotional landscapes for a truly one-of-a-kind musical experience.” Concertgoers aged 18 and under or with a college ID are admitted free to every SCSO concert. For more information about the Space Coast Symphony s 2026-27 season or the Symphony for Everyone discounted ticket program, visit SpaceCoastSymphony.org or call (855) 252-7276. The Florida Supreme Court is poised to decide whether Citizens Property Insurance's controversial arbitration system is constitutional, a ruling that could have major implications for homeowners across the state.WATCH BELOW: 'Big ramifications if the Supreme Court decides in favor of Citizens,' Aaron Bass tells Investigative Reporter Kate HusseyThe development comes after months of WPTV investigative reporting into the state-backed insurer’s mandatory arbitration process, which requires certain policyholders to resolve insurance disputes outside traditional court and before a single administrative law judge.Documents WPTV obtained show those judges are paid through contracts funded by Citizens.Attorneys challenging the system argue that arrangement creates an inherent conflict and strips homeowners of their constitutional right to a jury trial.“This is the textbook legal example of a thumb on the scale of the outcome here,” insurance attorney Aaron Bass told WPTV.WPTV has interviewed at least five attorneys who have raised concerns about the program.Emails WPTV obtained in a public records request show State Senator Erin Grall wrote to the state-run insurer, questioning its constitutionality, and Citizens' authority to enforce it, before the arbitration requirement took effect.A WPTV review of one year of Citizens final hearing decisions also found judges ruled in Citizens’ favor in 99% of the cases examined.“It’s unprecedented,” Bass said. “I’m not aware of anything anywhere else in the country where this occurs.”The constitutional fight escalated in May, when Miami-Dade Circuit Judge Milton Hirsch refused to force a Citizens policyholder into arbitration.“Citizens policyholders — and Floridians generally — are entitled to ask — indeed, cannot help but ask — why they must be stripped of their right to trial by jury — as a condition of insuring their homes,” Hirsch wrote.Citizens appealed.The Florida Supreme Court has now agreed to take up the case."Big ramifications if the Supreme Court decides in favor of Citizens," said Bass, who added the implications could extend well beyond Citizens policyholders.Last year, Florida lawmakers considered legislation that would have allowed other property insurers to require similar arbitration.If the Supreme Court ultimately sides with Citizens, Bass believes the decision could open the door for more Florida homeowners to have insurance disputes decided through arbitration systems funded by the insurers they are challenging."There would be no reason to have property insurance at that point. The constitutional battle comes as another Citizens policyholder is separately challenging what happened in her own arbitration case. The 12 elementary schools for 2026-27 will open at 7:40 a.m.; all four high schools, including Indiantown High School charter school, start at 8:30 a.m.; and five middle schools begin at 9:20 a.m. With the elementary schools, that means many students would be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for Jensen Beach Elementary students who meet the bus at the stop at Southeast Aster Lane and Southeast Astorwood Terrace at 6:10 a.m., according to Martin School District’s bus transportation schedules. As a result, the School District urges all parents/students/motorists to be extra cautious and to observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “As we prepare to welcome students back on Aug. 10, Martin County School District encourages families to take a few moments to review school bus safety with their children,” Kirstie Germaine, coordinator of public information community relations, said in a statement. “Students should arrive at their bus stop 5-10 minutes before their scheduled pickup time, remain off the roadway while waiting, and follow the bus driver’s instructions when boarding, exiting, or crossing the street,” she said. “We also encourage families to review their child’s bus stop location and schedule before the first day of school and ensure younger students have appropriate supervision at the bus stop. We are grateful for the partnership of families, our transportation staff, and local law enforcement agencies as we work together to keep students safe throughout the school year. The Martin County School District’s transportation page (www.martinschools.org/page/transportation) gives information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: • Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. • Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. • Ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: • Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street • Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. • Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: • Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. • Never play or run near traffic. • Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. • If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: • Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. • Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. • Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. • Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. • Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. • Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the web site. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend your driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. As the August election approaches, tensions are rising between the two political camps as incumbent Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steve Giordano in the race for mayor. So far, tensions have escalated beyond the polls, with campaign signs being removed or moved. The incidents prompted the Port St. Lucie Police Department to launch investigations into two separate cases involving campaign signs, one of which led to a confrontation. The first incident occurred Wednesday, Aug. 5, near the intersection of Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thanksgiving Avenue. PSLPD said one of its sergeants noticed mayoral candidate Steve Giordano and an unidentified woman near political campaign signs. An investigation was launched after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard. Investigators reviewed surveillance footage that showed Giordano and the woman approaching campaign signs displayed in the yard. PSLPD said the video then showed the woman removing a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before another sign was placed in the yard. PSLPD said officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement and authorization of the campaign signs. The August 7th Incident During the overnight hours Friday, Aug. 7, Giordano told CBS12 News that he and his campaign manager were putting up signs near Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thornhill Drive. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin. The two can be heard shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission. See also: South Florida Wendy's worker's lunch break sparks viral friendship PSLPD said investigators learned that one homeowner had given permission for one campaign sign to be placed on the property, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, told members of the opposing campaign they could also place a sign there. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. PSLPD said investigators are reviewing the video. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged. Lucie Police Department acknowledges that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process. As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy," PSLPD said in a news release. Following the incident, Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement: My campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of my campaign signs at different locations over several days. Signs were taken down without permission and replaced with Mr. In response, my husband simply restored the signs that had been removed. At no time were my opponent's signs stolen or damaged, one small sign was temporarily moved and put back in the ground. Lucie Police Department is investigating reports related to political campaign signs that occurred this week. We fully support a thorough, impartial review of the facts. I remain focused on the issues that matter to the city and will continue running a positive, transparent campaign. According to police, officers responded to the reported incidents, documented the scenes, collected available evidence and began interviewing those involved. Detectives are reviewing physical evidence, speaking with witnesses and verifying statements provided to investigators. The investigations remain active. Police said all available facts and evidence will be reviewed before any determination is made. Lucie Police Department said it remains committed to conducting a fair, impartial and fact-based investigation.
