What started as a routine drive home from work turned into a terrifying race against time for Debbie Spoelstra. Spoelstra says she was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound Friday evening when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her trapped on the tracks. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments that followed. A train's horn can be heard as it quickly moved closer and closer to Spoelstra's red car as it sat between the crossing gates. Then, a young man runs toward her. I was pretty much frozen, Spoelstra said. Then I thought about getting out of the car, and then at that moment I saw Josiah running across the railroad tracks. That man was 23-year-old Josiah Baur. Baur said he left work late that evening and was on his way home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing. He was on the other side of the tracks when he saw what was happening. You only get a couple seconds to react, Baur said. He immediately ran toward the crossing. I just took off running, he said. Baur reached the crossing and lifted the gate with both arms, giving Spoelstra enough time to back her car away from the tracks before the train came through. He said he first looked to see where the train was. It was on her side, so I ran up and pushed up on it and released it just in time for her to back up, Baur said. Another witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car when she saw what was happening. She and the others in her car could only watch. We were just saying, Please, God, please, God, please, God,’ Dominguez said. We were frozen in the car. After the rescue, Dominguez took a photo of Baur and posted it on social media , hoping to find him and thank him for what he had done. It was very emotional, Dominguez said. We thought, oh, we just witnessed a miracle. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday. When they saw each other, they hugged. Spoelstra said she's grateful to Baur and believes things could have turned out very differently if he hadn't been there. You know, first of all, that a total stranger, would help another person, she said. I won't ever forget what he's done for me. He is a true American hero. Baur, however, doesn't describe himself that way. I’m just very fortunate that God put me right where I was, he said. "He's got a plan and we just got to follow it sometimes. We don't understand why." Witnesses say the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. See also: Foodborne illnesses are rising. What not to eat right now. Spoelstra says she reported the problem to Florida East Coast (FEC) Railway line and was told someone would come out to inspect the gate. The incident remains a powerful reminder of how quickly a dangerous situation at a railroad crossing can unfold and how one person's decision to act can make all the difference. For Spoelstra, there is also a personal connection that makes the story feel even more remarkable. She says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who came to her rescue: Josiah.

A tree-trimming job turned into a rescue Saturday afternoon in Stuart after a man became trapped about 40 feet in the air on a broken lift. Martin County Fire Rescue says crews were dispatched around 1 p.m. When rescuers arrived, they found the man stuck on the lift after it stopped moving up and down. He had been trimming trees in the area when the equipment stopped working. Because access for a ladder was limited, firefighters used a specialized rescue approach. Crews first removed nearby tree limbs. They then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to safety. Once he was back on the ground, paramedics evaluated him and determined he had minor injuries. The man declined transportation to the hospital. Martin County Fire Rescue credited the C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, Battalion 2, EMS 2 and EMS 22 for the rescue.

A petition with nearly 800 signatures is mounting against a proposal that could transform Fort Pierce's Museum Pointe — a public waterfront park along the Indian River Lagoon — into a mega-yacht marina.WATCH BELOW: 'We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center,' Erick Gill tells WPTV's Kate HusseyThe proposal is part of the Port of Fort Pierce's updated 2026 Master Plan. It calls for redeveloping Museum Pointe, which is currently home to a history center, public waterfront access, fishing piers, and green space, into a facility featuring floating docks, a multi-story marina, an event center, a waterfront restaurant, and a clubhouse.Opponents fear the plan could privatize one of the city's most treasured public spaces."Giving public land to private folks," said Terry Howard, a volunteer at the History Center at Museum Pointe Park. Howard contacted WPTV's Kate Hussey after learning about the master plan. "Development is just rampant in Florida, and at least we can fight for this one particular area and keep it green," Howard said.He said the loss of public waterfront access is a concern — but his biggest worry is the fate of the museum itself."This is the place where this museum should be, right here on this Museum Pointe," said Howard. For more than 50 years, the museum has preserved artifacts from Florida's Native American tribes, Spanish shipwrecks, and more. The master plan's renderings place the proposed marina clubhouse exactly where the museum stands today."Basically taking away a gem — a public gem that belongs to the people and replacing it with a facility for mega yachts," Howard said. "We're trying to keep this area as it is." St. Lucie County spokesperson Erick Gill said the museum's future is not in jeopardy if the project moves forward."Staff's intent was never to close the museum," Gill said. "We have been talking for years about better locations for that history center; it is on a barrier island, in a flood zone, so it may not be the best place to store artifacts."Gill said the museum and its collection would be preserved and relocated if the project proceeds. He added that the master plan is designed to expand economic development, create jobs, and generate county revenue."I think all local governments are looking for a way to generate revenue, so we can continue to lower the taxes for St. Lucie County residents and generate revenue from economic development, and we already have dock space there," Gill said."Anything that's going to be a positive economic driver for the City of Fort Pierce, I'm going to embrace completely," Fort Pierce City Commissioner Michael Broderick added. Broderick said the city will have the final say on whether the project moves forward, and that commissioners will have to weigh economic benefits against preserving waterfront access.When asked which priority — economic development or waterfront access — would take precedence, Broderick said the answer is not simple."That's the challenging question right there. I believe that we can strike a balance," Broderick said. "We always have to be careful not to eliminate public access to the waterway. Period." For Howard, the stakes go beyond the present."This is a gem that once we develop around it, it'll never be replaced again," Howard said. "The museum has been here since the 1970s. If they want to boat docks for mega yachts, they can do it someplace else." St. Lucie County leaders are scheduled to discuss the proposal and its current status at a 9 a.m. Lucie County Commission Chambers.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested by the U.S. Marshals Service at his home in Mechanicsville, Va., on Aug. 4 as the fourth suspect in a St. Lucie County case involving the death of a 3-month-old infant in August 2025. LUCIE COUNTY -- A fourth arrest was made on Aug. 4 in the case of a 3-month-old child who died in August of 2025 in what St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office investigators called one of the worst cases of child neglect they have seen. Jason Gunter, 45, was arrested at his home in Mechanicsville, Va., by the U.S. Marshals Service on an outstanding warrant obtained by St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office detectives. Gunter is believed to be the natural father of the infant, whose name the sheriff’s office has not released. Gunter was charged with felony child neglect with great harm for his alleged role in the circumstances surrounding the child’s death, according to the sheriff’s office Facebook posting. Gunter is being held without bond in the Hanover County Jail, awaiting extradition to St. Lucie County, according to the Hanover County jail web site. Also charged in the case in St. Lucie County are the biological mother, Nicole Marie Maxwell, 27; the child’s grandfather, Robert Arthur Maxwell, 61; and Vikki Nicole Koon, 38, Robert Maxwell’s girlfriend, each on charges of aggravated manslaughter of a child and aggravated child abuse. Lucie County Jail on $1.5 million bond each, according to the jail web site. 20, 2025, deputies, detectives, and crime scene investigators with the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office responded to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce after a 3-month-old child was brought to the emergency room by the child’s grandfather, according to a St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Facebook posting. The infant was pronounced dead on arrival. The boy died of dehydration and malnutrition in a mobile home in the 800 block of Silverstream Circle, Fort Pierce which was in bad condition, according to investigators, who found an extreme bug infestation and a lack of food in the home. Four other children in the home – ranging in age from 2 to 10 years old – were placed in foster care through the state Department of Children and Families, investigators said. A Martin County community is restoring a mangrove island next to their marina that erosion has slowly destroyed. Residents at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club spent two years cultivating 6,000 mangroves in an on-site nursery. Now, they are planting them in the waterway to bring the island back to life. WATCH BELOW: "The mangroves were so thick and lush and we've watched them deteriorate and in some areas the island is dead now," Lisa Standing, a resident at Piper's Landing Yacht and Country Club, said. Standing rallied her neighbors to take action. The community built 10 planter pools to grow red and white mangroves. "We were able to collect just white and red seeds from our mangrove island," Standing said. The effort required extensive research and permitting before a single plant could go into the water. They say it was an elaborate operation that turned into a labor of love "We tried to match the habitat of all of our plants to the river habitat," Standing said. "We were here almost every day in the nursery and we inspected the plants, watered them if needed, monitored their health, matched salinity to the river." With the nursery phase complete, residents brought in Keith Rossin, CEO of Mang Consulting Services, to do the planting. "These are dredge filled little management areas and so they take that dredge fill and they actually bring it up to the right level for the elevation for the mangroves and that allows for us to plant these mangroves in here so this very unique way I've never actually seen this done before of how we can actually create mangrove habitat," Rossin said. What are now thousands of small trees are expected to grow into the foundation of a new ecosystem. "We will be able to go down to the mangrove island and enjoy beautiful lush island," Standing said. "It's just wonderful." This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Early voting for Florida's August primary begins Aug. 8 in Palm Beach County and across the Treasure Coast, with dates and hours varying by location. In Palm Beach County, early voting runs through Aug. Voters can cast their ballots at any of the 28 designated early voting sites in the county from 7 a.m. This differs from Election Day, when voters must go to their assigned polling place. Wendy Sartory Link, Palm Beach County supervisor of elections, shared advice for voters preparing for the primary. "Make sure they have a plan. The vote-by-mail deadline to request that we send you a ballot has already passed. If you need to come to our office to pick up a vote by mail ballot, you can do that," Link said. "And if you are waiting until Election Day, just make sure that you know where you're supposed to go." Voters should bring a current, valid photo ID with a signature. If the photo ID does not include a signature, a second form of identification may be required. Election officials recommend checking voter information and reviewing sample ballots before heading to the polls. The county's website also allows voters to check wait times and schedule optional early voting appointments. Early voting in Treasure Coast and Okeechobee counties runs from Aug. 15, with the following hours: Martin County: 8 a.m. Indian River County: 8 a.m. Okeechobee County: 8:30 a.m. Hours and locations vary, so voters should check with their county supervisor of elections before heading to the polls. Florida has closed primaries, meaning party registration determines which primary ballot voters receive. The deadline to change party affiliation has passed. However, all registered voters may still be eligible to vote in nonpartisan or universal-primary contests, depending on their location. Election Day is Tuesday, Aug. Italy defeated Pakistan to claim the 2026 Amerigol LATAM Cup championship on Sunday, with goalkeeper Rocco Bruno earning MVP honors in a game that highlighted hockey's expanding global footprint.The tournament, held in Florida, featured two countries not traditionally associated with the sport. Pakistan scored first, but Italy responded with two unanswered goals — including a decisive shot that sealed the championship.Bruno was a standout throughout the tournament."It means the world to me to be able to come out here and represent these colors. It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience; I'm just so thankful to be able to be a part of this team here," Bruno said.When asked about the MVP award, Bruno kept his focus on the bigger prize."I wasn't expecting it whatsoever. I go out there and play a game, and sometimes I get rewarded for it, but I like the big trophy; that one is more important to me," Bruno said.Italian team captain John Schiavo described the energy inside the arena."It was amazing; the atmosphere all tournament was awesome. Obviously, with this being the biggest game, the crowd was rocking, and there's no better feeling than to play in front of an awesome crowd," Schiavo said.For Pakistan's players, the experience carried meaning far beyond the scoreboard. Tariq Khan reflected on what competing on this stage represents."It's a huge honor to be able to show kids around the world that we have an ice hockey team; it shows that anything is possible no matter where you're from," Tariq Khan said.Zaakir Khan echoed that sentiment."It's nothing I've ever experienced. I'm not good enough to play for the United States, but just to be able to play for your country is something I wish everyone could feel; it's god's gift," Zaakir Khan said.Florida's hockey culture, fueled in part by the recent Stanley Cup championships of the Florida Panthers and Tampa Bay Lightning, has helped create a platform for the sport's international growth.

LUCIE – The Daytona Tortugas held off the St. Lucie Mets for a 5-4 victory in the series finale between the teams on Sunday at Clover Park. Daytona won the series 4-3. The Tortugas scored five runs across the fourth and fifth innings to take a 5-0 lead. The Mets scored three in the sixth and another run in the eighth to close the gap to one. But Daytona pitchers Lisnerkin Lantigua and Jesus Colina retired the last six Mets in a row to finish the game. Mets starter Joel Lara cruised through the first three innings, allowing just one base runner on a walk. However, Lara struggled with his command in the third, walking the first three batters. Lara threw a wild pitch that brought home Ichiro Cano for the first run. Then with two outs Anielson Buten hit a two-run single to make it 3-0. Jean Brito replaced Lara with one on and out in the fifth inning. Cano hit the first pitch from Brito for a two-run homer that made it 5-0. Meanwhile Daytona starter Justin Henschel was cruising. Henschel shut out the Mets over 5.0 innings on 75 pitches. He scattered three hits, walked one and struck out four. Elian Peña started the Mets comeback bid in the sixth inning with a leadoff double against Lantigua. The double extended Peña’s hitting streak to 11 games. Later in the inning with two outs Kuhio Aloy ripped a two-run double to get the Mets on the board. Simon Juan followed with a RBI single to make it 5-3. The first two Mets reached base to start the eighth inning vs. Lantigua but the Mets only got a sac fly by Juan to make it 5-4. Colina retired the side in order in the ninth with a fly out and back-to-back strikeouts to notch his first save. The first seven batters in the Mets order recorded a hit. Reed Stallman went 2 for 4. Julio Zayas went 1 for 3 win a single, walk and run to add to his bid for FSL Player of the Week. Austin Brown (undrafted 2025 – Chipola JC) made his team debut by pitching two scoreless innings in the seventh and eighth. The Mets (16-25, 49-58) are off on Monday. Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra — two strangers turned friends, brought together by an incredible act of courage.It happened last Friday around 5 p.m., when Spoelstra was driving along Southeast Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. Spoelstra made a turn, and suddenly a crossing arm came down on top of her car, trapping her on the tracks. Her car's antenna was caught on the crossing arm."I just went to turn and as soon as I turned, the gate came down on the top of my car," Spoelstra said. "Then I realized that I was trapped it was absolutely trapped.”Dash cam video obtained from a nearby driver shows the close call. As Spoelstra tried to figure out what to do, she hoped someone would come to her aid."I know for sure somebody might come up from behind and help me, but you know didn't happen and then all of a sudden I looked and I saw my guardian angel coming over the track," Spoelstra said.That's when Baur, who was on his way home from work, spotted her car. Baur was in a rush at the time and calls the moment a lesson, because he was forced to slow down and help."I looked down on my phone looked back up, and I see Miss Debbie's car stuck on the train tracks with the arm down behind it," Baur said. “As she's trying to move and I was like holy cow she's stuck in the tracks. She's going to get hit so I threw it in parking and just took off running," Baur said.As Baur ran toward her, he was tracking the approaching train. "As I was running, I was trying to see where the train was, how far off it was, how much time and also which side of the track it was on and when I noticed it was on her side of track I'm like okay now or never we gotta do this," Baur said.Baur lifted the crossing arm, allowing Spoelstra to reverse to safety — just before the train came through."It was incredible and after he had he had lifted the gate off I don't know how many seconds passed by and then the train came right by so it was a close call. It was very close," Spoelstra said.For Baur, it was a close call, but the right thing to do. "Don't hesitate to help others when they're in need. I didn't sit there and think about it, if I sat there and he hesitated who knows if I would've got there in time," Baur said. "People say she's a stranger to me but she's a child of God just like I am.”The two believe the moment was meant to be."I think it was a God thing and for those if you don't believe, I don't know it was just a miracle," said Spoelstra.Spoelstra plans to take Baur and his family out for dinner as a thank you. She also noted an interesting connection — she has a 9-month-old grandson named Josiah. She says she will never forget what Baur did."He's an amazing individual. He is my guardian angel," Spoelstra said. "I'll never forget what he's done ever. I'm truly grateful and indebted to him.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie police are investigating the death of 77-year-old Michael Joseph Kramer, who was found unresponsive in a pond near his home on Friday afternoon after being reported missing earlier that day. At approximately 1:18 p.m. today, officers responded to a residence on the 1400 block of SW Mockingbird Drive regarding a missing adult. Kramer was last seen by his wife inside their home at approximately 10 p.m. the following morning, Kramer was no longer inside the residence. Kramer’s personal belongings, including his shoes, wallet, and cellphone, were still inside the home. His wife searched for him and contacted local hospitals before reporting him missing to law enforcement at approximately 1:18 p.m. Officers began searching the neighborhood and, during the canvass, located an unresponsive person in a pond directly across the street from Kramer’s residence at approximately 2 p.m. The individual and clothing matched Kramer’s description. Lucie Police Department Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water near the shoreline of the pond, where he was confirmed deceased. The circumstances surrounding Kramer’s death remain under investigation. Police said there are no known indications of foul play at this preliminary stage of the investigation. Authorities encourage the public to promptly contact law enforcement when a person is believed to be missing, emphasizing that timely reporting allows officers to begin investigative and search efforts as quickly as possible.

Lucie Police Department on Sunday identified the victim and suspect involved in the domestic-related murder-suicide that occurred the night before at a residence. The victim has been identified as Elizabeth Ortega and the shooter as Ralph Varela Sr., both 50. As the August election approaches, tensions are rising between the two political camps as incumbent Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steve Giordano in the race for mayor. So far, tensions have escalated beyond the polls, with campaign signs being removed or moved. An investigation was launched after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard. Investigators reviewed surveillance footage that showed Giordano and the woman approaching campaign signs displayed in the yard. PSLPD said the video then showed the woman removing a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before another sign was placed in the yard. PSLPD said officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement and authorization of the campaign signs. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin. The two can be heard shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. PSLPD said investigators are reviewing the video. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged. Lucie Police Department acknowledges that Aaron Martin is employed by the department. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process. As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy," PSLPD said in a news release. Following the incident, Mayor Shannon Martin said in a statement: My campaign is aware of recent incidents involving the unauthorized removal of my campaign signs at different locations over several days. Signs were taken down without permission and replaced with Mr. In response, my husband simply restored the signs that had been removed. At no time were my opponent's signs stolen or damaged, one small sign was temporarily moved and put back in the ground. Lucie Police Department is investigating reports related to political campaign signs that occurred this week. We fully support a thorough, impartial review of the facts. I remain focused on the issues that matter to the city and will continue running a positive, transparent campaign. According to police, officers responded to the reported incidents, documented the scenes, collected available evidence and began interviewing those involved. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is asking for donations, foster homes, adopters, and help from rescue organizations after taking in more than 100 animals from what the Martin County sheriff described as the worst animal hoarding case in the county’s history. "We need adopters and fosters. Anyone that's willing to adopt and has been thinking about getting a pet, the time is now," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson, Humane Society of the Treasure Coast. Employees and volunteers have been working around the clock to care for the animals while the Palm City shelter continues its regular operations. A total of 108 animals were brought to the humane society for medical treatment and care after 77-year-old Gail Giustino was arrested July 20. Since then, 10 cats and 17 dogs from the case have been adopted, while five microchipped cats have been reunited with their owners. "I think she thought she was doing a good thing. She thought she was rescuing cats from the outdoors and unfortunately, she was way in over her head, couldn't care for it and ended up in a terrible situation," Fisher said. The shelter’s workload has continued to grow. Following the initial case, the Martin County Sheriff’s Office reportedly received an influx of requests for animal welfare checks. Last week, the humane society took in 26 cats from another situation and five dogs from a separate case. We expect more animals in the coming weeks due to the calls that have come in requesting animal welfare checks and the initial information we are receiving from Animal Services, which is following up on these calls, Humane Society Director of Operations Lori Tucker said. Many calls have been cleared, but there are cases that are requiring further follow-up. The organization said monetary donations are its greatest immediate need because of the continuing costs of medical care, food and housing while the animals await placement. Donations may be made through the shelter’s emergency medical fund. The humane society is also urging residents to adopt or foster animals already in its care. Officials said the influx doubled the shelter’s animal population even as normal admissions and services continued. Adopting or fostering a dog, cat, rabbit or guinea pig would free space for rescued animals still receiving treatment and preparing for adoption. See also: Road rage ends in violent 4-vehicle crash on U.S. Lucie man arrested We are still in need of people to adopt working cats, that is, cats that are suitable for safe outdoor living, Tucker said. We also are in desperate need of adopters and rescue groups willing to help take some of our animals. The shelter is offering a Name Your Price adoption special until further notice. Short- and long-term foster opportunities are also available. Information about adoptable animals is available at hstc1.org/Adopt , and foster information is available at hstc1.org/foster . Prospective adopters may call 772-223-8822 . Foster inquiries may be sent to catfoster@hstc1.org or dogfoster@hstc1.org , or made by calling 772-600-3220 . The Humane Society will also offer public microchipping services from 10 a.m. Registration is available at hstc1.org/Clinic . The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is a private, locally operated nonprofit at 4100 SW Leighton Farm Ave. The no-kill animal welfare organization has served the Martin County area since 1955 and relies on donations to support its programs and services.

The victim in a weekend murder-suicide in Port St. Lucie has been identified as a communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Fifty-year-old Elizabeth Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last 10 years. The shooting happened Saturday night both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. In a video statement released Monday, police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. "One of the neighbors actually located that victim after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive," Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department said. On Monday afternoon, PBSO posted about Ortega on social media, saying, in part, "She was a respected and cherished part of our PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room." Police said the shooter was Ortega’s longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr. After killing Ortega, Varela went back inside the home and killed himself. McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. "Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Ralph could find other living arrangements," McNally said. Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. The couple’s son, Varela Jr., had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine. "There’s no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting," McNally said. Varela Jr., is a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue. The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega’s co-workers cope with the loss. Lucie Police Department is investigating the death of a 77-year-old man who was found in a pond, according to a press release from the PSLPD . PSLPD says that on Friday, around 1:18 p.m., officers were called to a residence on SW Mockingbird Drive in reference to a missing adult who was later identified as Michael Joseph Kramer, 77. The investigation revealed that Kramer was last seen by his wife inside of their residence at around 10:00 p.m. However, when Kramer’s wife woke up at approximately 7:00 a.m. on Friday, Kramer was nowhere to be found despite all of his personal belongings remaining in the residence. See also: Delray Beach body shop owner accused of insurance fraud stemming from 2024 claims After an extensive search of the area, PSLPD says that they located an unresponsive man that matched Kramer’s description in a pond directly across the street from the residence at around 2:00 p.m. The PSLPD Dive Team recovered Kramer from the water, and he was pronounced deceased. PSLPD says that currently, the circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear, but no indications of foul play seem apparent.

Lucie Police Department has released an update on 2 separate investigations involving political campaign signs, both occurring this week in the area of SW Airoso Boulevard.Although both incidents involve political campaign signs in the same area, police say they are being investigated as separate cases, with each evaluated independently based on their own facts, evidence, and applicable law.The first incident occurred on August 5, 2026, near the intersection of SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thanksgiving Avenue.A Port St. Lucie Police sergeant observed Steven Giordano and an unidentified adult female near political campaign signs at a residence and initiated an investigation after one campaign sign was found on the ground while another had been placed in the yard.Detectives reviewed surveillance video from the area, which appears to show Giordano and the unidentified adult female arrive at the residence, approach campaign signs displayed in the yard, and interact with the signage. The video further appears to show the unidentified female remove a campaign sign supporting Mayor Shannon Martin before a different campaign sign was placed in the yard.Detectives collected the video evidence and are evaluating it alongside statements, physical evidence, and all other information gathered during the investigation.Officers and detectives are working to determine the circumstances surrounding the placement, movement, and authorization of the campaign signs, including whether the movement or replacement of the signs was authorized by the property owner at the time the incident occurred.The second incident occurred on August 7, 2026, near SW Airoso Boulevard and SW Thornhill Drive, where officers responded to a disturbance involving political campaign signs.During the investigation, officers learned that Aaron Martin and Steven Giordano were involved in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of campaign signs at a nearby residence.Officers reviewed video recordings provided by the involved parties, which depict Martin and Giordano engaged in a verbal confrontation regarding the placement and movement of political campaign signs at the residence.Investigators interviewed the homeowners and learned that both residents believed they had separately granted permission for campaign signs to be placed on the property. Officers determined that one homeowner communicated permission for one campaign's sign, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, separately conveyed permission to individuals associated with the opposing campaign.Investigators believe the language barrier contributed to a misunderstanding regarding which campaign signs were authorized to be displayed and whether previously placed signs could be moved or replaced.The preliminary investigation indicates that both individuals believed they had permission from residents of the property to place campaign signs. At this time, there is no indication that any campaign signs associated with this incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.Information related to the placement of the campaign signs has been forwarded to the City of Port St. Lucie Code Compliance for review.Many residents were taken back after learning of the incidents.“I think it’s childish and if they’re going to be childish with their personalities and who they are then they probably shouldn't be in that position,” said resident Trumaine Pearson.The Port St. Lucie Police Department acknowledged that Aaron Martin is employed by the department."The fact that Mr. Martin is a department employee will not influence the investigative process," the department said. "As with every investigation, the facts and evidence will determine the outcome, and this investigation will be conducted fairly, impartially, and in accordance with department policy."The department said that should the investigation identify any potential policy violations involving a department employee, the matter will be handled in accordance with established department procedures. Consistent with Florida law, department employees are afforded the rights and protections provided under the Florida Law Enforcement Officers' Bill of Rights. Any related administrative review will proceed following the completion of the ongoing criminal investigation.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Homes wants to rezone in order to build a 135,000-square-foot indoor and outdoor recreation area known as the Riverland-West Sports Recreation complex. Because so many residents both emailed the city and spoke out in protest during the July 27 quasi-judicial rezoning hearing, the City Council voted unanimously that day to table the request until Aug. 24 to give the applicant time to hold a neighborhood meeting. LUCIE – City Council members found themselves defending their actions to frustrated Tradition-area residents July 27, prompting them to table a quasi-judicial rezoning request from the developer of the Riverland/Kennedy Development of Regional Impact. The delay will give the developer’s representatives time to meet with area homeowners and address their concerns. Planner Francis Forman introduced the controversial agenda item that evening to a packed Chambers. “The item before you is the Riverland-West Sports Recreation Master Planned Unit Development rezoning,” he said. “The applicant is Azlina Goldstein with Riverland/Kennedy II LLC. This site is located south of Southwest Discovery Way and east of Southwest Sundance Vista Boulevard. The request is to rezone approximately 33.23 acres from St. Lucie County Agricultural to Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD.” Forman proceeded to provide more details on the GL Homes request to develop the site in a manner that many Riverland homeowners claim is different than what was planned when they purchased their properties years ago. “This site is designated Neighborhood Village Commercial, which allows a mixture of residential and non-residential uses such as commercial and offices, personal and household services, institutional, public facilities, parks, playgrounds and similar services,” he explained. “Any Neighborhood Village Commercial area must contain at least two of those uses. Currently the Riverland-West Sports Recreation MPUD is proposing to provide about 135,000 square feet of indoor recreation with some commercial as well as some outdoor RV/boat storage areas.” Because the city had received numerous emails from nearby residents in opposition, Vice-Mayor Jolien Caraballo immediately asked City Attorney Richard Berrios to describe the formalities of the quasi-judicial process. “This is a rezoning, which is limited to what Mr. Forman presented,” Berrios said. “Not part of it are things like landscaping, indoor and outdoor features and specifics of what it will ultimately be. Those things are better suited for the site-plan process. As far as the process here, the legislators take off their legislative hats and put on their judge robes, and it’s limited to taking sworn testimony and the facts presented and applying them to a specific problem.” Councilman Anthony Bonna, however, believed more information was needed for the area residents. “Can you go into more detail about what evidence is allowed to be weighed [and] is a rezoning discretionary?” he asked. While Berrios admitted the Council’s hands were tied as far as any pre-existing DRI entitlements, he deferred Councilman Bonna’s question to Planning Zoning Director Mary Savage-Dunham. The latter emphasized the legal framework of controlling agreements and city codes. A pre-existing Development of Regional Impact (DRI) is a large-scale project approved under older Florida growth laws that retains vested development rights despite later changes to local plans or the elimination of the state’s formal DRI program. “The DRI document talks about what’s going to be built there,” Savage-Dunam said. “We also have the comprehensive plan. As staff testified, this rezoning was found to be consistent with the comprehensive plan, [which] follows the DRI. Those are the road maps that guide development in that section of the city. So, you would be looking at the totality of what the applicant submitted showing their intended uses there and how that aligns with the comp plan and the DRI.” Vice-Mayor Caraballo then chimed back in with her own perspective. “If you’re confused, I understand,” she said. “It’s not our process – it’s the way it’s legally required by the state. It’s definitely not the simplest thing for anybody to understand.” After the applicant’s contracted Land Use Attorney Goldstein provided her own presentation, 10 nearby homeowners aired their complaints, beginning with Southwest River Rock Road resident Jim Riordan. “My property is located at the southern end of the proposed Riverland-West Sports Recreation Center,” he said. “I spoke at the July 7 Planning Board meeting, and the chairman encouraged me to meet with Ms. At that time, I gave her our primary concerns with the project. On Friday, she did contact me, but none of those concerns were addressed. What she did say was exactly what she said right now: This is not the time – the time is later – but we feel this is the time before we move forward.” Riordan pointed out that GL Homes had “1,300 other acres where they could build this complex.” “GL has already sold parcels in the new section advertising the fitness center,” he continued. “So, I guess it’s a done deal based on this picture and what they’re advertising. We purchased our property, as well as every citizen here, from The Grove with the understanding that this parcel will be a city park. Now they’re basically trying to make this something different.” Both Harriet Gallas and her husband Lawrence agreed. “We chose to move here for quality of life,” the former said. “When we bought our house, we were told there was going to be a park over the berm next to us. They’re [now] talking 72 pickleball courts, bocci courts, tennis courts, a dog park and RV park, and that’s going to destroy my quality of life. Noise pollution’s a real thing: It causes stress, and pickleball is loud, stabbing and sharp. I respectfully beg you to not pass this rezoning.” The other residents echoed similar fears, resulting in more staff explanations and Council debate until Mayor Shannon Martin asked Goldstein a pivotal question. “Has their been a public meeting with the neighbors with regard to this issue?” she asked. Riordan regarding the issue of the buffer,” Goldstein responded. That response gave Mayor Martin the impetus she needed. “Being that there are so many concerns from the residents, is GL willing to have a meeting with the residents in order to address the issues?” she prodded. Goldstein, however, resisted the delay at first. “This is a straight-forward rezoning,” she insisted. “We don’t have all those details yet for the site plan because that’s not this process. When we’re ready to get there and we have those details, we’d be more than happy to meet with everybody to discuss what’s planned.” That response brought a loud uproar of protest from the audience and a plea from the vice-mayor. “I would really appreciate very much if you’d be willing to just table this,” Caraballo said. “I’m sorry to slow it down, but even this part of the process I don’t think they comprehend.” The City Council then voted unanimously to table the request until the Aug. This week I'm at Vero Beach High School where students are getting ready to go back to school, and I decided to do something I've never done before – I joined the marching band! I crashed band camp at Vero Beach High School just a few days before school started, and let me tell you, it was an incredible experience.WATCH: The first time I stepped onto that practice field, I could feel the history before I even picked up my instrument. This wasn't just another high school band – this was a tradition stretching back to 1934, when the Fighting Indians Band was founded as part of the Federal Music Project during the Great Depression. Every student who had ever worn that uniform had helped build an incredible legacy.I got to meet some amazing students who are keeping that tradition alive, like Annabel Robbins who plays flute piccolo and is a drum major. Brady, an incoming senior, is the woodwind captain and section leader."It's kind of scary, you know," Brady said. "You're in charge of a lot of kids, so you got to make sure they're all doing good.The band director, Sean Srigley, has a special connection to this program that goes way back. "I'm actually alumni of Vero Beach High School. I was in the band myself," Srigley explained. "The cool thing about Vero is we've got awesome academics, awesome athletics. Our band is right there with them. We've marched in pretty much every big parade you could have in America."And he's not exaggerating! This band has an absolutely incredible resume. They performed in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in 1988, marching through the streets of New York City and playing "Alexander's Ragtime Band" for millions of television viewers. That single performance became one of the defining moments in the program's history and remains a source of pride for every new generation of members.But that's not all – they've also performed in the Tournament of Roses Parade, the Fiesta Bowl Parade, the Orange Bowl and even Carnegie Hall! The program has earned decades of Superior ratings and national recognition while representing our Treasure Coast with pride.After learning about all this amazing history, it was time for me to get to work. But honestly, that wasn't really my thing, so I tried the drums next.But joining the marching band for practice meant more than just learning music and drill. It meant discipline and the ability to stand for a long time in that Florida heat – something these kids do with incredible dedication.As I marched onto the football field, I couldn't help but imagine all the students who had stood in that same place before me. Some had gone on to march through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Others had performed in famous bowl games or international parades.As I left Vero Beach High School that day, I was thankful for the opportunity to be part of something so special, even for just one practice. These students aren't just making music – they're carrying on a legacy that's been building for nearly 90 years.

A school crossing guard in Martin County waits at an intersection for youngsters to ensure they cross streets safely. The 2026-2027 school session for students begins in Martin County on Monday, Aug. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. MARTIN COUNTY – Public school for all students in Martin County begins on Monday, Aug. The 12 elementary schools for 2026-27 will open at 7:40 a.m.; all four high schools, including Indiantown High School charter school, start at 8:30 a.m.; and five middle schools begin at 9:20 a.m. With the elementary schools, that means many students would be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for Jensen Beach Elementary students who meet the bus at the stop at Southeast Aster Lane and Southeast Astorwood Terrace at 6:10 a.m., according to Martin School District’s bus transportation schedules. As a result, the School District urges all parents/students/motorists to be extra cautious and to observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “As we prepare to welcome students back on Aug. 10, Martin County School District encourages families to take a few moments to review school bus safety with their children,” Kirstie Germaine, coordinator of public information community relations, said in a statement. “Students should arrive at their bus stop 5-10 minutes before their scheduled pickup time, remain off the roadway while waiting, and follow the bus driver’s instructions when boarding, exiting, or crossing the street,” she said. “We also encourage families to review their child’s bus stop location and schedule before the first day of school and ensure younger students have appropriate supervision at the bus stop. We are grateful for the partnership of families, our transportation staff, and local law enforcement agencies as we work together to keep students safe throughout the school year. The Martin County School District’s transportation page (www.martinschools.org/page/transportation) gives information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: • Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. • Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. • Ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: • Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street • Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. • Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: • Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. • Never play or run near traffic. • Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. • If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: • Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. • Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. • Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. • Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. • Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. • Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the web site. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend your driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. European soccer's governing body UEFA said Thursday it is maintaining its demand for FIFA President Gianni Infantino to resign and is not ruling out a boycott of FIFA events, including the next men's and women's World Cups.The threat comes after Infantino faced criticism over his failed plan to bring in private investors to buy into some of FIFA's competitions. FIFA admitted to mistakes in the plan, but the UEFA said its demands have not been met, leaving FIFA's leadership and the stability of international soccer in question.RELATED STORY | Senior FIFA official resigns over Infantino's World Cup sell-off plan"UEFA's associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non participation in FIFA competitions," it said in a statement obtained by the Associated Press. "First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.""These conditions have not been met. In addition, UEFA made it abundantly clear in it's statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | The 2026 World Cup is officially the most attended ever, according to FIFAIn response to the recent international backlash, FIFA called an emergency meeting this week in attempt to present a united front as concerns grow over finances and tensions with international associations. Following the meeting, FIFA announced that Infantino had the full support of those in attendance.Nonetheless, the feud could have major implications for the future of international soccer and billions of dollars in revenue tied to the world's most popular sport.

A road rage confrontation erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four injured and a Port St. Officers with the Port St. Lucie Police Department say they responded around 6:45 p.m. to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where investigators determined that a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road-rage incident. "These two vehicles were involved in an active road rage incident just prior to the crash, and this is based off the dash camera and witness statements that we've collected," said Officer Brittany McNally with the Port St. Detectives say the pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection. According to witness statements and dash-camera video, the motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. See also: Miami man faces prison after pleading guilty to online threats against Rubio, Noem Police say Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center , per PSLPD. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Investigators say the motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition.\ Based on witness statements, dash-camera video and the investigation, police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. The investigative findings indicate that the pickup truck was actively pursuing that motorcyclist just moments prior to that crash, said McNally. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m. This case does, though, serve as hopefully a powerful reminder that allowing your anger to dictate your actions behind the wheel can put multiple innocent lives at risk, McNally said.

Distributing donated backpacks to Pinewood Elementary School in Stuart are, from left, Costco Membership Manager Ray Perry, Pinewood Elementary Principal Amy Porter, Education Foundation of Martin County Executive Director Lisa Rhodes, Pinewood Elementary Assistant Principal Dana Carroll, and Costco Administrative Manager Mike Fabis. Education Foundation of Martin County Costco Stuart presents a $500 gift certificate to Murray Middle School Assistant Principal Robert Beasley and Principal Tiffany Roth. Education Foundation of Martin County Executive Director Lisa Rhodes joins Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth and Assistant Principal Robert Beasley unloading backpacks donated by Costco. STUART — Thanks to the partnership-building efforts of the Education Foundation of Martin County and the generosity of Costco, approximately 750 students will head into the 2026-27 school year with a new backpack in hand. On Thursday morning, Stuart Costco Administrative Manager Mike Fabis and Membership Manager Ray Perry arrived at Pinewood Elementary School with pickup trucks loaded with hundreds of backpacks. The donation marked the second consecutive year Costco has provided backpacks for local students, but this year’s contribution was significantly larger. “We received backpacks last year, but this year we had almost 400 coming in, which is incredible,” said Pinewood Elementary Principal Amy Porter. “Our kids were so excited when they got them last year, so I can’t wait to see their faces this year.” The deliveries continued across Stuart, where Fabis and Perry unloaded another truckload of backpacks at Murray Middle School, ensuring hundreds more students will be prepared for the first day of classes. “Anytime we have an opportunity to help our families, making sure that they have access to new resources for back to school to relieve that financial burden is always so appreciated,” said Murray Middle School Principal Tiffany Roth. In addition to the backpacks, Costco donated a $500 gift card to each school to help meet additional student needs. School leaders say the donation is an example of the Education Foundation of Martin County’s unique role in connecting community partners with schools to provide meaningful support for students and families. “The Education Foundation of Martin County is really the powerhouse of our school district and our schools,” Roth said. “They really act as a liaison, helping to connect us with all of our community partners.” Porter echoed that sentiment. “We want to thank Costco and the Education Foundation, who does so much for our students,” she said. The Foundation coordinated the partnership between Costco and both schools, helping transform a corporate donation into direct assistance for local families. By fostering relationships with businesses and community organizations, the Education Foundation continues to expand opportunities that benefit students throughout Martin County. When students arrive at Pinewood Elementary and Murray Middle School next month, they will be able to choose from patterned, solid-color, or clear backpacks. For many families facing the rising costs of back-to-school shopping, the new backpacks represent more than just school supplies—they provide financial relief and help ensure every child begins the school year with confidence. For the Education Foundation of Martin County, the backpack giveaway reflects its broader mission: bringing together community partners and schools to remove barriers to learning and create opportunities for every student to succeed. hero.headline: Indian River County deputies talk man off 17th Street Bridge after two-hour standoff
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies safely took a man into custody after a two-hour standoff on the 17th Street Bridge early Tuesday morning. The incident began around 1 a.m. when deputies responded to a call from Port St. Lucie police about a man wanted for burglary who had called his mother and told her he wanted to kill himself.

Body camera footage showed the man sitting on a platform over the bridge railing with his feet dangling in the air. Traffic Deputy Edouard Gast, a member of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office Crisis Negotiation Team, worked to establish a connection with the man. Gast said the man at first did not want to talk, and it took time to get him to open up. At one point, the man appeared ready to jump. Gast continued to plead with him, saying, "Come on, man, don't do this to your mom."

Gast said the man flipped a switch and climbed on top, positioning himself to jump. Gast talked to him repeatedly until the man climbed back over and stood on the platform. The sheriff's office marine unit and fire rescue crews were stationed in the water below as a safety precaution.

After two hours of negotiation, the man climbed back to the top of the bridge and shook the negotiator's hand. The man was taken into custody without incident. Sgt. from the sheriff's office said that even though the man was wanted out of Port St. Lucie, deputies still treated him with due care to make sure he was safe and could answer for his crimes.

You got a lot on your mind?” The man responded, “Yeah, I do, and I’m trying to think about it.” At one point, the man appeared ready to jump. cards.headline: Vehicle connected to fatal hit-and-run in Indian River County recovered
cards.teaser: The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Wednesday that a vehicle connected to a deadly hit-and-run crash on Sunday has been recovered.
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced Wednesday that a vehicle connected to a deadly hit-and-run crash on Sunday, Aug. 9, has been recovered. The sheriff's office said its Real-Time Crime Center assisted the Florida Highway Patrol in the investigation, which led to the discovery.

A vehicle matching the description of the suspected truck was identified by the Real-Time Crime Center analyst. The truck was missing a passenger-side mirror. Using other technology, the analyst identified the truck's license plate and associated driver information. The information was immediately given to FHP, which located the truck and confirmed it was involved in the crash with a bicyclist.

The investigation continues in identifying the driver of the truck.

hero.headline: Martin County deputies save senior from $600,000 gold bar scam
hero.teaser: A Martin County senior citizen nearly lost $600,000 to a scam in which a fraudster posed as a bank representative and convinced the victim to buy gold bars, but deputies intervened to stop the transaction.
hero.body:
A Martin County senior citizen nearly lost $600,000 to a gold bar scam, but deputies helped avert the loss. The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the victim was contacted by a fraudster claiming to be from his financial institution and was told that his bank account had been compromised. The scammer then convinced the senior citizen that he needed to protect his money by backing it up with gold.

According to the sheriff's office, the victim was instructed to send $600,000 to a legitimate gold vendor. The scammer told the victim that the gold would then be picked up by a third-party driver and delivered to the bank. After going through with the transaction, the victim quickly realized something was wrong and immediately went to his bank. The bank recognized the situation as potential fraud and advised him to contact the sheriff's office.

The responding deputy spoke directly with the gold vendor and helped the victim stop the transaction from going through. The sheriff's office said the victim confirmed he received a full refund of his $600,000.

cards.headline: Trail camera, AirTags fuel sign theft allegations between Martin County candidates
cards.teaser: A Martin County Commission candidate says he caught a campaign sign thief on a trail camera and tracked stolen signs with AirTags, igniting a public clash between political candidates in the final days before the August election.
cards.body:
Chris Collins, running for Martin County Commission Seat Two, posted a video to Facebook claiming he caught a man stealing his campaign signs using a hunting trail camera. In the video, Collins stands in front of a still photo showing a man in a darkened area at night holding one of his campaign signs. Collins, formerly the Mayor of Stuart, said he set up the trail cam after some of his signs went missing and put Apple AirTags on some of the signs to track their location.

Collins identified the man as Jim Gallegos and said the signs were tracked to Gallegos' house. Collins claimed Gallegos is a campaign advisor to Merritt Matheson, another political candidate, though not in the same race as Collins. Gallegos denied the accusation, saying he was taking down signs that the property owner had requested be removed. Merritt Matheson sent a text saying Gallegos is not his campaign advisor.

The story of the stolen signs prompted Derreck Ogden, who is running for election to be a Stuart City Commissioner, to confront Gallegos. Their argument about the campaign signs was caught on camera and posted on Facebook. Gallegos said he removed about 30 campaign signs for various candidates, not just Chris Collins' campaign, because the property owner did not want the signs on his property. Gallegos said he no longer has the campaign signs.
cards.article_text: We are less than a week away from the August election and we have another story about campaign signs and bad blood and mud-slinging between candidates. Chris "Doc Collins, running for Martin County Commission Seat Two, posted a video to Facebook on a rant about his signs being stolen. In the video he claims the sign thief is in cahoots with a political enemy. Candidates try to increase their name recognition by putting out campaign signs along roads. One candidate for Martin County Commission says some of his campaign signs were missing recently, and he found out who the culprit is who took them. "Many people have been asking me, do you know who this guy is? What time of day?" Collins said in a video posted on Facebook, as he stands in front of a still photo of a man in a darkened area at night holding one of Collins' campaign signs. Chris Collins, formerly the Mayor of Stuart is now running for Martin County Commission Seat Two. He wanted to figure out why some of his campaign signs were disappearing, so he came up with a plan. See also: Third victim dies after South Bay crash that killed woman, two 13-year-old girls "I set up a hunting trail cam to get some receipts and we found out who's been doing it. This is Jim Gallegos at 3:58 in the morning on August 5, while biking down Palm City Road, you'll notice the bike shorts, taking my sign out of the ground," Collins said in the Facebook video. Collins goes on to say, he put Apple Airtags on some of the signs, and was able to pinpoint their location. He says they were at man named Jim Gallegos' house. He says Gallegos is a campaign advisor to Merritt Matheson. Matheson is another political candidate, though not in the same race as Collins. "Listen, I don't want to get the cops involved. Guys, bring me the signs back. Let's have a clean election," Collins said in the Facebook video. We met with Jim Gallegos and asked him about the accusations. "What we were doing was taking the signs down that the owner of the property had requested us to remove and that's what we were doing. That's what I was doing at that particular time," Gallegos explained. Merritt Matheson sent CBS12 News a text. He says Gallegos is not his campaign advisor. Nevertheless, the story of signs being stolen prompted a man named Derreck Ogden to confront Gallegos. Ogden is also running for election to be a Stuart City Commissioner. Their argument about the campaign signs was caught on camera. Gallegos, if you want to return the signs I don't think the other slow-growth candidates are gonna press charges. So if you want to ask your campaign, your campaign team to return the signs," Ogden says in a video posted on Facebook. "I never touched one of your signs! And that's an attack on me personally!" Gallegos says in the video posted on Facebook. "While our campaign is following the rules, other campaigns are not and I think it's important that people know that and we're the only ones that hold anybody responsible as the residents. So we have to hold these people to, you know, their feet to the fire," Ogden told CBS12 News. Gallegos says he no longer has the campaign signs. He says he removed about 30 campaign signs for various candidates, not just Chris Collins' campaign, because the property owner did not want the signs on his property.

hero.headline: Palm City home condemned after woman charged with hoarding 36 Border Collies in 'worst case ever seen'
hero.body:
The Martin County Building Department condemned a Palm City home on Wednesday after authorities arrested Paige O'Donnell on 72 charges in connection with hoarding 36 Border Collies in what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast called the worst animal hoarding case in its history. The notice posted to the gate states occupancy is prohibited as the structure is unfit for human occupancy under section 21.75.3, citing an unsanitary single-family residence.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrested O'Donnell on Monday following a lengthy investigation into animal welfare concerns at her residence. When deputies executed a search warrant, they discovered dogs covered in feces and urine living in a home with no functioning air conditioning and floors covered in waste and garbage, according to a probable cause affidavit. Deputies noted the condition of the dogs and surrounding environment was such that the animals were difficult to distinguish from the heavily soiled areas of the residence.

Animal Control Officer Tabitha Queen documented approximately 20 related incidents at the address spanning from 2020 through 2026. During an August 3 meeting at Jock Leighton Park in Palm City, O'Donnell told the officer she owned only four dogs, but records from Boulevard Animal Hospital identified approximately 38 adult dogs associated with O'Donnell. The clinic employee said there were so many puppies brought in with O'Donnell that it was impossible to get an accurate count, with the last recorded visit on June 25, 2022.

O'Donnell faces 72 total charges, including 36 counts of felony animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts for failing to provide the dogs with proper exercise or air. A judge set her total bond at $275,000 and ordered that she may not own or possess any animals as a condition of her bond. The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is providing urgent care for the 36 Border Collies, including three puppies up to six months old, with staff working around the clock to medically groom, bathe and examine the dogs.

hero.headline: Indian River County school district plans to sell around 10 properties including 4 older schools
hero.teaser: The School District of Indian River County is looking to put around 10 properties on the market for potential buyers, including 4 older schools, older office buildings and district-owned land.
hero.body:
William Dodds, CFO of the School District of Indian River County, said the properties are spread across the county and include 4 older schools, older office buildings and district-owned land. After consolidating multiple schools throughout the district, Dodds said some of the properties are no longer necessary. Money made from the sale of the properties would go back to the district's capital budget to help keep buildings up, enhance some buildings and do things in capital that the district would not be able to do otherwise.

Ken Krasnow with Cushman and Wakefield, a real estate company working with the school district to sell the properties, said the buildings vary in condition and potential. Krasnow said some buildings, like Rosewood Magnet School, could be transformed into medical office or quasi-flex space. Krasnow said larger schools and properties could be redeveloped with commercial and retail along the front and residential in the back.

No decisions have been made yet. Dodds said the district is gauging interest from potential buyers before moving forward. Dodds said the district will reexamine interest in the properties and whether they need to be sold around December or January. The school board will have final approval.

cards.headline: Indian River County Sheriff's Office locates truck in deadly Vero Beach e-bike hit-and-run
cards.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff's Office has located the vehicle allegedly involved in a deadly hit-and-run crash that killed a 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle Sunday night near 8th Street and 14th Avenue. An IRCSO analyst located a vehicle matching the truck's description, including a missing passenger-side mirror, while reviewing leads with the Florida Highway Patrol. Deputies used Flock Safety technology and other investigative resources to identify the vehicle, its license plate and information about the driver.

The crash occurred at about 8:57 p.m. Sunday when the man was riding an e-bike near 8th Street and 14th Avenue. Investigators said a light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind the man in the same lane. As the pickup approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action, traveling southwest and partially entering the eastbound lane. However, the driver was unable to avoid the bicyclist, and the right side of the pickup struck him.

The bicyclist was thrown onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane of 8th Street. FHP said the driver fled the scene without rendering aid or contacting law enforcement. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

The information from IRCSO's Real Time Crime Center allowed FHP to locate the vehicle and confirm its connection to the crash. IRCSO has not identified the driver or released the identity of the bicyclist who was killed.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police arrest man in hit-and-run that seriously injured 7-year-old boy
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce Police Department arrested a man in connection with an Aug. 1 hit-and-run crash that left a 7-year-old boy seriously injured. Police arrested Demetrius Johnson at 2905 U.S. Highway 1 and charged him with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury and driving with a suspended license.

The crash occurred at 8:55 p.m. on Aug. 1 at the intersection of North 25th Street and Avenue M in Fort Pierce. Two children were crossing the roadway in a marked crosswalk when Johnson struck one of them, according to police.

Surveillance video from a nearby business shows two children running across the street in the crosswalk as a vehicle makes a sharp left turn and strikes the 7-year-old boy. Johnson, 34, briefly exited his vehicle to check on the child before returning to the vehicle and driving away, police said.

The 7-year-old boy has been released from the hospital and is recovering. The investigation remains ongoing, and anyone with additional information is asked to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department at 772-462-6800 or Treasure Coast Crime Stoppers.

hero.headline: South Fork High School freshman describes hot, crowded bus ride on first day of school
hero.teaser: A Martin County parent says her daughter came home in tears after her first bus ride home from South Fork High School, describing extreme heat and overcrowding on the bus Monday.
hero.body:
Sherri Lindemann's daughter is a freshman at South Fork High School. Lindemann said she was caught off guard when she learned what had upset her child. Lindemann said her daughter described a miserable experience on the ride. She said the bus was extremely hot with no air or ventilation and that there was overcrowding with four kids to every seat, with everybody sweaty and upset. The bus ride took an hour and 15 minutes to get home.

The Martin County School District said it understands why the experience would be concerning for students and families, especially on the first day of school when routines are new and students are adjusting to the year ahead. The district's Transportation team confirmed that 57 students were on the bus on Monday, which falls within regulation for high school buses, and that no seat had 4 students in it. Staff also confirmed the bus's air conditioning system was operating properly, but the district acknowledged that mid-August heat can make any bus ride feel particularly warm.

Lindemann's concerns come after the school district consolidated 3 school bus routes to make transportation more efficient without impacting students. In a statement, the district said the delays had nothing to do with the consolidation. The district said Transportation staff are closely monitoring ridership and routes as drivers become more familiar with traffic patterns and students become accustomed to safely exiting the bus. Families can track their child's bus through the MyReaxiumApp. Those who need help setting up an account can contact the transportation department at 772-219-1287.

hero.headline: Republicans Build 40,000-Vote Lead in Florida Primary as Democrats Turn Out at Higher Rate
hero.body:
Republicans hold a 40,114-vote lead over Democrats in Florida's primary election with less than a week before Election Day, even as Democrats vote at a significantly higher rate relative to their party registration, according to Fresh Take Florida's statewide turnout tracker.

As of 3:30 p.m. Wednesday, more than 1.3 million Floridians had already voted. Republicans accounted for 585,423 ballots compared with 545,309 Democrats. Another 177,542 ballots came from voters outside the two major parties. Republicans enter this election with a registration advantage of roughly 1.54 million voters, with 5.6 million registered Republicans and 4.06 million Democrats. Democrats still lead in mail ballots, with 409,358 Democrats voting by mail compared with 356,500 Republicans, a Democratic lead of 52,858 ballots. Republicans have overwhelmed that advantage at early voting sites, where 228,923 Republicans have voted early in person compared with 135,951 Democrats, a GOP advantage of 92,972 votes.

When turnout is measured against the size of each party, 13.43 percent of registered Democrats have voted compared with 10.45 percent of registered Republicans, almost a three-percentage-point Democratic advantage. About 10.08 percent of registered Democrats have already voted by mail compared with 6.37 percent of Republicans. Republicans have the edge in early in-person participation, 4.09 percent to 3.35 percent. Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said the political environment is shifting and argued the Republican supermajority in the Legislature is breakable this cycle. Republican Party of Florida Chair Evan Power said Republicans have taken the vote lead and will not look back, predicting a big vote lead on Election Day.

Florida's primary Election Day is August 18, with the state's mandatory early voting period continuing through Saturday, August 15. Political analyst Susan MacManus said enthusiasm only matters if campaigns can turn it into votes. For Democrats, the challenge is proving that dissatisfaction over affordability and the party in power can translate into enough turnout to overcome Florida's Republican registration advantage. For Republicans, it is showing that their larger voter pool and established turnout operation can dominate when all ballots are counted.
