cards.headline: Hobe Sound man rescues woman trapped on railroad tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway
cards.teaser: Josiah Baur lifted a railroad crossing gate to free Debbie Spoelstra's car from the tracks seconds before a freight train passed through Friday evening in Hobe Sound.
cards.body:
Josiah Baur, 23, rescued a woman whose car became trapped on train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound on Friday evening, lifting the crossing gate seconds before a freight train passed through. Debbie Spoelstra was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her stuck between the gates. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments as a train's horn sounded while it moved closer to Spoelstra's red car.

Baur was leaving work and heading home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing on the other side of the tracks. He saw the car stuck and Spoelstra still inside, threw his car in park and ran across the tracks. He looked to see which side the train was on, saw it was on her side, and lifted the gate with both arms to release her car just in time for her to back up before the train came through.

Spoelstra said she put her car in reverse but the gate got stuck on top of her car on the antenna, preventing her from backing up. A witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car and took a photo of him after the rescue, posting it on social media to find and thank him. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday and hugged. Spoelstra says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who saved her: Josiah.
cards.article_text: An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash from a freight train. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Paige O'Donnell, 62, was arrested and charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. Approximately eight Border Collies had been removed from the home by Monday afternoon, with deputies and animal services officers continuing to work to safely remove the remaining dogs.

Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the dogs were running loose in the house and described the conditions as deplorable. The house was stacked with garbage and had feces over every square inch, making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals. It was extremely hot inside and the home may not have had air conditioning.

O'Donnell will face at least 40 charges and is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home.

hero.headline: Florida awards $1 million to fire departments for cancer prevention equipment
hero.body:
Florida Chief Financial Officer Jimmy Ingoglia announced Monday the allocation of $1 million to fire departments across the state through programs designed to protect firefighters from cancer-causing chemicals. Ingoglia made the announcement at West Palm Beach Fire Station 1, joined by state Rep. Anne Gerwig, state Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, and West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James. The funds come from the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program, the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program, and projects appropriated in the state's fiscal 2025-2026 budget.

The program provides financial assistance to fire departments, including volunteer departments, to procure equipment, supplies, and educational training designed to mitigate exposure to hazardous, cancer-causing chemicals. Ingoglia explained that modern fires pose greater health risks than decades ago because burning structures now contain materials beyond wood and concrete that release substances absorbed through the skin, eyes, and lungs of firefighters. West Palm Beach received $19,635, Greenacres received $6,806, and Highland Beach received $5,962 from Monday's allocation. West Palm Beach Fire Chief Diana Matty said the grants fund second sets of gloves, particulate blocking hoods, on-scene cleansing wipes, and specialized washers.

The state still has $1 million available through the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program and another $1 million available for the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program in this year's state budget. Ingoglia urged fire chiefs across Florida to apply for the remaining funds.

Ingoglia also addressed concerns about an upcoming property tax amendment vote and funding worries expressed by cities and first responders. He said county budgets have increased between 60 to 160 percent over the past six years and counties have benefited from historic property tax revenue. Ingoglia stated he believes there is room to offer property tax relief while still funding necessary items for first responders, despite anxiety from sheriffs, police chiefs, and fire chiefs about potential budget cuts and layoffs. He said the vast majority of their budgets are controlled by county commissioners or mayors and there is more than enough money available.

Anne Gerwig, R-Wellington, and state Rep. Peggy Gossett-Seidman, R-Highland Beach, and West Palm Beach Mayor Keith James at West Palm Beach Fire Station 1 off North Dixie Highway.WATCH BELOW: Florida CFO holds news conference in West Palm BeachIngoglia awarded $1 million to local fire departments through the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program, the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program and projects that were appropriated in the state's fiscal 2025-2026 budget.According to the CFO's website, this program was established "to help protect the health and safety of firefighters and provide financial assistance to help departments, including volunteer fire departments, procure equipment, supplies and educational training designed to mitigate exposure to hazardous, cancer-causing chemicals.""Fighting fires today is much different than fighting fires 40 years ago," Ingoglia said. "When a structure burned, it was most likely concrete, it was wood. But today, when we ask our firefighters to go into burning structures, there's a lot more than just wood and concrete that are burning. there are things that are being lit up and being absorbed into the skin, into the eye, into the lungs of our firefighters, and unfortunately this has caused occupational cancers, and there's a higher risk of contracting and getting those cancers because of their profession."Funds allocated to local departments on Monday included:West Palm Beach received $19,635 Greenacres received $6,806 Highland Beach received $5,962 "The state of Florida's firefighter cancer decontamination grant is making a real difference here in the West Palm Beach Fire Department and at fire departments across the state," West Palm Beach Fire Chief Diana Matty said. "Whether it is for second sets of gloves, particulate blocking hoods, or on-scene cleansing wipes, or specialized washers, these are very important items that they're accenting in our budgets."The CFO said that the state still has $1 million available through the Firefighter Cancer Decontamination Grant Program, and another $1 million available for the Firefighter Assistance Grant Program in this year's state budget, urging other fire chiefs to reach out to the state and apply."We must ensure that our fire stations and our firefighters have the equipment they need to keep Florida safe and their families safe," Ingoglia said.Also at Monday's news conference, Ingoglia took questions regarding the upcoming property tax amendment vote and some of the funding concerns that cities and first responders are discussing if the amendment passes.In support of the amendment, Ingoglia said that many county budgets have "exploded over the last six years.""I don't think there is any one of these counties that their budgets have not increased anywhere between 60 to 160% over six years," the CFO said. "They have been an enormous beneficiary of a historic amount of property tax revenue that has flowed into the coffers. Right now, what I'm worried about is an affordability issue here in the state of Florida."Ingoglia said he believes there is a lot of room to offer property tax relief and still fund the necessary items for our first responders."I understand the anxiety of sheriffs and police chiefs and fire chiefs around the state where they're saying that their budgets may wind up being gutted and they might have to lay off people. I don't necessarily agree with that, but I think that also goes to their distrust of the people who are holding their budget because across the state the vast, vast, vast majority of their budgets are controlled by their county commissioners or their mayors. I will tell you that there's more than enough money to go around," Ingoglia said.Matty said at the moment she did not have concerns over response time lagging or budget cuts regarding the property tax amendment.

hero.headline: Palm City woman arrested after deputies rescue 24 Border Collies from hoarding home on SW Alligator Street
hero.body:
Martin County sheriff's deputies arrested Paige O'Donnell, 62, on Monday after rescuing 24 Border Collies from her home in the 1200 block of SW Alligator Street in Palm City. O'Donnell faces charges of felony animal cruelty and improper confinement, with Sheriff John Budensiek saying she will face at least 40 charges total, one felony and one misdemeanor for each dog rescued.

Deputies and Martin County Animal Services officers executed a search warrant at the property following an ongoing investigation. The conditions inside the home were described as deplorable, with feces covering every square inch of the house. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said it was extremely hot inside and that O'Donnell may not have had air conditioning.

The search warrant came after WPTV reporting revealed that Martin County Animal Control officers and sheriff's deputies had visited homes in the area at least 11 times since 2020, all related to concerns about dogs and their owners. After the news station began asking the sheriff's office about the house, investigators conducted days of surveillance. O'Donnell agreed last week to surrender one dog, which appeared to be malnourished, giving deputies probable cause to execute the warrant.

Budensiek said the dogs were running loose inside the house and described it as stacked with garbage. The rescued dogs were taken to the Humane Society in Martin County for care. O'Donnell is expected to make her first appearance before a judge on Tuesday. The case comes weeks after a U.S. Postal Service carrier was arrested after more than 100 dogs and cats were found in her Palm City home.

The search follows an ongoing investigation by Martin County Animal Services officers and sheriff’s detectives, who have been working to determine the scope of the situation and the condition of the animals. Authorities said approximately eight Border Collies had been removed from the home so far, while deputies and animal services officers continued working to safely remove the remaining dogs. Investigators said it was unclear exactly how many animals remained inside but that there was at least 29. The woman who was arrested was identified as Paige O'Donnell, 62. She is being charged with felony animal cruelty and improper confinement. The conditions inside the home were described as extremely concerning. Deputies and animal services officers were required to wear Tyvek protective clothing because of extensive accumulations of feces, urine-soaked materials, boxes and other debris throughout the residence. Authorities said those conditions were making it difficult and time-consuming to locate and safely remove the animals; they also said it was extremely hot and that she may not have had AC. Investigators and animal services personnel are continuing to assess the condition of the dogs and determine the full scope of the case. cards.headline: Hallandale Beach man arrested in Indian River County on charges of traveling to meet minors for sex
cards.teaser: Emaad Mir, 27, of Hallandale Beach was arrested Saturday in Indian River County after deputies say he drove two hours to Vero Beach to meet what he believed was an underage girl.
cards.body:
Emaad Mir, 27, of Hallandale Beach was arrested on Saturday in Indian River County on charges of traveling to meet a minor for unlawful sexual activity, transmitting harmful information to minors and unlawful use of a two-way communication device. Indian River County Sheriff's Office deputies responded to a home on Thursday, Aug. 6, where a mother reported her daughter was sexually battered by an adult man who went by the name of Adam.

The victim said she was contacted by the suspect on the messaging application TextNow and that the suspect picked her up near her residence during the early morning hours on July 31. The sheriff's office report notes that Adam allegedly had sexual contact with other underage girls who knew each other that occurred between June and July. In one instance, another female victim told deputies she attempted to purchase THC vape pens from the suspect, and when she met him and entered his vehicle, sexual contact occurred.

Deputies created a TextNow account and contacted the suspect while pretending to be the victim who attempted to purchase THC vape pens. Deputies persuaded the suspect to travel two hours to Vero Beach to meet. On Aug. 8, deputies stopped a dark blue Kia sedan near the 1300 block of 29th Avenue in Vero Beach. The victim who attempted to purchase THC vape pens was given a photo lineup and selected Mir as the person she believed was Adam. A court ordered Mir not to have contact with the victim, and he is being held in the Indian River County Jail on $1.75 million bail. Mir was previously arrested on Feb. 11, 2026, in Brevard County on allegations involving sexual activity with an underage female at Anderson Park in Rockledge. He was released from Brevard County Jail on Feb. 13 after posting $150,000 bond and has a scheduled court date in Brevard County on Aug.

cards.headline: Centennial High School student hit by car while crossing Crosstown Parkway in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was struck by a vehicle Monday morning at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard while attempting to cross against the pedestrian signal.
cards.body:
A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while attempting to cross a Port St. Lucie intersection against the pedestrian signal. The incident occurred shortly after 7 a.m. at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and Southwest Cameo Boulevard, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

Police say the preliminary investigation indicates the teenager attempted to cross Crosstown Parkway against the pedestrian signal, entering the roadway in front of oncoming traffic that had the right of way. The teen told investigators they believed they could make it across the street before an approaching vehicle reached them. However, the driver was unable to avoid striking the student.

The 16-year-old sustained superficial injuries but declined medical transport at the scene. The teen's guardians were notified of the incident. The vehicle involved in the crash sustained minor cosmetic damage. In March 2024, a 15-year-old student was hit by a car making a right turn onto Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard and was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

cards.headline: Four Indian River County schools reach 90% reading proficiency milestone through Moonshot Moment program
cards.teaser: Four elementary schools in Indian River County have achieved a 90% reading proficiency goal through a community-driven literacy program called the Moonshot Moment, drawing national attention to the effort.
cards.body:
Four schools in Indian River County have reached a 90% reading proficiency goal through a community-driven literacy program called the Moonshot Moment, a program born in 2012 through The Learning Alliance. The nonprofit was co-founded by parent Liz Remington, whose son struggled with reading. When Remington first launched the effort in 2017, just 56% of third graders in the district were reading at grade level.

The nonprofit brings together schools, philanthropists and business owners to fund added resources, including reading coaches in elementary classrooms. Rosewood Magnet School principal Adam Faust said the achievement came down to the final day. Six students had to test to make the 90% threshold, and the school needed three to be at proficiency or above. Five of those students made it. At Osceola Magnet School, principal Jennifer Norris said students will return to a new campus building and a new reading challenge after the school also cleared the 90% threshold. Norris said the school is shooting for 95% this year.

The stakes behind that goal are significant. If students are reading at grade level by third grade, data show they are going to be proficient readers for the rest of their life, Norris said. Other school districts across Florida are now looking at adopting the Moonshot Moment model, a continuation of a mission that started with one parent's child and has since helped thousands of students.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce approves 36-unit temporary family housing at GraceWay Village on Hartman Road
hero.body:
The Fort Pierce City Commission voted unanimously on August 3 to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit allowing GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct 36 dwelling units of temporary family housing at 1780 Hartman Road. The project will be built on 7.84 acres near the nonprofit's existing cafe and clothing boutique, with a density of 4.5 units per acre, well below the maximum of 15 units per acre allowed under the city's comprehensive plan for general commercial land use.

The development will proceed in three phases. Phase 1 will occupy 10,200 square feet and contain 10 dwelling units with support facilities. Phase 2 will add six buildings totaling 17,800 square feet, with each building containing three dwelling units. Phase 3 will expand the first facility by 6,300 square feet, adding eight additional dwelling units and support facilities. Each unit will be approximately 990 square feet, and 73.72 percent of the site will remain open space.

Assistant Planning Director Chris Suneson told the commission that the project met all code requirements and had been coordinated with the Technical Review Committee, with all departments supporting the application. St. Lucie County has required the applicant to provide a sidewalk in front of the property from north to south. The Planning Board had previously recommended approval unanimously at a July 13 meeting.

GraceWay Village CEO Chrystal Netherton told the Planning Board in July that the facility focuses on temporary stays to help families become self-sufficient. Project Engineer Mark Landsman said many residents might only need a three-month stay. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky made the motion for approval on August 3, which was seconded by Commissioner Michael Broderick and passed unanimously.
hero.article_text: The current view of the 7.84-acre property at 1780 Hartman Road owned by the not for profit Graceway Village. The City Commission voted unanimously Aug.3 to recommend to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit to enable GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct 36 dwelling units of temporary family housing on Hartman Road. The location of the 7.84 acre property at 1780 Hartman Road owned by the not-for-profit Graceway Village. The Fort Pierce City Commission voted unanimously Aug. 3 to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit to enable GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct 36 dwelling units of temporary family housing on the parcel. FORT PIERCE – The City Commission voted unanimously Aug. 3 to approve a major site plan and conditional use permit to enable GraceWay Village, Inc. to construct temporary congregate housing for adults and families on Hartman Road near the non-profit entity’s existing cafe and clothing boutique. The Planning Board previously heard the same requests on July 13, unanimously recommending approval. Assistant Planning Director Chris Suneson introduced the agenda item during the latest meeting. “This is a request this evening to review and approve an application for a major site plan with conditional use to allow adult congregate living facilities at 1780 Hartman Road,” he said. “The owner of Graceway Village Inc. proposes to construct a family shelter community centered on temporary housing with associated site improvements on 7.84 acres. The property contains two buildings [with] a combined 7,563 square feet that houses the applicant’s cafe program, clothing boutique and offices. The facilities were remodeled in 2009 and got some roofing permits in 2021.” Suneson proceeded to emphasize that the property’s underlying General Commercial Future Land Use enabled the location of just such a congregate living facility on the parcel as a conditional use. “The land development code sets forth several basic standards that adult congregant living facilities must meet,” he continued. “The most important of these is that maximum residential densities may not exceed the level determined by the comprehensive plan for general commercial. That maximum is 15 dwelling units to the acre, and with the proposed 36 dwelling units, the project has a density of 4.5 units to the acre.” The assistant planning director also described the site plan, which the applicant proposes to construct in three separate phases. “Phase 1 occupies 10,200 square feet and contains 10 dwelling units and support facilities,” he explained. “Phase 2 contemplates six additional buildings, comprising 17,800 square feet, with each building containing three dwelling units. The final phase is an expansion of the first facility with tri-plex cottages. Each unit will be about 990 square feet. It is an extension of the Phase 1 building, which would expand the family shelter building by an additional 6,300 square feet while also providing eight additional dwelling units and support facilities. Most of the site, 73.72 percent, will be left to open space. This project has been coordinated with the Technical Review Committee [and] all departments have supported the application.” Commissioner Michael Broderick was the first Board member to comment afterward and pose a question to Suneson. “If it was our job to just sit up here and rate the application based on need in the community, this would receive 110 percent approval,” he said. “However, that’s not what we’re here to do: We’re here to participate in a quasi-judicial hearing and determine facts. I reviewed this application in detail, site plans, everything. My only question is, is there any portion of the code that you’re aware of that this application does not meet?” “Not that I’m aware of sir,” Suneson replied. Commissioner Chris Dzadovsky raised a question to staff. “Due to the future use of this, congregant living and the possibility of families, is there any provision for transportation at this location, a local bus set aside for transportation?” he asked. Suneson did not have a positive reply to him on that inquiry, however, instead describing other planned improvements on the parcel. “First off, I do not believe this is on a public bus route,” he said. “Second, the applicant has been required by St. Lucie County to provide a sidewalk in front of the property from north to south. Thirdly, if you’re talking about private facilities, I think there’s plentiful parking and driveway access in order to provide that type of service if it’s contemplated in the future by the applicant.” GraceWay Village’s contracted Landscape Architect Brad Currie also addressed the Commission. “Tonight, I’m very grateful to be representing GraceWay Village and their request to expand their existing facility,” he said. Broderick, this is one of the few projects that I’ve brought before the City Commission that I didn’t think you were going to have any comments on, and you did still.” The commissioner, however, admitted this particular development had no apparent controversy or protest. “We usually tend to have a little bit of a friction point, but on this, I think we’re all in agreement,” Broderick explained. “I actually think this is a great location for the project.” Currie did acknowledge some concerns expressed by Planning Board member Krista Story on July 13 about potentially locating so much residential in a commercial use. The applicant’s contracted Project Engineer Mark Landsman attempted to allay her fears that same night. “This is not a permanent residence,” he said during the prior meeting. “These are temporary residences to help people get back on their feet, so it’s not going to be a long-term resident.” While GraceWay Village CEO Chrystal Netherton did not come to the podium during the Commission meeting, she did addressed Storey’s concerns as well during the Planning Board meeting. “The first day of coming to Graceway Village, we are talking about your exit strategy to get into your own permanent housing,” she said July 13. “This really is an opportunity for this family to be self-sufficient [and] learn the skills. Many of them might only need a three-month stay with us.” After no member of the public came forward to comment on Aug. 3, Commissioner Dzadovsky made a motion for approval, with was seconded by Commissioner Broderick and passed unanimously. hero.headline: Indian River County schools launch real-time bus tracking feature for parents
hero.teaser: The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child's bus in real time and receive push notifications when buses are running late.
hero.body:
The School District of Indian River County is rolling out a new feature in its free app this school year that allows parents to track their child's bus in real time. Parents can tap the bus icon in the district's app to see where the bus is and get an estimated arrival time. The app will also send push notifications when a bus is running late.

Superintendent David K. Moore says the new feature is designed to give parents more peace of mind. "You feel good as a parent, speaking as a parent, when your kid's in school. But when they are on the bus, there's just a little bit of angst until they get off that bus and walk in that front door," Moore told CBS12 News. "Now parents have greater access when they are walking in that front door."

The district is also adding another layer of security for students. Students will scan their school ID when they board the bus, allowing the district to keep better track of who is riding each bus. Moore says every school bus driver position is filled, meaning the district is fully staffed.

cards.headline: Troopers seek Ford F-150 driver after deadly e-bike hit-and-run in Vero Beach
cards.body:
A 48-year-old Vero Beach man riding an electric bicycle was killed after being struck by a pickup truck that fled the scene Sunday night in unincorporated Indian River County. The Florida Highway Patrol said the crash happened around 8:57 p.m. Sunday at the intersection of 8th Street and 14th Avenue.

The man was traveling west on an e-bike in the westbound lane of 8th Street as he approached 14th Avenue. A light-colored Ford F-150, believed to be a 2015 to 2020 model, was traveling behind him in the same lane. As the truck approached the bicyclist, the driver took evasive action and moved southwest, partially entering the eastbound lane. The truck still struck the bicyclist with its right side. The man was thrown onto the roadway and came to rest in the eastbound lane.

The driver fled without stopping to provide aid or contact law enforcement. Investigators say the truck may be missing its right-side rearview mirror due to the crash. The bicyclist was taken to Lawnwood Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

Both eastbound and westbound lanes of 8th Street were temporarily blocked during the investigation. The crash remains under investigation, and troopers are seeking the public's help in locating the truck driver. Anyone with information about the vehicle or driver is asked to contact FHP.

hero.headline: Centennial High School student hit by car at Port St. Lucie intersection
hero.body:
A 16-year-old Centennial High School student was hit by a vehicle Monday morning while crossing against the pedestrian signal at the intersection of Crosstown Parkway and SW Cameo Boulevard in Port St. Lucie. The crash occurred shortly after 7 a.m., according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.

The preliminary investigation indicates the teenager attempted to cross Crosstown Parkway against the pedestrian signal, entering the roadway in front of oncoming traffic that had the right of way. The teen told investigators they believed they could make it across the street before an approaching vehicle reached them. The driver was unable to avoid striking the student.

The 16-year-old sustained superficial injuries but declined medical transport at the scene. The teen's guardians were notified of the incident. The vehicle involved in the crash sustained minor cosmetic damage.

In March 2024, a 15-year-old student was hit by a car making a right turn onto Crosstown Parkway at Southwest Cameo Boulevard and was taken to the hospital with minor injuries.

cards.body:
Sunshine State of Mind Boutique opened in early June on Second Street in downtown Fort Pierce, offering Fort Pierce souvenirs, locally made works of art, and Florida-inspired apparel and gifts. The shop is owned by Kim Brant, who has worked in downtown Fort Pierce for many years, including 10 years at the Original Tiki Bar and the past five years at Cobbs Landing.

Brant said she saw the need for a shop dedicated to showcasing the city's charm and character. She designs most of the shirts and sweatshirts herself and keeps vendors as local as possible. One wall features a shelf labeled Locals Only, showcasing work by local artists and crafters.

Sunshine State of Mind Boutique is located at 102 N. 2nd St., Unit B, Fort Pierce. The shop is a family affair, with Brant's husband Chris and their children helping so she can continue working at Cobbs Landing.

hero.headline: Martin County schools cut three bus routes, saving $255,000 annually as students return
hero.body:
Martin County Public Schools reduced its bus routes from 58 to 55 as students returned to classrooms Monday, a move the school board voted to approve that will save the district $255,000 per year. Superintendent Michael Maine said the district is combining underused routes serving the same areas rather than eliminating any stops, and every bus will continue to operate within its legal capacity.

Maine said the district is right-sizing its transportation system because it does not make sense to have 16 or 20 students on a 77-passenger bus. Some routes may take a little longer, but drivers will be paid for any additional time they work. All buses have seatbelts, and depending on the age, students have to be buckled up.

The district will never run a transportation route or a bus that is over capacity, Maine said. While bus stops are not changing, some students may see a different bus number this year. The transportation department reports all 55 bus routes are covered with 56 drivers available.

Maine said families should expect the usual first-week delays as drivers settle into their new routes. Parents can check their child's bus assignment in the focus parent portal or track their bus in real time using the MyReaxium app. Some employees have raised concerns about what the route cuts could mean for already-crowded buses.

cards.article_text: Martin County Public Schools has earned its second consecutive A rating from the state, marking a significant turnaround from seven years of B-level performance through innovative teaching methods that prioritize individual student needs over traditional classroom instruction. Superintendent Michael Maine announced the district's back-to-back A grades for the 2024-25 and 2025-26 school years, crediting teachers and administrators who shifted away from whole-group instruction to personalized learning approaches that close achievement gaps The transformation centers on what Maine calls a "game changer" — moving beyond traditional classroom lectures to small-group instruction tailored to each student's skill level. "Instead of focusing on all whole group instruction, when the teacher is standing up in front of the classroom and just teaching the entire class, that's happening to introduce lessons," Maine explained. "But teachers are spending a lot more time individualizing the instruction for individual kids, pulling small groups, having smaller groups of students around the kidney table with them." Teachers now use education technology to track student progress in real-time and intervene quickly when students struggle. The data-driven approach allows educators to identify learning gaps and provide targeted remediation through small-group sessions. Martin County's success comes as Florida school districts face increasing pressure to improve academic outcomes while managing budget constraints and staffing challenges. The district's model demonstrates how strategic teaching methods can drive measurable results without reducing class sizes or significantly increasing costs. The district maintains regular class sizes mandated by state rules but transforms instruction delivery through centers and rotations that keep all students engaged at appropriate levels. "The teachers are doing a really good job making sure that while he or she's pulling a small group of students, the other students are also in groups working on things that they need," Maine said. Students rotate through differentiated instruction centers, with some working on advanced materials while others receive targeted support. Martin County enters the new school year nearly fully staffed, with 29 teaching vacancies remaining as of early August, with 16 candidates already in the onboarding process. Maine expects the district to be "in a really, really good position" when students return August 10. The transportation department reports all 55 bus routes covered with 56 drivers available. Student enrollment remains steady at approximately 16,000 students, consistent with recent years. Construction continues at Murray Middle School following significant tornado damage that destroyed two buildings and severely damaged a third. The multi-phase rebuilding project will deliver new facilities including band and chorus rooms, agricultural education spaces, a media center, administrative building, and additional classroom space. Maine said certain construction phases will be completed by December 2027, with others finishing by August 2027, depending on progress. The district launched a flexible education program, dubbed "flex tech," offering families alternatives including single-course enrollment, partial schedules, and fully virtual learning through Martin eSchool. "We really truly want to be the premier choice, the first choice for all of our families here in Martin County," Maine said. The program targets homeschool families who may need specific courses like advanced chemistry or algebra while maintaining connection to the district. Traditional high school students can also access evening courses or additional classes to enhance their academic preparation. Martin County continues expanding career and technical education programs that provide pathways to skilled trades and high-paying positions immediately after graduation. Programs include HVAC technician training, certified welding, construction trades, certified nursing assistant certification, drone flight operations, and entrepreneurship courses. "We have a lot of students that might want to go into a skilled trade right after high school and earn a really high-paying earning job," Maine said. The district continuously evaluates and upgrades security systems, including additional cameras, updated crisis alert badges, hardened front offices, and perimeter fencing improvements. "We're always going to be thinking first and foremost about the safety of our students," Maine said. "Anytime we see an area that needs to be improved, our safety and security team is quick to move in and get those fixed." Maine emphasized the district's commitment to living within its means while protecting classroom instruction from budget reductions. "We are great stewards of their taxpayer dollars. We do not spend more than we bring in," he said. Any operational adjustments have occurred at the district office level or through efficiency measures, not classroom programs. Looking ahead, Maine set an ambitious target for Martin County to rank among Florida's top 10 school districts while maintaining its A rating. "I want to be in the top 10 school districts in the state of Florida. We're working our way towards that goal," he said, emphasizing continuous improvement and professional development for staff. hero.headline: Man rescues woman trapped on railroad crossing in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
Josiah Baur rescued a woman whose car became stuck on train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound on Friday evening. Debbie Spoelstra was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway when a railroad crossing arm came down on her car, trapping her between the gates as a freight train approached. Baur was on his way home to Port St. Lucie when he stopped at the crossing and saw Spoelstra's red car stuck on the tracks.

Baur put his car in park and ran across the tracks to help. He lifted the crossing gate with both arms, allowing Spoelstra to back her car away from the tracks seconds before the train passed through. Dash camera video captured the rescue. Lizzy Dominguez, who witnessed the incident from behind Baur's car, posted a photo of Baur on social media to find and thank him.

Spoelstra said the crossing arm got stuck on her car antenna when she tried to reverse, preventing her from moving. She said she was not texting or distracted while driving and was taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. Witnesses reported the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. Spoelstra reported the malfunction to Florida East Coast Railway, which told her someone would inspect the gate.

Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing on Sunday and hugged when they saw each other. Spoelstra said her baby grandson shares the same name as Baur. Both attributed the rescue to faith and said they have bonded over the experience. Spoelstra urged other drivers to always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks.
hero.article_text: An act of bravery and compassion is bringing two strangers together on the Treasure Coast. A young man rescued a woman whose car got stuck on a railroad crossing in Hobe Sound, saving her from near disaster. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Just a few days ago, Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra didn’t know each other, but now, they share a special connection. “Friday, I was leaving work, and I was heading back home. I was trying to get home for a tire appointment, funny enough, and running late for it. Train crossing went down, and I looked down on my phone, and I glimpsed up, and I saw the car stuck behind the railroad crossing,” Baur said. Spoelstra was still inside that car, stuck on the train tracks at Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. What I did is, I put my car in reverse, and apparently the gate got stuck on top of my car on the antenna. So, when I tried to reverse, it would not let me reverse. I sat there, I saw the train,” Spoelstra said. Baur, realizing she was still in the car, didn’t hesitate and jumped out of his car to help. “I threw it in park and just took off running. Try to see what side the train was on to see if it would clear her or not. But it was on her side and didn't really want to take a chance. So, I ran across and tried to push up on the thingy to release her,” Baur said. That split-second decision helped to avoid what could have been a devastating crash from a freight train. “He came just like a hero. And lifted the gate up off of my car. And I was able to reverse and get off the tracks. And as soon as he did that, within seconds, the train passed by me. So it was very scary, you know, life-changing experience for me,” Spoelstra said. “We think of heroes, I think police officers and military, not what I did. It was just a good, good thing to do,” Baur said. The two said they’ve now bonded over this unique experience, attributing it to their shared faith. “He was put in one place, I was put in one place, and it was just fate. And it was a God thing, you know, and then once I told him my grandson was Josiah, and then he was just like, ‘Oh, wow. It's definitely a God thing.’ So, I don't know. I would just say, like I said, I'm so grateful for him,” Spoelstra said. He puts us exactly where we need to be. If you're running late for something, it's probably for a reason. Just trust his plan,” Baur said. Spoelstra said she wasn’t texting or distracted while driving and was simply just taken off guard by the railroad crossing arms lowering. She wants to pass this message on to other drivers: always be careful and look both ways before crossing train tracks. Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

hero.headline: Man lifts railroad crossing gate to rescue woman trapped on tracks in Hobe Sound
hero.body:
A 23-year-old man lifted a railroad crossing gate with his bare hands Friday evening to free a woman whose car became trapped on the tracks as a train approached on Bridge Road in Hobe Sound. Josiah Baur was driving home to Port St. Lucie from work when he stopped at the railroad crossing and saw Debbie Spoelstra's red car stuck between the crossing gates. A railroad crossing arm had come down on her car as she turned onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway, and dash-cam video captured a train horn blaring as the train moved closer.

Baur ran across the tracks toward the crossing. He lifted the gate with both arms, giving Spoelstra enough time to back her car away from the tracks before the train came through. Spoelstra said she was frozen in her car until she saw Baur running toward her. Another witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car and posted his photo on social media to find and thank him.

Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday and hugged. Spoelstra called Baur a true American hero and said she believes things could have turned out very differently if he had not been there. Baur said he was fortunate that God put him where he was at that moment.

Witnesses said the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. Spoelstra reported the problem to Florida East Coast Railway and was told someone would come out to inspect the gate. Spoelstra said her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who rescued her.
hero.article_text: What started as a routine drive home from work turned into a terrifying race against time for Debbie Spoelstra. Spoelstra says she was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound Friday evening when a railroad crossing arm suddenly came down on her car, leaving her trapped on the tracks. Dash-cam video captured the tense moments that followed. A train's horn can be heard as it quickly moved closer and closer to Spoelstra's red car as it sat between the crossing gates. Then, a young man runs toward her. I was pretty much frozen, Spoelstra said. Then I thought about getting out of the car, and then at that moment I saw Josiah running across the railroad tracks. That man was 23-year-old Josiah Baur. Baur said he left work late that evening and was on his way home to Port Saint Lucie when he stopped at the crossing. He was on the other side of the tracks when he saw what was happening. You only get a couple seconds to react, Baur said. He immediately ran toward the crossing. I just took off running, he said. Baur reached the crossing and lifted the gate with both arms, giving Spoelstra enough time to back her car away from the tracks before the train came through. He said he first looked to see where the train was. It was on her side, so I ran up and pushed up on it and released it just in time for her to back up, Baur said. Another witness, Lizzy Dominguez, was behind Baur's car when she saw what was happening. She and the others in her car could only watch. We were just saying, Please, God, please, God, please, God,’ Dominguez said. We were frozen in the car. After the rescue, Dominguez took a photo of Baur and posted it on social media , hoping to find him and thank him for what he had done. It was very emotional, Dominguez said. We thought, oh, we just witnessed a miracle. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing Sunday. When they saw each other, they hugged. Spoelstra said she's grateful to Baur and believes things could have turned out very differently if he hadn't been there. You know, first of all, that a total stranger, would help another person, she said. I won't ever forget what he's done for me. He is a true American hero. Baur, however, doesn't describe himself that way. I’m just very fortunate that God put me right where I was, he said. "He's got a plan and we just got to follow it sometimes. We don't understand why." Witnesses say the crossing arm malfunctioned during the incident. See also: Foodborne illnesses are rising. What not to eat right now. Spoelstra says she reported the problem to Florida East Coast (FEC) Railway line and was told someone would come out to inspect the gate. The incident remains a powerful reminder of how quickly a dangerous situation at a railroad crossing can unfold and how one person's decision to act can make all the difference. For Spoelstra, there is also a personal connection that makes the story feel even more remarkable. She says her baby grandson shares the same name as the man who came to her rescue: Josiah.

hero.headline: Indian River County students head to school before sunrise as new year begins Monday
hero.body:
Indian River County public schools begin the 2026-2027 school year on Monday, with buses picking up students sometimes in the dark. High schools open their doors to students at 7:20 a.m., middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m., and elementary schools at 9 a.m. Many students will be walking to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. Students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road are scheduled for pickup at 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district's strategic communications and marketing.

The School District and Indian River County Sheriff's Office are urging caution regarding school bus safety throughout the year. Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page that all schools are changing and new students entering schools will go through metal detectors. He asked parents to be patient during drop off periods. Flowers said all of the safety measures will take some time for everyone to get used to.

Vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children at two-lane paved roads and at multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to 6 months.

School district officials recommend children arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early and stay at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas. Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation, as well as the district's Facebook and Instagram accounts.
hero.article_text: Buses will be picking students sometimes in the dark as Indian River County public schools begin the 2026-2027 year. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – Public school for all students in Indian River County begins on Monday, Aug. High schools open their doors to students at 7:20 a.m.; middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m.; and elementary schools at 9 a.m. That means many students could be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district’s strategic communications and marketing. “Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas,” she said in a statement. “We also encourage families to remind students to wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street.” Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation , as well as the district s Facebook and Instagram accounts. The School District and Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urge all parents/students/motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “There will be new challenges with drop offs, pickups, buses,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff’s office’s Facebook page. “All the schools are changing and we want to make sure your kids are safe. We’ve got measures in place to make sure that it is a smooth beginning to the school year.” “Please be patient as during drop off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors,” he said. “All of the safety measures we have in place will take some time for everyone to get used to.” School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: * Have the child arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early. * Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. * Teach children to stay well off the roadway until the bus comes to a complete stop. * Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. * Ensure backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: * Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street * Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. * Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: * Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. * Never play or run near traffic. * Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. * If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: * Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. * Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. * Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. * Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. * Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. * Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. “Motorists also play an important role by slowing down, remaining alert in school zones and neighborhoods, and always stopping when required by (state) law for a school bus displaying its stop arm and flashing red lights,” Schafte said. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. hero.headline: Man rescues woman trapped on railroad tracks in Hobe Sound seconds before train arrives
hero.body:
Josiah Baur lifted a railroad crossing arm and pulled a trapped driver to safety seconds before a train passed through the intersection at Southeast Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound on Friday evening around 5 p.m. Debbie Spoelstra was turning onto Bridge Road from Dixie Highway when a railroad crossing arm came down on top of her car, trapping her on the tracks. Her car's antenna was caught on the crossing arm.

Baur, 23, was driving home to Port Saint Lucie from work when he stopped at the crossing and saw Spoelstra's red car stuck between the gates. Dash cam video from a nearby driver captured the moment Baur ran across the tracks toward Spoelstra's car as a train approached. Baur lifted the crossing arm with both arms, allowing Spoelstra to reverse her car away from the tracks just before the train came through on her side of the tracks.

Lizzy Dominguez witnessed the rescue from her car behind Baur's vehicle at the crossing. After the rescue, Dominguez took a photo of Baur and posted it on social media to find and thank him. Spoelstra and Baur met again at the railroad crossing on Sunday and hugged when they saw each other.

Spoelstra reported the crossing arm malfunction to Florida East Coast Railway and was told someone would inspect the gate. Spoelstra plans to take Baur and his family out for dinner as a thank you. She noted that her 9-month-old grandson shares the same name as her rescuer, Josiah.
hero.article_text: Josiah Baur and Debbie Spoelstra — two strangers turned friends, brought together by an incredible act of courage.It happened last Friday around 5 p.m., when Spoelstra was driving along Southeast Bridge Road and Dixie Highway in Hobe Sound. Spoelstra made a turn, and suddenly a crossing arm came down on top of her car, trapping her on the tracks. Her car's antenna was caught on the crossing arm."I just went to turn and as soon as I turned, the gate came down on the top of my car," Spoelstra said. "Then I realized that I was trapped it was absolutely trapped.”Dash cam video obtained from a nearby driver shows the close call. As Spoelstra tried to figure out what to do, she hoped someone would come to her aid."I know for sure somebody might come up from behind and help me, but you know didn't happen and then all of a sudden I looked and I saw my guardian angel coming over the track," Spoelstra said.That's when Baur, who was on his way home from work, spotted her car. Baur was in a rush at the time and calls the moment a lesson, because he was forced to slow down and help."I looked down on my phone looked back up, and I see Miss Debbie's car stuck on the train tracks with the arm down behind it," Baur said. “As she's trying to move and I was like holy cow she's stuck in the tracks. She's going to get hit so I threw it in parking and just took off running," Baur said.As Baur ran toward her, he was tracking the approaching train. "As I was running, I was trying to see where the train was, how far off it was, how much time and also which side of the track it was on and when I noticed it was on her side of track I'm like okay now or never we gotta do this," Baur said.Baur lifted the crossing arm, allowing Spoelstra to reverse to safety — just before the train came through."It was incredible and after he had he had lifted the gate off I don't know how many seconds passed by and then the train came right by so it was a close call. It was very close," Spoelstra said.For Baur, it was a close call, but the right thing to do. "Don't hesitate to help others when they're in need. I didn't sit there and think about it, if I sat there and he hesitated who knows if I would've got there in time," Baur said. "People say she's a stranger to me but she's a child of God just like I am.”The two believe the moment was meant to be."I think it was a God thing and for those if you don't believe, I don't know it was just a miracle," said Spoelstra.Spoelstra plans to take Baur and his family out for dinner as a thank you. She also noted an interesting connection — she has a 9-month-old grandson named Josiah. She says she will never forget what Baur did."He's an amazing individual. He is my guardian angel," Spoelstra said. "I'll never forget what he's done ever. I'm truly grateful and indebted to him.”This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. hero.headline: Daytona Tortugas rally to beat St. Lucie Mets 5-4, take series at Clover Park
hero.body:
The Daytona Tortugas defeated the St. Lucie Mets 5-4 on Sunday at Clover Park, winning the seven-game series 4-3. The Tortugas scored five runs across the fourth and fifth innings to build a 5-0 lead before holding off a late Mets rally.

Mets starter Joel Lara cruised through the first three innings, allowing just one baserunner on a walk. Lara struggled in the fourth, walking the first three batters. A wild pitch brought home Ichiro Cano for the first run. Anielson Buten hit a two-run single with two outs to make it 3-0. Cano hit the first pitch from reliever Jean Brito for a two-run homer in the fifth inning that made it 5-0.

The Mets mounted a comeback in the sixth inning when Elian Pea led off with a double against Lisnerkin Lantigua, extending his hitting streak to 11 games. Kuhio Aloy ripped a two-run double with two outs to get the Mets on the board, and Simon Juan followed with an RBI single to make it 5-3. Juan added a sacrifice fly in the eighth to pull the Mets within one at 5-4.

Daytona pitchers Lantigua and Jesus Colina retired the last six Mets batters in a row to secure the win. Colina earned his first save by retiring the side in order in the ninth with a fly out and back-to-back strikeouts. The Mets fell to 16-25 in the second half and 49-58 overall. They begin a six-game commuter series at the Jupiter Hammerheads on Tuesday with first pitch at Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium set for 6:30 p.m.
hero.article_text: Elian Peña started the Mets comeback bid in the sixth inning with a leadoff double against Lantigua. LUCIE – The Daytona Tortugas held off the St. Lucie Mets for a 5-4 victory in the series finale between the teams on Sunday at Clover Park. Daytona won the series 4-3. The Tortugas scored five runs across the fourth and fifth innings to take a 5-0 lead. The Mets scored three in the sixth and another run in the eighth to close the gap to one. But Daytona pitchers Lisnerkin Lantigua and Jesus Colina retired the last six Mets in a row to finish the game. Mets starter Joel Lara cruised through the first three innings, allowing just one base runner on a walk. However, Lara struggled with his command in the third, walking the first three batters. Lara threw a wild pitch that brought home Ichiro Cano for the first run. Then with two outs Anielson Buten hit a two-run single to make it 3-0. Jean Brito replaced Lara with one on and out in the fifth inning. Cano hit the first pitch from Brito for a two-run homer that made it 5-0. Meanwhile Daytona starter Justin Henschel was cruising. Henschel shut out the Mets over 5.0 innings on 75 pitches. He scattered three hits, walked one and struck out four. Elian Peña started the Mets comeback bid in the sixth inning with a leadoff double against Lantigua. The double extended Peña’s hitting streak to 11 games. Later in the inning with two outs Kuhio Aloy ripped a two-run double to get the Mets on the board. Simon Juan followed with a RBI single to make it 5-3. The first two Mets reached base to start the eighth inning vs. Lantigua but the Mets only got a sac fly by Juan to make it 5-4. Colina retired the side in order in the ninth with a fly out and back-to-back strikeouts to notch his first save. The first seven batters in the Mets order recorded a hit. Reed Stallman went 2 for 4. Julio Zayas went 1 for 3 win a single, walk and run to add to his bid for FSL Player of the Week. Austin Brown (undrafted 2025 – Chipola JC) made his team debut by pitching two scoreless innings in the seventh and eighth. The Mets (16-25, 49-58) are off on Monday. They return to action on Tuesday when they begin a six-game commuter series at the Jupiter Hammerheads. First pitch from Roger Dean Chevrolet Stadium is 6:30 p.m. Your comment has been submitted. hero.headline: Indian River County students head to school Monday with some bus stops before sunrise
hero.body:
Public school begins Monday, August 10, for all students in Indian River County, with some bus stops scheduled before sunrise. High schools open at 7:20 a.m., middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m., and elementary schools at 9 a.m. The earliest bus stop is scheduled for 5:51 a.m. near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district's strategic communications and marketing.

Many students will be walking to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas, Schafte said. The School District and Indian River County Sheriff's Office urge all parents, students, and motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff's office's Facebook page that there will be new challenges with drop offs, pickups, and buses. He asked parents to be patient during drop off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors. All of the safety measures in place will take some time for everyone to get used to, he said.

Vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children at two-lane paved roads and at multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to 6 months. Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested on animal cruelty charge after video shows dog being kicked
hero.body:
A 68-year-old Port St. Lucie man was arrested on August 6 on an animal cruelty charge following the circulation of a video on social media that appeared to show the abuse of a small dog. Ricky Lee Schieferstein was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail as of August 7 on a $7,500 bond on a charge of cruelty to animals, according to the jail website.

The investigation began after numerous members of the community shared the video and tagged the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office across its social media platforms, according to the sheriff's office Facebook posting. The information was then turned over to the sheriff's office criminal investigations division for investigation. Detective Dawn Dale, through her investigation, developed probable cause and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Schieferstein with animal cruelty.

In the 16-second video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page with a viewer discretion warning, a man can be seen walking behind a dog at a concrete pool and yelling out, out, out ... in the grass several times and kicking the dog in its right hip at least once before the dog and the man went out of range.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office stated in its Facebook posting that while it appreciates the public's assistance in bringing this incident to attention, residents should remember that the fastest and most effective way to report a crime in progress or suspicious activity is by calling 911. The sheriff's office noted that while it actively monitors its social media platforms, they are not monitored continuously and should never be relied upon to report emergencies or crimes requiring an immediate law enforcement response.

hero.headline: American Paint Horse stolen from pasture in Port St. Lucie, sheriff's office seeks public help
hero.teaser: A 2-year-old stallion named Strait from Above was last seen Sunday afternoon at 2801 Williams Road near St. Lucie West.
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is asking for the public's help locating a missing American Paint Horse believed to have been stolen from its owner's pasture in Port St. Lucie. The 2-year-old stallion named Strait from Above was last seen at approximately 3 p.m. Sunday at 2801 Williams Road near St. Lucie West and west of Interstate 95 in a rural area.

Distinctive features include a white forelock and mane with a black and white tail, and a pinto coat with distinctive black and white spots. The breed typically stands 56-64 inches and weighs between 950 and 1,200 pounds, according to the American Paint Horse Association. The agency asked residents, property owners, horse enthusiasts, agricultural communities, and anyone who may have seen or been offered a horse matching this description to take a close look at the identifying information.

Anyone with potential sightings or information can report them to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-7300 or submit a tip by email at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com. Every detail could help bring Strait from Above home safely, the agency posted Saturday on Facebook.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office employee killed in Port St. Lucie murder-suicide
cards.body:
Elizabeth Ortega, a 50-year-old communications officer with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, was killed in a murder-suicide Saturday night in Port St. Lucie. The shooting happened both inside and outside a home in the 2000 block of Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Ortega had been employed at PBSO for the last 10 years.

Police said a man began shooting at the woman inside their home, chased her outside, and continued firing, hitting her multiple times. One of the neighbors located Ortega after they observed her lying in the front yard unresponsive, according to Officer Brittany McNally of the Port St. Lucie Police Department. The shooter was Ortega's longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr., who went back inside the home and killed himself after killing Ortega.

McNally said Ortega and Varela had been together for about 30 years, but Ortega had recently ended the relationship. Although the relationship had ended, it appears the two had agreed to live together until Varela could find other living arrangements. The couple's son, Varela Jr., a firefighter with Palm Beach County Fire Rescue, had left the home just minutes before the shooting and told police everything seemed fine.

Investigators are working to determine what led to the violence. There is no evidence to suggest that there was a disagreement, a disturbance or an argument that occurred directly prior to the shooting, McNally said. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office posted about Ortega on social media Monday afternoon, saying she was a respected and cherished part of the PBSO family, known for her kindness, compassion, and a warm smile that could brighten any room. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office has provided therapy dogs to help Ortega's co-workers cope with the loss.

The investigation began after numerous members of the community shared the video and tagged the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office across its social media platforms. The information was then turned over to the sheriff's office criminal investigations division for investigation. Detective Dawn Dale, through her investigation, developed probable cause and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Schieferstein with animal cruelty.

In the 16-second video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page with a viewer discretion warning, a man can be seen walking behind a dog at a concrete pool and yelling out, out, out, in the grass several times and kicking the dog in its right hip at least once before the dog and the man went out of range.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office stated in a Facebook posting that while it appreciates the public's assistance in bringing this incident to its attention, it also wants to remind residents that the fastest and most effective way to report a crime in progress or suspicious activity is by calling 911. The sheriff's office stated that while it actively monitors its social media platforms, they are not monitored continuously and should never be relied upon to report emergencies or crimes requiring an immediate law enforcement response.

hero.headline: Indian River County students head back to school Monday with some bus pickups before sunrise
hero.body:
Public school begins Monday for all students in Indian River County, with high schools opening at 7:20 a.m., middle and K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m., and elementary schools at 9 a.m. Some students will walk to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter, particularly those meeting the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district's strategic communications and marketing.

Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas. Students should wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street. The School District and Indian River County Sheriff's Office urge all parents, students, and motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year.

Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page that new challenges with drop offs, pickups, and buses will require patience. All schools are changing and new students entering through metal detectors will take some time for everyone to get used to. Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation, as well as the district's Facebook and Instagram accounts.

Vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children at two-lane paved roads and at multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to 6 months. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie police release 911 call from weekend murder-suicide on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police on Wednesday released the 911 call from a neighbor following a weekend murder-suicide at a home on Southeast Oxmoor Terrace. Authorities identified the victim as 50-year-old Elizabeth Ortega, a communications officer for the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office. Investigators believe Ortega was shot and killed by her longtime boyfriend, 50-year-old Ralph Varela Sr., who then shot and killed himself.

According to police, Ortega had recently ended their 30-year relationship, but the two were still living together while Varela searched for a new place to live. The neighbor who called 911 said she had been in her backyard with her children when they heard the gunshots. There were six of them, the neighbor said during the call, adding that she thought it was fireworks at first but the sound made her house rattle.

The caller said she did not know her neighbors' names but mentioned she often heard them yelling. When asked by the dispatcher if her neighbors were fighting, the caller said she did not know if they were fighting but that they were always cursing at each other. Police arrived at the scene and began their investigation, which they are calling a murder-suicide.

The National Domestic Violence Hotline is available 24 hours a day at 800-799-SAFE. Locally, 2-1-1 also provides resources around the clock.

hero.body:
The Costco at 3173 Kanner Highway in Stuart has reopened following an electrical fire that temporarily closed the store on Thursday. Store management told the Stuart Police Department that only dry goods are available for purchase because the refrigeration unit is not operational.

The Stuart Police Department said the electrical fire at the Kanner Highway location has been extinguished. Shoppers and travelers were asked to avoid the area while the store was closed.

The fire disrupted normal operations at the Martin County location. The store has since resumed limited service while the refrigeration system remains down.

Customers visiting the Stuart Costco can purchase dry goods but will not be able to buy refrigerated or frozen items until the refrigeration unit is repaired.
