hero.headline: St. Lucie County schools reopen Monday with new bus safety warnings
hero.body:
Public school for all students in St. Lucie County begins Monday, Aug. 10, with the St. Lucie County School District and St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office urging parents, students, and motorists to exercise caution around school buses throughout the 2026-27 school year. The seven high schools will open for students as early as 7:33 a.m., and the daily start of school for eleven K-8 grade schools is 7:35 a.m. Lincoln Park Academy in Fort Pierce begins its days at 7:23 a.m. Dan McCarty and Forest Grove middle schools start sessions at 9:30 a.m., while the start of school for Southern Oaks and Southport middle schools is at 9:40 a.m.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said motorists must obey school zone speed limits and always stop when a school bus displays its flashing red lights and extended stop arm. Parents should review bus stop safety with their children, and students should remain attentive, follow the bus driver's instructions, and never cross the street until they are signaled to do so safely. Lydia Martin, chief communications officer for St. Lucie County School District, said families should allow extra travel time during the first few weeks of school as traffic patterns increase and students adjust to their routines.

Drivers are required by Florida law to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to 6 months.

School district officials recommend parents have children arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early, supervise younger children while they wait, and ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. Students should stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting, never play or run near traffic, and stay out of the bus's danger zone. The Here Comes The Bus app can be downloaded at www.herecomesthebus.com. Anyone who sees unsafe driving around school buses, dangerous conditions at bus stops, or suspicious activity near bus stops can report it to local law enforcement or the St. Lucie Public Schools Transportation Department at 772-204-RIDE.

At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after video shows alleged dog abuse
cards.teaser: Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, was arrested following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man appearing to kick a small dog in his backyard near a pool.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man abusing a small dog, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office. Video from the sheriff's office shows Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, appearing to kick a small dog in his backyard near a pool. The video made rounds on social media, and the outrage sparked an investigation from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office.

Following the investigation, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office's findings gave detectives probable cause to charge Shieferstein with animal cruelty. Shieferstein is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $7,500 bond.

The Costco at 3173 Kanner Highway in Stuart has reopened following an electrical fire that temporarily closed the store on Thursday. The Stuart Police Department said the fire has been extinguished.

Store management told police that only dry goods are available for purchase because the refrigeration unit is not operational. The Stuart Police Department asked shoppers and travelers to avoid the area while the store was closed.

The electrical fire forced the closure of the location on Kanner Highway. The Stuart Police Department confirmed the incident and said the fire had been put out.

The store has resumed operations with limited merchandise available. Shoppers can purchase dry goods but cannot buy refrigerated or frozen items until the refrigeration system is restored.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested after social media video shows alleged dog abuse
hero.teaser: A Port St. Lucie man was arrested after a video circulating on social media appeared to show him abusing a small dog in his backyard.
hero.body:
Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, of Port St. Lucie was arrested August 6 on an animal cruelty charge after the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office investigated a video that circulated on social media. The 16-second video shows a man walking behind a dog at a concrete pool and yelling out, out, out ... in the grass several times and kicking the dog in its right hip at least once before the dog and the man went out of range.

The investigation began after numerous members of the community shared the video and tagged the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office across its social media platforms. Detective Dawn Dale developed probable cause and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Shieferstein with animal cruelty. Shieferstein was being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $7,500 bond as of August 7.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office warns against using social media to report crimes
cards.teaser: The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office reminded residents to call 911 for crimes in progress after an animal cruelty case was reported through social media tags.
cards.body:
Following the arrest of Ricky Lee Schieferstein on animal cruelty charges after a social media video showed alleged dog abuse, the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office issued a reminder about how to report crimes. The sheriff's office said that while it appreciates the public's assistance in bringing incidents to its attention, social media platforms are not monitored continuously and should never be relied upon to report emergencies or crimes requiring an immediate law enforcement response.

The fastest and most effective way to report a crime in progress or suspicious activity is by calling 911, according to the sheriff's office. The case began after numerous members of the community shared a video and tagged the sheriff's office across its social media platforms before the information was turned over to the criminal investigations division.

The information was then turned over to the sheriff’s office’s criminal investigations division for investigation. Dawn Dale, through her investigation, developed probable cause and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Schieferstein with animal cruelty, according to the Facebook posting. hero.headline: Indian River County approves expansion of Westside Racquet Club in Vero Beach
hero.body:
The Indian River County Commission approved a special exception use and Phase 1 site plan on August 4 for the renovation and expansion of the Westside Racquet Club, a 1970s-era facility in Vero Beach that has fallen into disrepair in recent years. The 6.89-acre property is located east of 43rd Avenue Southwest, north of 6th Lane Southwest and south of Fifth Place Southwest.

Phase 1 of the project will restore the existing eight tennis courts, construct four new padel courts and construct associated site improvements including utilities, stormwater, parking and landscaping. The existing 2,400-square-foot clubhouse will be restored in Phase 2, which will also add two padel courts. Phase 3 will include a pool house and four pickleball courts, while Phase 4 will add two additional tennis courts. The Planning Zoning Commission voted unanimously to recommend approval on June 11 but added a special condition due to concerns about potential noise pollution and light infiltration onto adjacent properties.

Vice-Chairwoman Laura Moss expressed concerns about voting on the special exception use that would cover all four phases while only approving the Phase 1 site plan, saying commissioners were being asked to vote in the blind. She also raised concerns about pickleball noise and lighting impacts on neighboring residents. Planning Development Services Director John Stoll said the county can require traffic studies once the project exceeds 400 average daily trips and can implement noise mitigation measures including limiting nighttime lighting and operational hours, requiring special paddles and balls, and increasing separation from neighbors.

District 3 Commissioner Joseph Earman pointed out the continuity of use on the parcel and said he had heard from residents who think the improvements will add value to their property. Mark Jaffe, a 4th Lane Southwest resident, was the only public speaker and said he would like to see the project move forward. The County Commission voted unanimously to approve the requests.
hero.article_text: The aerial and location map for the 6.89-acre property home to the current Westside Racquet Club whose new owner had requested a conditional use permit and Phase 1 site plan approval for a significant remodeling and expansion project. The aerial and location map for the 6.89-acre property home to the current Westside Racquet Club whose new owner had requested a conditional use permit and Phase 1 site plan approval for a significant remodeling and expansion project. VERO BEACH – The Indian River County Commission approved the special exception use and Phase 1 site plan Aug. 4 for the renovation and expansion of the existing Westside Racquet Club, a 1970s-era facility that in recent years has fallen into disrepair. The Planning Zoning Commission previously heard the same requests on June 11, voting unanimously to recommend approval but adding a special condition of approval due to concerns about potential noise pollution and light infiltration onto adjacent property owners. Senior Planner Kelly McKinley introduced the agenda item during the latest meeting. “Before you today is the Westside Racquet Club’s special exception use and site plan approval request to expand the existing facility with the intent of restoring it, as well as providing additional enhancements,” she said. “The subject parcel is 6.89 acres located east of 43rd Avenue Southwest, north of 6th Lane Southwest and south of Fifth Place Southwest. The special exception use will cover all four phases, [but] only Phase 1 is before you for site plan approval at this time. The additional phases will subsequently be approved.” McKinley proceeded to provide further details on the color-coded phasing plan for the property, which currently houses a small, existing racquet court building and eight tennis courts. “The white [Phase 1] is going to restore the existing eight tennis courts, construct four new padel courts and construct associated site improvements like utilities, stormwater, parking and landscaping,” she continued. “The green will restore the existing 2,400-square-foot clubhouse and construct two additional padel courts. Phase 3, the pink, will include the pool house as a clubhouse amenity and construct four pickleball courts. Phase 4, the blue, will consist of two additional tennis courts.” McKinley also described the proposed stormwater improvements and landscaping plan, which will include a stormwater pond along the southern part of the project and a swale. Additional landscaping will include a 20-foot buffer along 43rd Avenue Southwest and a 30-foot-Type B landscape buffer around the other three perimeters. Foundation plantings will be installed around the pool and the existing clubhouse building. After she recommended approval and described the P Z Commission’s additional condition of approval, Vice-Chairwoman Laura Moss posed her first question and initial concerns to staff. “I’m just confirming what they’re adding,” she said. “So, it’s four padel courts, a pool and four pickleball courts. Is that reason why this is a special exception?” “The site is zoned RS-3,” McKinley replied. “Within that zoning district, the use itself is the special exception.” Chairman Deryl Loar chimed in with another important fact. “I think it’s also because you’re going over a threshold and you’re expanding the existing use by more than 10 percent,” he said. Vice-Chairwoman Moss then addressed the heart of her concern, the fact that all subsequent phases would be administratively approved and not require any further public hearings. “I think to vote on this, we’re in effect being asked operationally to vote in the blind because I don’t know what it’s going to be in totality,” she continued. “Once we grant the special exception, basically anything goes [and] we lose control of it. On top of that, if we change it, that land maintains the special exception designation no matter who owns it.” Vice-Chairwoman Moss acknowledged that she’d viewed the June Planning Zoning Commission hearing and lamented what she viewed as a lack of technical expertise for the concerned neighboring residents. She also bemoaned the fact the applicant’s representative was not present that day. “Pickleball is very loud, [and] somebody made a really good point,” she said of the earlier hearing. “The noise ordinance only applies when it’s a sustained level of sound. Pickleball’s not a sustained level of sound, so they really don’t have protection in terms of the noise. It was mentioned that the lighting would end up in peoples’ backyards. A privacy fence was suggested. I’m not comfortable that this was thoroughly addressed and will not adversely affect the public interest.” While Chairman Loar responded by insisting her comment about losing control was “not an exact description of our professional staff,” Deputy County Attorney Susan Prado provided a legal opinion of the exact task before commissioners that morning. She also attempted to alleviate some of the vice-chairwoman’s concerns about the lack of technical expertise during the P Z Commission hearing. “As was stated, none of the other phases will come back,” Prado said. “If you’re wanting to place conditions on the other phases, that will need to be placed today as well as for all phases. As far as evidence presented, affected persons can come forward and present their evidence as to issues. If there is that [pickleball noise] concern, there is case law that says both sides have to bring their own professionals and that will also include the people impacted.” For his part, District 3 Commissioner Joseph Earman pointed out the continuity of use on the parcel and local community support for the planned improvements. “Commissioners understand this has always been what it’s always been – it’s nothing different,” he said. “It just went silent because it had no ownership. I’ve heard from a few of the residents out there that think it’s great because it’ll add value to their property and everything as a whole because it is run down right now.” Vice-Chairwoman Moss’ final concern was related to potential traffic impacts, which were addressed by Planning Development Services Director John Stoll, who also touched on her noise and lighting concerns. “The traffic studies will be cumulative,” he explained. “As soon as they have a use that kicks them over the 400 average daily trips, we’ll require a traffic study. We have a number of noise-mitigation measures that we’ve found, including a new noise study specifically to pickleball. We can limit nighttime lighting and operational hours, require special paddles and balls and increase the separation from the neighbors if we need to.” There was only public speaker that evening, 4th Lane Southwest resident Mark Jaffe. “I travel on 5th Street Southwest every single day since 1996 and pass this neighborhood many times a day,” he said. “When I moved here, Westside Neighborhood was there. I drive past that dilapidated racquet club almost every single day. I would like to see this move forward.” The County Commission then voted unanimously to approve the requests. hero.headline: American Paint Horse stolen from Port St. Lucie pasture, sheriff's office seeks public help
hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is asking the public for help locating a missing American Paint Horse believed to have been stolen from its owner's pasture in Port St. Lucie. The 2-year-old stallion named Strait from Above was last seen at approximately 3 p.m. Sunday at 2801 Williams Road near St. Lucie West and west of Interstate 95 in a rural area.

The horse has distinctive features including a white forelock and mane with a black and white tail, and a pinto coat with distinctive black and white spots. The breed typically stands 56 to 64 inches and weighs between 950 and 1,200 pounds, according to the American Paint Horse Association.

The sheriff's office posted on Facebook Saturday that every detail could help bring Strait from Above home safely. Authorities are asking residents, property owners, horse enthusiasts, agricultural communities, and anyone who may have seen or been offered a horse matching this description to take a close look at the identifying information.

Anyone with information can report potential sightings or tips to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at 772-462-7300 or submit a tip by email at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com.

hero.body:
Port St. Lucie police arrested Ricky Lee Shieferstein, 68, on Aug. 6 following an investigation into a social media video that shows a man abusing a small dog. The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office received numerous reports from community members who shared the video and tagged the agency across its social media platforms. The video shows a man walking behind a dog at a concrete pool and yelling out, out, out in the grass several times and kicking the dog in its right hip at least once.

The information was turned over to the sheriff's office criminal investigations division. Detective Dawn Dale developed probable cause through her investigation and obtained an arrest warrant to charge Shieferstein with animal cruelty.

Shieferstein is being held at the St. Lucie County Jail on a $7,500 bond. The video circulated widely on social media, sparking outrage and prompting the investigation.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office posted the case to its Facebook page with a viewer discretion warning. The agency reminded residents that the fastest and most effective way to report a crime in progress or suspicious activity is by calling 911, stating that while it actively monitors social media platforms, they are not monitored continuously and should never be relied upon to report emergencies or crimes requiring an immediate law enforcement response.

cards.headline: Road rage ends in four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 in Port St. Lucie, man arrested
cards.teaser: A road rage confrontation between a motorcyclist and a pickup truck driver erupted into a violent four-vehicle crash on U.S. 1 Wednesday, leaving four people injured.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie police responded around 6:45 p.m. Wednesday to the intersection of South U.S. Highway 1 and SE Lyngate Drive/SE Tiffany Avenue, where a red Harley-Davidson motorcycle and a black Ford Super Duty pickup truck were involved in an ongoing road rage incident. The pickup, driven by 54-year-old Kevin Lonergan, was pursuing the motorcycle as both vehicles traveled northbound on U.S. 1 and approached the intersection, according to witness statements and dash-camera video.

The motorcycle entered the intersection against a red light and collided with a black Chevrolet Silverado, throwing the 31-year-old rider from the bike. Lonergan then entered the intersection against the red signal, struck the ejected motorcyclist, and crashed head-on into a blue Toyota RAV4. The motorcyclist and two people inside the RAV4 were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center. The Silverado driver was transported to St. Lucie Medical Center.

The motorcyclist suffered serious injuries, including a brain bleed and facial fractures, and lost consciousness after the crash. He remains hospitalized in stable condition. Police arrested Lonergan for two counts of reckless driving causing serious bodily injury and one count of reckless driving causing injury. After being medically cleared, Lonergan was booked into the St. Lucie County Jail. The intersection remained closed for hours while investigators processed the scene before all lanes reopened around 2 a.m.

hero.headline: Indian River County schools open Monday with some bus pickups before sunrise
hero.body:
Public schools in Indian River County open Monday, Aug. 10, for the 2026-2027 school year, with high schools starting at 7:20 a.m., middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m., and elementary schools at 9 a.m. Some students will be walking to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter, particularly students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district's strategic communications and marketing.

The School District and Indian River County Sheriff's Office urge all parents, students, and motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety. Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff's office Facebook page that all schools are changing and there will be new challenges with drop-offs, pickups, and buses. He asked parents to be patient during drop-off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors.

At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. The same rule applies to two-lane paved roads. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to six months.

Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop-off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas, Schafte said. Families should remind students to wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street. Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation, as well as the district's Facebook and Instagram accounts.
hero.article_text: Buses will be picking students sometimes in the dark as Indian River County public schools begin the 2026-2027 year. At multi-lane paved roads without a raised median or physical barrier, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. At two-lane paved roads, vehicles traveling in both directions must stop when a school bus is stopped to pick up or discharge children. INDIAN RIVER COUNTY – Public school for all students in Indian River County begins on Monday, Aug. High schools open their doors to students at 7:20 a.m.; middle school K-8 schools at 8:10 a.m.; and elementary schools at 9 a.m. That means many students could be walking to bus stops sometimes in the dark on a on a daily basis as the days grow shorter. That is especially true for students who meet the bus at the stop near State Road 60 and Rollins Ranch Road, scheduled for 5:51 a.m., according to Dr. Kyra Schafte, executive director of the school district’s strategic communications and marketing. “Parents who drive their children to bus stops should park a safe distance away from buses during both morning pickup and afternoon drop off to help maintain clear visibility and safe loading areas,” she said in a statement. “We also encourage families to remind students to wait until the school bus has come to a complete stop and the stop arm is fully extended before approaching or crossing the street.” Transportation details are available on the Indian River County schools webpage at www.indianriverschools.org/o/sdirc/page/transportation , as well as the district s Facebook and Instagram accounts. The School District and Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urge all parents/students/motorists to be cautious and observe rules and laws pertaining to school bus safety throughout the 2026-27 school year. “There will be new challenges with drop offs, pickups, buses,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said in a video posted on the sheriff’s office’s Facebook page. “All the schools are changing and we want to make sure your kids are safe. We’ve got measures in place to make sure that it is a smooth beginning to the school year.” “Please be patient as during drop off periods as new students entering the schools are entering through metal detectors,” he said. “All of the safety measures we have in place will take some time for everyone to get used to.” School district officials offer these tips that parents are encouraged to review with their children regarding bus safety: * Have the child arrive at the bus stop at least 10 minutes early. * Supervise younger children while they wait for the bus. * Teach children to stay well off the roadway until the bus comes to a complete stop. * Remind children to wait for the driver’s signal before crossing the street. * Ensure backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors. When walking to a bus stop, children should: * Make eye contact with the driver before crossing the street * Cross at least 10 feet in front of the bus. * Never cross behind a school bus. At bus stops, students should: * Stand at least 10 feet away from the roadway while waiting. * Never play or run near traffic. * Stay out of the bus’s ‘danger zone’—the area around the front sides, and rear where the driver may not see anyone. * If something is dropped near the bus, tell the driver instead of reaching under the bus. When on the bus, students should: * Stay seated in assigned seats and wear seat belts (when equipped) while the bus is moving. * Keep hands, arms, and head inside the bus. * Keep aisles clear of backpacks and personal items. * Speak quietly so the driver can focus on driving safely. * Do not eat, drink or throw objects on the bus. * Follow the driver’s instructions at all times. “Motorists also play an important role by slowing down, remaining alert in school zones and neighborhoods, and always stopping when required by (state) law for a school bus displaying its stop arm and flashing red lights,” Schafte said. Drivers also must stop on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier, according to the state Department of Transportation’s web site As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver’s license for 90 days up to 6 months A driver does not have to stop when traveling in the opposite direction only if the roadway is divided by a raised median, a physical barrier or an unpaved median at least five feet wide, according to the DOT web site. In addition, the driver’s cell phone must be “hands-free” in a school zone. Using a wireless communications device in a handheld manner while driving in a designated school crossing, school zone, or active work zone area is against the law, according to the DOT web site. hero.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is seeking the public's help locating a missing American Paint Horse believed to have been stolen from its owner's pasture in Port St. Lucie. The 2-year-old stallion named Strait from Above was last seen at approximately 3 p.m. Sunday at 2801 Williams Road near St. Lucie West and west of Interstate 95 in a rural area.

The horse has distinctive features including a white forelock and mane with a black and white tail and a pinto coat with distinctive black and white spots. The breed typically stands 56-64 inches and weighs between 950 and 1,200 pounds, according to the American Paint Horse Association.

The sheriff's office is asking residents, property owners, horse enthusiasts, agricultural communities, and anyone who may have seen or been offered a horse matching this description to report any potential sightings or information to the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office at (772) 462-7300 or submit a tip by email at PatrolTips@stluciesheriff.com.

hero.headline: Martin County firefighters rescue tree trimmer trapped 40 feet in air in Stuart
hero.body:
Martin County Fire Rescue crews on Saturday afternoon freed a tree trimmer who became trapped about 40 feet in the air after his lift stopped working in Stuart. Firefighters were dispatched around 1 p.m. to find the man stuck on the lift, which had stopped moving up and down while he was trimming trees in the area.

Limited access for a ladder forced crews to use a specialized high-angle rescue approach. Firefighters first removed nearby tree limbs, then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to the ground.

Paramedics evaluated the man once he reached the ground and determined he had minor injuries. The man declined transportation to the hospital.

Martin County Fire Rescue credited C-Shift crews from Heavy Rescue 23, Battalion 2, EMS 2 and EMS 22 for completing the rescue.

He had been trimming trees in the area when the equipment stopped working. Because access for a ladder was limited, firefighters used a specialized rescue approach. Crews first removed nearby tree limbs. They then used a series of high-angle rescue maneuvers to secure the man, transfer his weight and carefully bring him to safety. Once he was back on the ground, paramedics evaluated him and determined he had minor injuries. The man declined transportation to the hospital. cards.headline: F-bombs fly in confrontation over Port St. Lucie campaign signs
cards.teaser: A profanity-laced confrontation was captured on video between mayoral challenger Steve Giordano and the husband of incumbent Mayor Shannon Martin.
cards.body:
As the August election approaches, tensions are rising between the two political camps as incumbent Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin faces challenger Steve Giordano in the race for mayor. The incidents prompted the Port St. Lucie Police Department to launch investigations into two separate cases involving campaign signs, one of which led to a confrontation.

During the overnight hours Friday, Aug. 7, Giordano told CBS12 News that he and his campaign manager were putting up signs near Southwest Airoso Boulevard and Southwest Thornhill Drive. Giordano said he saw a man remove a sign from the ground and throw it. Giordano then grabbed his cellphone and began recording the encounter. The man appears to be Shannon Martin's husband, Aaron Martin, a lieutenant with the Port St. Lucie Police Department. Video shows a profanity-laced confrontation between Giordano and Martin, with the two shouting at each other and making accusations about campaign signs being placed in the community without property owners' permission.

Police said investigators learned that one homeowner had given permission for one campaign sign to be placed on the property, while another resident of the home, who has limited English proficiency, told members of the opposing campaign they could also place a sign there. Investigators said the language barrier contributed to the confrontation over the campaign signs and whether the previously placed sign could be moved or removed. At this time, police said there is no indication that any campaign signs involved in the incident were stolen or intentionally damaged.

hero.headline: Martin County schools open Monday with new school bus safety measures and earlier start times
hero.body:
The 2026-2027 school year begins Monday, Aug. 10 for all students in Martin County, with 12 elementary schools opening at 7:40 a.m., four high schools including Indiantown High School charter school starting at 8:30 a.m., and five middle schools beginning at 9:20 a.m. The earlier elementary school start times mean many students will be walking to bus stops in the dark on a daily basis as the days grow shorter, particularly Jensen Beach Elementary students who meet the bus at the stop at Southeast Aster Lane and Southeast Astorwood Terrace at 6:10 a.m., according to Martin School District bus transportation schedules.

The Martin County School District is urging parents, students and motorists to observe school bus safety rules throughout the 2026-27 school year. Students should arrive at their bus stop 5 to 10 minutes before their scheduled pickup time, remain off the roadway while waiting, and follow the bus driver's instructions when boarding, exiting, or crossing the street, said Kirstie Germaine, coordinator of public information community relations. She encouraged families to review their child's bus stop location and schedule before the first day of school and ensure younger students have appropriate supervision at the bus stop.

Florida law requires drivers to stop for a school bus displaying flashing red lights and an extended stop arm on two-lane roads and on multi-lane roads without a raised median or physical barrier. As of May 1, Florida began issuing citations for illegal passing of a stopped school bus with stop arm extended and red lights flashing, with a $225 fine for the offense. For a second or subsequent offense within five years, the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles may suspend a driver's license for 90 days up to six months.

The Martin County School District's transportation page at www.martinschools.org/page/transportation provides information including links to download bus routes, bus stop rules, and safety guidance. The page also has instructions on downloading MyReaXium app, which gives parents details on the location of the school bus which will pick up and drop off their children. Parents are encouraged to supervise younger children while they wait for the bus, remind children to wait for the driver's signal before crossing the street, and ensure that backpacks, clothing, and drawstrings cannot get caught in bus handrails or doors.
